#6307. Dreaming of Country Living? These Renovated Barn Airbnbs Got You Covered

Country living, with its beautiful nature, relaxing atmosphere, and stunning wildlife, makes it incredibly easy to forget your day-to-day stressors and embrace the slower path. And where better to enjoy this peace and quiet than from an Airbnb converted from a barn—provided, of course, you’re not actually sleeping next to a pitchfork and a pile of hay? Across the US, old dairy barns, horse stables, haylofts, and grain silos that once kept America’s farms running are finding dreamy second lives as vacation rentals. These sturdy structures are getting some very glamorous redesigns, but keeping the soaring ceilings, original timber beams, weathered wood, and old architectural details that no new build can quite replicate.

From sprawling farmhouses with enough room for the whole gang, to intimate hayloft hideaways made for a national park trip, to old grain silos that are surprisingly stylish places to sleep, there’s something interesting in every corner of the country. Expect modern interiors tucked behind century-old barn doors, outdoor soaking tubs overlooking rolling pastures, and properties where the resident animals are still very much part of the picture (morning coffee with a few curious goats, anyone?).

Whether you’re after a little farmyard nostalgia, a design-forward country escape, or simply a storied home just steps away from the wild, these barn Airbnbs make a pretty compelling case to trade your average stay for something with a little more hay-day history.

Number of guests: 2Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Proximity to Nashville, floor-to-ceiling windows, fully equipped kitchen, optional farm tours and event bookings

Bloomsbury Farm is a family-owned and -operated organic farm just outside Nashville. The 400-acre retreat is pastorally posh—the kind of place where wild turkeys and deer roam free, hawks swoop overhead, and coyotes howl in the night. The one-bedroom, one-bath rental is tastefully decorated: It’s where Martha Stewart meets Modern Farmer. That said, intentionality permeates every design choice, from the handsome leather headboard to the subway-tiled bath with Aesop hand soap. Guests are given farm-fresh eggs and a box of fruits and vegetables that are grown on-site; these come in handy when preparing meals on the kitchen’s professional gas range or grilling over the outdoor firepit.

City: Smyrna, TennesseeThings to do nearby: Brewer Farms, Cedar Stone Park, The Barn at Sycamore Farms, Arrington Vineyards

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 1.5 bathsWhy we love it: Proximity to NYC, wood-burning fireplace, reading nooks, meadow and valley views, vintage arcade and board games

Just around a two-hour drive from NYC, this charmingly restored barn cottage awaits in the Hudson Valley. The space pairs a cozy wood-burning fireplace with expansive windows overlooking a meadow—one that the host notes becomes a “veritable bird sanctuary for most of the year.” It’s a harbor of hidden nooks made for cozying up with a book, and features a well-stocked kitchen and dining space for cooking, as well as a vintage arcade and board games for fun nights in with your crew. Previous guests have raved about its proximity to Hudson Valley hot spots: There’s no shortage of places to hike, ski, see art, or dine, as well as some fun local breweries and wineries. The property is within a 10- to 25-minute drive of six quaint Hudson Valley towns. (You can also request bikes from the hosts if you’re inclined to venture out on two wheels.)

City: Red Hook, New YorkThings to do nearby: Pine Plains, Stissing Mountain (and iconic restaurant Stissing House), Thompson Pond

Number of guests: 2Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Desert views, on-site animals, proximity to Zion National Park, fully equipped kitchen, firepit, sauna

With a classic red-barn build, friendly farm animals, and a sauna practically made for stargazing, this dreamy Airbnb is an oasis—especially if Zion National Park is on your itinerary. Just one hour from the park, you’ll find this whimsical base for two set between Utah’s red rock cliffs, sweeping canyons, and heaps of local hiking paths. Inside, enjoy tasteful touches everywhere. Sunlight pours through the studio; a vintage-style soaking tub sits on black-and-white checkered flooring, and the kitchenette has modern appliances as well as some plants and pastel green cabinets. You’ll have some company when walking outside, too: This farm stay comes with two adorable Highland cows as well as a chicken coop. There’s also a sauna and firepit, just in case you need another reason to visit.

City: Hildale, UtahThings to do nearby: Water Canyon Winery, Squirrel Canyon Trailhead, Coral Pink Sand Dunes, Zion National Park

Number of guests: 6Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 2 bathsWhy we love it: Outdoor firepit, central location, private stargazing deck, wood-burning fireplace, vinyl player

A silo in the Catskills? Now that's a fun place to spend a weekend. From the outside, this three-story converted tower is fairly understated, but step inside, and you'll find a surprisingly airy, thoughtfully designed little escape that makes every inch count. There's an open living room that flows into a stocked kitchen, two spacious (and stunningly modern) bathrooms, and a private deck for soaking up the quiet. The interiors have a cool, pared-back feel, with just the right amount of personality to make it feel like somewhere you'd actually want to hang out (board games and a puzzle marathon are very much encouraged). And while it feels nicely tucked away, Woodstock's galleries, shops, and restaurants are just 10 minutes down the road.

City: Willow, New YorkThings to do nearby: Mount Tremper, Emerson Kaleidoscope, Phoenicia Diner, Overlook Mountain

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 2 bathsWhy we love it: Ocean views, stereo system, heated floors, wood-burning stove, open and modern kitchen

What could be better—or more endearing—than this modern Northern California barn in a forest clearing? Renovated by San Francisco architect David Crimmins, this gem leans into its sleek agrarian style, with airy, open-beam ceilings, heated concrete floors, a redwood slab dining table, and windows on all sides, bringing the outside in. The house sits along a rocky coastline, primed for whale watching and trips to coastal wineries between the Redwoods and the Pacific. The high-design stay stands tall on Anchor Bay along the Mendocino Coast; you’ll have your very own one-acre yard amid the state’s dreamy Redwoods, and it’s just a 20-minute walk to the beach.

City: Gualala, CaliforniaThings to do nearby: Whale Watch Point, Gualala Arts Center, Point Arena Lighthouse, Bonham Trail to Cooks Beach

Number of guests: 3Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 1 bathWhy we love it: Sauna, firepit, outdoor shower, proximity to Lake Michigan

Not every barn stay comes with Lake Michigan practically in its backyard. Tucked among 12 wooded acres in Leelanau County, this country base holds its former farm structure while offering its guests a fresh and pretty new lease. Once part of a 30-acre farm that stretched across both sides of the road, you can still appreciate a little of that history in its beautifully restored bones. These days, it's a two-bedroom hideaway that makes a wonderful home base for exploring Northern Michigan's wine country, with Northport's small-town charm and the peninsula's wineries and breweries just a hop and a skip away. There’s no need to leave your Airbnb for a fun day out: Spend the afternoon wandering out in nature, then make your way to the nearby secluded Lake Michigan beach. Peruse the guest reviews, and you’ll notice a telling pattern: Most travelers don't just stay once or twice—they return time and time again.

City: Northport, MichiganThings to do nearby: Cherry Basket Farm, Onomonee Road Beach, Fischer’s Happy Hour Tavern, Bay Front Park

Number of guests: 3Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Silo design, mountain views, fully equipped kitchenette, private patio, firepit, proximity to Glacier National Park

On an 80-acre family farm in Montana’s Flathead Valley, this converted grain silo is truly one of a kind. Alongside jaw-dropping mountain views, the structure itself is a treat—and happens to be more homey than one might think at first glance. Inside, the lofted king bedroom is spacious and comfy, the kitchenette is stocked with all you might need for a long weekend, and kid-friendly amenities are at your ready, from a pack-and-play to a portable high chair. That said, it’s best for one or two, or a couple traveling with a little one, since there aren’t full walls between the sleeping area.

Embrace the outdoors as much as you can here: According to previous guests, this barn puts you in a prime spot for stargazing around the firepit, jumping in the glittering Flathead Lake, and taking advantage of Glacier National Park—only 30 minutes away.

City: Kalispell, MontanaThings to do nearby: Glacier National Park, Conrad Mansion Museum, Flathead Lake, Wild Horse Island

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#6306. The 6 Best Electric Snowblowers Are Plenty Powerful—and Quieter Alternatives to Gas Models

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Two more reasons to go green: Battery-powered outdoor equipment is also easier to operate and store.

If you’re looking for the quickest, least labor-intensive way to dig out after a big snowstorm this winter, a snowblower is it. While it’s only fall, it’s not too early to think about getting a snowblower if you found yourself wanting one during last year’s winter storms but struggled to find a retailer that wasn’t already out of stock. Getting ahead of the game is a good idea.

Electric models are more capable than ever, and in some cases meet or exceed their gas-powered brethren in some respects. Cordless, battery-electric blowers can clear a path up to roughly 2 feet wide through as much as 20 inches of snow. They start with the push of a button, require less maintenance than gas machines, and run relatively quietly. They’re also easier to store than their gas-powered counterparts.

Ahead, we review both two-stage snow blowers and single-stage snow throwers and recommend models from Toro, Ego, Milwaukee, and more.

Our selections for this list are based on our years of testing snow blowers of all varieties. Most of these examples we’ve tested in the last few years, and others are updated versions of models we’ve tested. We are also planning for a substantial update to this guide in the coming weeks with new models.

Tony Carrick, the original author of this article, is a regular PopMech contributor and writes about everything from landscaping to home improvement. He grew up in rural Pennsylvania, where he became well-acquainted with blizzards and the backbreaking labor of digging out after them. His recommendations are based on his personal experience testing snow blowers at home, along with plenty of research to inform the picks. He compared specs for a variety of corded and cordless models, while also plowing through recommendations and feedback from dozens of customer reviews.

Ego Power+ 21-Inch Single-Stage Snow Blower

Ego claims this single-stage snow blower is able to clear a 14-car driveway on a single charge. Plus, it has heated handles.

Ryobi’s latest single-stage blower comes with two 40-volt, 8-amp-hour batteries for long runtime. It also has a tall clearing depth of 11.5 inches.

Wild Badger Power 20-Inch Single-Stage Snow Blower

We’re checking out this single-stage budget option to see if it can achieve effective snow removal for a small property.

This is Ego’s latest two-stage blower, which we’re evaluating to see if it can hold its own against a gas-powered two-stage snow blower.

Electric snow blowers may not be able to match the power of their gas-powered counterparts, but this self-propelled two-stage model from Ryobi comes close. It sports four rechargeable 40-volt 6-amp-hour batteries, which Ryobi claims can power the snow blower for up to 45 minutes, and move the same amount of snow as a 252-cc gas-powered two-stage snow blower. It has the power to scoop up a path that’s 24 inches wide and 21 inches deep, then chuck it up to 55 feet away.

We’re also impressed with the cockpit, which allows you to control the speed of the drive wheels and the auger, change the direction of the chute, and toggle the LED headlights without missing a beat. The handlebar even heats up so your hands don’t get numb as you're working.

Our only concern is with the charger. While we like the fact that this Ryobi supports rapid charging, the charger only has two slots, which means you’ll have to go through two rounds of recharging before you’re back to full power.

If you don’t relish the idea of pushing heavy machinery through heavy snow, Snow Joe makes a lightweight single-stage snow blower that’s fairly easy to push around. At less than 38 pounds with batteries installed, the Snow Joe 24V-X2-SB18 is easy to roll out of storage, push down the driveway, and maneuver through turns.

The scraper bar clears snow right down to the pavement, and it can launch snow up to 20 feet away. On top of that, it’s very cheap—one of the most affordable cordless snow blowers we’ve found.

Unsurprisingly, that light weight and low price come with some compromises. The 18-inch-wide chute cuts a narrow path, so you’ll need to take a few extra passes to get the job done right compared to a wider machine. Meanwhile, its two 24-volt batteries offer a modest 40-minute run time.

Combine those two things, and the 24V-X2-SB18 is best reserved for smaller jobs like clearing decks, walkways, and compact driveways. If that’s what you need, though, it makes snow removal cheap and easy.

We like Ego’s battery-powered outdoor equipment because it’s among the best when it comes to power and run time—and this two-stage snow blower is no exception. With its two 56-volt, 7.5-Ah batteries and 24-inch-wide intake, the Power+ SNT2405 can clear a 8-inch layer of snow from an 18-car driveway on a single charge.

We also like the cockpit on this self-propelled machine. You can change speeds while in forward or reverse, adjust the auger speed, and change the chute direction all without having to leave the controls. It also comes equipped with four bright LED headlights, useful in the event your snow clearing efforts take you past sundown.

We also like the fact that Ego uses mostly steel construction with this machine, so you can expect it to hold up for many a winter.

Ego claims its 21-inch Power+ snow blower can throw snow up to 40 feet with a 180-degree, adjustable chute, which is pretty far for a cordless machine. In the wet sawdust test, we were able to throw 24 feet with the heavier, denser material—longer distances are certainly achievable with lighter, drier snow. It took the Power+ 4 minutes 16 seconds to clear the sawdust down to pavement in our area test.

Like most single-stage blowers, the Power+ is not self-propelled, so we needed to push it into the snow. In our dense, heavy sawdust, that took some effort to make forward progress. It’s not a bad thing, though, as it makes it easier to prevent the machine from digging in too deep and bogging down. In very wet or ice-packed snow, we expect you’ll have to put in a similar effort.

The Power+ has a variable-speed auger, so we were able to adjust speed for the conditions and conserve battery when less power was needed. There isn’t too much to worry about in the battery department, since it comes with two 5-Ah batteries, enough to clear 8 inches of snow on a 12-car driveway—that’s six cars long by two cars wide.

The Power+ comes with a dual-port charger, so the two batteries can be charged simultaneously to get you ready for the next round faster. Ego rounds things out with front-mounted LEDs for low-light and dark conditions, plus an easy-folding handle for stowing the unit when not in use.

The 60-volt 26-inch Power Max e26 is one of the models we tested in November 2025, and it’s among the burliest two-stage cordless snow blowers we’ve used. It is built virtually the same as a gas model, except with an electric motor and two batteries. That includes the frame, drive system, auger, and auger housing.

Since it’s built the same, we can confirm it performs the same—so it could easily replace a similar gas model. No caveats here; the Power Max e26 isn’t a compromise in any significant way that we could determine. It comes with two batteries and a (claimed) runtime of up to 70 minutes—enough to clear a driveway 30 car spaces long.

Operating the Power Max e26 was a pleasant experience, if you can call snow blowing pleasant. It has effective heated hand grips, and an axle with a differential that allows you to turn quickly, on a dime—no having to muscle it around.

The e26 easily handled our testing with wet sawdust, throwing it far enough to cross an average driveway—even when making a full 26-inch-wide pass. If you’ve questioned whether a cordless snow blower could ever be as good as a gas machine, the e26 answers that affirmatively.

Milwaukee’s M18 single-stage snow blower is the second machine we tested in November 2025, and it also impressed us. It's noticeably heavier than many other similar cordless models, which seems to be due to its metal frame. At 90 pounds, it isn’t heavy, at least in comparison to two-stage machines, but the weight is an advantage, helping prevent the blower from bouncing around or riding up when encountering denser, crusty snow.

We tested this snow blower with wet sawdust, which always presents a little bit of a challenge with single-stage snow blowers, as they have to lift the snow and eject it in one operation. Milwaukee’s M18 blower did this well enough in testing—and if it can throw wet sawdust, it will really throw the snow.

To facilitate ejecting snow, the M18’s chute is wider than that of most other models. This eliminates potential bottlenecks and ultimately clogs, where the snow passes from the blower body into the chute. Milwaukee's single auger is edged with a rubber paddle that both sweeps the pavement clean and pulls the machine forward. It does this well enough that, in some instances, we had to hold it back a little in testing.

The chute has a remote adjustment—you can crank a knob just below the handlebar to change the direction of the chute, allowing you to put snow where it needs to go. However, ejection elevation is manually adjusted at the top of the chute—but this isn't something you typically need to adjust as often.

Milwaukee claims the M18 blower can clear up to 11 parking places, or 500 feet of sidewalk on the two included 12.0-Ah batteries. But with two extra battery ports, you can double the runtime by adding another pair of batteries. We’ll be testing this more as we have snow available.

There are two types of snow blowers for homeowners, based on the number of “stages” in the mechanical process they use to collect and distribute snow.

Single-stage snow blowers have an auger that pulls the snow into a large intake at the front of the snow blower, and propels it out of a chute mounted to the top of the machine. Single-stage blowers, also frequently referred to as “snow throwers,” are small, lightweight and easy to maneuver, making them ideal for clearing light snowfall and smaller driveways and walks.

Dual-stage snow blowers, as the name suggests, have a two-stage process for collecting and expelling snow. Like single-stage models, they have an auger that pulls snow into the intake. The dual-stage snow blower follows up by pushing the snow into an impeller that ejects it out through the chute.

The one-two punch of auger and impeller allows a two-stage snow blower to remove more snow quicker, and throw it a longer distance. That makes them perfect for large driveways. That said, they are larger and heavier than single-stage machines, so they may not be able to maneuver around narrow walking paths as easily.

The width and depth of a snow blower’s intake determine how much snow it can move with each pass, and thus, how long it takes you to get the job done. Most single-stage electric snow blowers have a clearing width of around 20 inches and a clearing depth of around 8 inches. That’s good for carving out walks and medium-sized areas. Some heavy-duty two-stage electric snow blowers can remove a 24-inch-wide and 20-inch-deep swath of snow, which will make quick work of a large driveway.

Throwing distance refers to how far a snow blower can launch snow out of the chute. This gives you a sense of how to plan when and how you’ll dispose of the snow in your path. The average single-stage snow blower typically has a short throwing distance—around 25 feet. Unsurprisingly, a two-stage snow blower can send its snow as far as 50 feet.

Snow blowers typically have a throttle that allows you to change their mechanical speed, which will adjust how far it throws your snow. There are also controls that allow you to rotate the chute to change the direction of the flow of snow. If you can map out your snow-blowing route, check and make sure your snow blower throws the snow far enough to keep it out of your way until it melts.

Most electric snow blowers receive power from multiple large rechargeable batteries, which allow them to produce nearly as much power as a gas snow blower. No battery supplies uninterrupted power for as long as a tank of gas, though: On average, you should expect a battery-powered snow blower to run for about 30 to 45 minutes on a single charge. You can extend that time if you have multiple batteries, but the low run time still caps how much ground they can cover.

Though we largely consider them to be obsolete, some manufacturers also still produce corded electric snow blowers, which plug into a standard electrical outlet. They’re often cheaper than battery-powered models and run as long as you need them to. However, having a power cord substantially reduces their range: You will likely need to purchase an extension cord to extend its reach slightly beyond the length of the area you need to clear. No matter how much slack you have, though, the cable makes the whole process a little more awkward.

“Cordless snow blowers are easier, better, and safer to use,” says Popular Mechanics Test Editor Brad Ford. “Corded is old, out-of-date tech in most cases.”

They’re also limited to smaller, 15-amp motors that run on the power an outlet can provide. That usually translates to narrower clearing widths, shallower clearing depths, and shorter throw distances. Unless you have a very tight budget, we highly recommend going with a battery-powered electric snow blower rather than a corded one.

The most important thing you can do to keep your electric snow blower running season after season is to simply make sure that you store your charger and batteries indoors when you aren’t charging or using them. Lithium cells aren't able to hold the same amount of charge when the temperature drops below freezing. By storing and charging those batteries indoors, you’ll get the most run time out of them.

If you use a corded snow blower, you shouldn’t plug it into any old extension cord. These machines draw a lot of power, and not every cord can handle it. Using the wrong one can create a fire hazard or damage your snow blower. Make sure to check your snow blower’s specs before buying an extension cord to pair with it, so you can be sure it can handle its amperage.

Most corded electric snow blowers have a 12-amp rating, in which case you’ll want a 12-gauge extension cord that can provide at least 12 amps of power. You’ll also want to make sure it’s long enough for you to reach the far end of whatever walkway or road you plan to clear, preferably with some slack to spare for maneuverability. We recommend starting with 100 feet and scaling up based on your property.

Regardless, it would be wise to buy an extension cord to match the specs you need for your snow blower, rather than using one that you happen to have lying around.

With advancements in battery technology, there are now powerful two-stage cordless snow blowers capable of clearing deeper, heavier snow.

That said, the most powerful electric snow blowers still don’t match the snow-moving capabilities of the largest gas-powered snow blowers on the market. The most powerful electric snow blowers work best at maximum depths of about a foot, while some gas-powered models can clear snow up to 2 feet deep.

Tony Carrick is a full-time freelance writer who specializes in technology, home improvement, DIY, home security, and outdoor recreation. He’s tested and written about everything from home security systems to power tools to gas grills. His product guides, how-to articles, and feature stories can be found in such publications as Bob Vila, Angi, U.S. News and World Report, Field & Stream, Futurism, and Switchful. When Tony isn’t writing, he can be found working on his latest home improvement effort at his home in North Carolina.

#6305. In National Geographic’s “Expedition: Saving Our Seas,” it’s all hands on deck

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Narrated by Auli’i Cravalho, the documentary dives into how oceanographers are racing to understand the world’s changing waters

Aerial imagery of research vessel Star Keys safe harboring in Abel Tasman, New Zealand.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

As documentaries about Earth’s accelerating climate crisis go, Expedition: Saving Our Seas is surprisingly buoyant.

The ocean covers more than two-thirds of Earth’s surface. And “as the climate heats up, our seas are under pressure like never before,” narrator Auli’i Cravalho, the voice of the title character in Disney’s Moana, says at the opening of The National Geographic Society’s new documentary. The film documents how oceanographers are racing to document and mitigate climate change’s impacts on ocean and coastal habitats.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Expedition: Saving Our Seas premieres November 13 on the National Geographic Channel at 9pm EST and streams the next day on Disney+ and Hulu.

Despite that solemn mission, Expedition: Saving Our Seas is full of hope — and stunning visuals. The documentary offers a window into the scientists’ wonder and joy in their work as they discover new life forms in the depths of the Southern Ocean, or successfully nurture young corals threatened by warming in the Pacific Ocean.

The film opens with a twist on the usual world map: At the center is one great ocean, surrounded by land. Trivia buffs know Earth has five oceans: the Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Southern and Arctic. But geographic names aside, these five oceans are just one, linked by a global system of currents known as the Great Ocean Conveyor Belt.

“It’s this giant connected ocean that ignores all of the political boundaries, ignores all of the names we call them,” says Andrew Thurber, a biological oceanographer at the University of California, Santa Barbara, whose research is among those featured in the film.

The documentary loosely follows the current’s path as it zips around the world from project to project.

The first project in the documentary is Thurber’s. He’s on board a research vessel in the frigid Southern Ocean, which rings Antarctica. Using a remotely-operated vehicle dubbed SuBastian, Thurber and his colleagues are scanning the seafloor, hunting for the world’s southernmost hydrothermal vent.

Hydrothermal vents spew superhot, chemically-enriched seawater. In the generally nutrient-poor Southern Ocean, that makes these vents a potential food oasis to support deep sea life.

Throughout the night, as the ROV scans the seafloor, Thurber and his colleagues stay glued to the video it sends back, oohing and aahing as never-before-seen life-forms come into view. “It was a marathon of excitement,” he says now.

Then they see it: A large black smoker, the southernmost hydrothermal vent ever found. And all around it: swarms of pregnant female krill.

“That blew all of our minds,” Thurber says. Krill are the keystone species of the entire Southern Ocean food web, a crucial food source for baleen whales, seals, penguins and fish. But krill are threatened by both industrial fishing and climate change. This discovery, Thurber says, helps make the case for a marine protected area, a region where fishing and other human activities should be restricted.

From the Southern Ocean, the Great Ocean Conveyor Belt flows thousands of kilometers to the north, where marine ecologist Maiyai Taal Hocheimy is tracking how the rising waters of the Atlantic Ocean are encroaching on Banjul, the capital of The Gambia in West Africa. Her hope is that salt-tolerant mangrove trees along the coast, with their dense network of soil-retaining roots, might help hold back the sea in the coming decades — provided that the community can be enlisted to help maintain the mangroves.

I found Hocheimy’s work especially inspiring because she is working to shape the future of oceanography. In 2017, she founded the GREAT (Gaining Research Experience in Africa for Tomorrow) Institute, the first aquatic and coastal science research institute in The Gambia. The mangrove project recruited young local scientists to help conduct the research.

“The goal is to train the next generation of environmental stewards,” Hocheimy says. “We have to show that mangroves have value, so they’ll understand and want to protect them. It is their future at stake.”

That sentiment is echoed many times in the film — the importance not only of enlisting young scientists but also centering local scientists who pose new questions that oceanographers who parachute in from other places may not think to ask, says marine biogeochemist Kristina Brown.

In the documentary, Brown, of the University of Manitoba in Canada, co-leads an expedition to explore the waters of Sherman Basin, a large bay north of the Arctic Circle in Nunavut, Canada. This region has been hunted and fished by Inuit people for centuries.

But it might change beyond all recognition in the next few decades, Brown says. So, the local Inuit community invited her to help create the first catalog of what species are present in the waters and on the seafloor. “[It’s] the first project I’ve been involved in where the local community both defined the research questions and have brought their own unique expertise to the research project.”

Watching how communities around the world are increasingly taking ownership of studies in their own waters was, for me, the most exciting takeaway of this documentary.

“We want to democratize access to the deep sea, to enable people who haven’t had access to these kinds of tools to ask more and new questions,” says Katy Croff Bell, the founder and president of the Ocean Discovery League, a nonprofit ocean exploration group based in Saunderstown, Rhode Island.

As a result of inaccessibility, little of Earth’s vast ocean has been mapped, particularly the deep sea. Bell’s organization is developing inexpensive technologies such as a hardy little camera and sensor system dubbed DORIS, for Deep Ocean Research and Imaging System. It can descend to 6,000 meters and costs less than $10,000.

Expedition: Saving Our Seas offers just a few scant minutes to each project before moving on around the globe to the next, so there’s no time to learn about each project in depth. But the overall takeaway of watching these vignettes, back to back, is that there is a young, energetic community of scientists taking on the challenge.

Mitigating climate change’s impacts on the oceans is, after all, a race against time. So it’s nice to think we might have all hands on deck.

Carolyn Gramling is the earth & climate writer. She has bachelor’s degrees in geology and European history and a Ph.D. in marine geochemistry from MIT and the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution.

Recently, researchers used AI to "decode" segments of birdsong. In the wake of this, Live Science asks its readers which animal they'd want to communicate with.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The idea of talking to animals like Dr. Dolittle might sound far-fetched, but researchers are making progress toward understanding how other species communicate. In a recent Live Science interview, University of California, Berkeley ethologist Julie Elie explained how she used artificial intelligence (AI) and behavioral experiments to decode the calls of zebra finches (Taeniopygia guttata). For instance, Elie was able to determine which calls the birds used to communicate over short distances versus longer distances.

Birds aren't the only animals scientists are hoping to understand. Researchers with Project CETI are using AI to decipher the clicks and calls of sperm whales, while a separate team (with the search for extraterrestrial intelligence, or SETI) conducted what they described as the first "conversation" between humans and a humpback whale. The whale, named Twain, responded to recorded calls played by researchers over a 20 minute period, a "conversation" scientists believe could help us figure out how to communicate with extraterrestrial life someday.

Closer to home, cats have already figured out how to use meows to get their human's attention, whether they're demanding food, affection or simply that we open the door for them (again). Whether this means they understand the human language or not is still up for debate, but it raises an interesting question: If we could understand what animals were saying, which species would you most want to talk to? Vote in our poll and let us know what you'd ask in the comments below!

Kenna Hughes-Castleberry is the Content Manager at Live Science. Formerly, she was the Content Manager at Space.com and before that the Science Communicator at JILA, a physics research institute. Kenna is also a book author, with her upcoming book 'Octopus X' scheduled for release in spring of 2027. Her beats include physics, health, environmental science, technology, AI, animal intelligence, corvids, and cephalopods.

#6301. NRCC Chairman Richard Hudson loses reelection in North Carolina

NRCC Chairman Richard Hudson, right, here at a hearing in June, lost his reelection bid in North Carolina's 9th District. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

North Carolina Rep. Richard Hudson, the chairman of the National Republican Congressional Committee, has lost his race for reelection, a stinging defeat for the man charged with preserving the House majority for the GOP.

Hudson fell to Democrat Richard Ojeda, a former West Virginia state senator who was leading  51 percent to 49 percent Thursday afternoon  when The Associated Press called the race in North Carolina’s 9th District.

Hudson had already conceded the race Wednesday, when it became clear that his path to victory was closing off.

“[The] voters of North Carolina’s 9th District made their choice and I respect it,” he said in a statement. “Since 2013 I’ve worked for North Carolina families. That includes the soldiers and families at Fort Bragg, who sacrifice more for this country than most people will ever know.”

Hudson is now the second party campaign chief to lose his seat during a midterm election this decade. In 2022, New York Rep. Sean Patrick Maloney lost reelection while serving as chair of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee.

Republicans across North Carolina experienced devastating losses on election night. As of Thursday afternoon, Democrats had also flipped the seats of Reps. Addison McDowell, Brad Knott and Tim Moore, as well as the open seat of retiring Rep. Chuck Edwards. The races for five other GOP-held seats remain uncalled, while Democratic Rep. Don Davis was reelected despite being targeted for defeat under a new GOP-drawn congressional map. Republicans also lost control of the North Carolina House and lost seats in the state Senate.

North Carolina’s 9th District, which includes the Eastern Piedmont region and the Fayetteville area, was far from the House battlefield for much of the midterm cycle. President Donald Trump carried the seat by 16 points in 2024, according to calculations by Inside Elections with Nathan L. Gonzales, and Hudson won a seventh term the same year by nearly 19 points. Hudson also held a financial advantage over Ojeda, raising $4.2 million to Ojeda’s $2.9 million through mid-October.

But in the waning weeks of the campaign, signs of Republican concern grew and Hudson’s campaign began spending on ads.

Ojeda was first elected to the West Virginia Senate in 2016. He ran for the U.S. House two years later as a Trump-voting Democrat but lost that race to Republican Carol Miller. He then briefly ran for the 2020 Democratic presidential nomination and also challenged GOP Sen. Shelley Moore Capito later that cycle but lost in the Democratic primary.

Ojeda moved to North Carolina in 2020, he told CityView, a local magazine, and he announced his challenge to Hudson last year.

Throughout the campaign, he attacked the incumbent over his support for Trump’s agenda, particularly the war in Iran. Ojeda is a retired Army major and the district is home to Fort Bragg, the nation’s largest Army base by population, where the Democrat was previously stationed for more than a decade.

“We did the impossible,’’ Ojeda told supporters Tuesday night. “We took on the chair of the National Republican Congressional Committee, a man with political connections, the billionaire donors, and the entire Washington establishment standing beside him.”

Hudson, 55, is finishing his seventh term in the House and his second term as NRCC chair. He had no primary opponent this year and had grown used to winning reelection by comfortable margins.

As a legislator, Hudson focused much of his policy agenda on health issues such as federal pandemic preparedness programs. He serves on the House Energy and Commerce Committee and chairs the panel's Communications and Technology Subcommittee.

#6300. Most transgender youth satisfied after choosing hormone therapy

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Taking gender-affirming hormone therapy was the right decision for 97 percent surveyed

Demonstrators rally at the U.S. Supreme Court in 2025 in support of gender-affirming health care for transgender youth. The vast majority of transgender and gender diverse young people are satisfied with their decision to take hormone therapy, according the largest survey on the topic.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

An overwhelming percentage of transgender and gender diverse young people in the United States express satisfaction with gender-affirming hormone therapy.

Almost 400 transgender and gender diverse young people reflected on their decision to take hormone therapy in the largest such survey to date. Nearly 97 percent affirmed it was the right decision, researchers report November 9 in JAMA Pediatrics. Only about 3 percent, or 10 individuals, said they regretted the step, and of those, seven felt the experience was harmful.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

With concerns around youth well-being fueling limits on gender-affirming hormone therapy, the researchers write, “the results provide further support for the existing standards of care [and] do not support efforts to categorically restrict or ban access.”

Gender-affirming hormone therapy — with the masculinizing hormone testosterone or the feminizing hormone estrogen — allows a person’s body to better match their gender identity. Around 3 percent of 13- to 17-year-olds in the United States identify as transgender.

Among the study’s 376 young people, who were former patients of a clinic for transgender and gender diverse youth, nearly 92 percent began hormones at 17 or younger. Thirty percent took estrogen and 70 percent took testosterone, with the amount of time since starting the hormones averaging five years.

As per clinical guidelines for transgender health care, young people interested in medical treatment, joined by parents or guardians, began with an assessment visit with a mental health professional. For the study, participants took a yearly survey, filled out anytime from one month prior to six months following the anniversary of this initial visit. The research team analyzed surveys submitted from 2023 to 2025.

The new research adds to growing evidence on the benefits of gender-affirming hormone therapy for transgender young people. Gender-affirming hormones improve the alignment these young people experience between their appearance and their gender, increase their satisfaction with life and reduce depression and anxiety.

But state bans have curtailed young people’s access to gender-affirming care, which can include hormone therapy and puberty blockers. As of November 2026 in the United States, 28 states have laws or policies that limit this care, according to the health policy organization KFF. More than half of transgender young people age 13 to 17 reside in states that restrict gender-affirming care. The American Academy of Pediatrics and the Endocrine Society support gender-affirming health care for young people and provide evidence-backed guidelines for treatment.

Nearly 50 years after launch, NASA's Voyager 1 probe will pass the one light-day mark on Nov. 18, a symbolic milestone for the agency's longest-running mission. Scientists reflect on the Voyager program's legacy and what comes next.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

NASA's Voyager 1 probe, already the farthest human-made object in space, is about to set another record. On Nov. 18, the spacecraft will be so far from Earth that light, the universe's ultimate speed limit, takes a full 24 hours to reach it.

For researchers who worked on the Voyager program and continue to study its data, the symbolic milestone of being a full light-day from Earth celebrates a mission that continues half a century after it began. Since launching in September 1977, the twin Voyager probes have outlasted many of the engineers who built them, and their flybys of the outer solar system planets remain some of the best close-up observations scientists have of those distant worlds.

"Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 are transcending generations," Pascal Lee, a planetary scientist at the SETI Institute who was part of the Voyager 2 team at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) during its Neptune flyby in 1989, told Live Science. "Not only is their data relevant, but they themselves are still out there, moving into the unknown."

Here is what the Voyagers have revealed about the solar system and interstellar space, what happens when their power finally runs out, and whether anyone — or anything — might ever intercept the messages from Earth they carry.

A NASA simulation showing where Voyager 1 is relative to the sun and solar system planets.

Voyager 1, cruising through space at nearly 38,000 mph (61,000 km/h), is just shy of 16 billion miles (about 26 billion kilometers) from Earth. That's the distance light travels in 24 hours, also known as one light-day. The spacecraft will reach this milestone on Nov. 18 at 5:16:07 a.m. ET, after traveling through space for 49 years, two months and 11 days.

As long as that sounds, "it's still pathetically slow in the grand scheme of things," Lee told Live Science.

If anything, it reminds us of the sheer vastness of space and time, and how this spacecraft is just a little mote of dust that's barely drifted out of the solar system still.

Scientifically speaking, Voyager 1 hasn't even left its home neighborhood yet. In 2012, the probe traveled beyond the heliosphere, the bubble of plasma blown outward by the sun that shields the planets from incoming cosmic radiation. But it still remains within the sun's gravitational grasp, which extends past the Oort Cloud — a vast spherical shell of icy bodies surrounding the solar system. Voyager 1 will need about 300 more years just to reach the cloud's inner edge, and possibly 30,000 years to fly beyond it, according to NASA.

"If anything, it reminds us of the sheer vastness of space and time, and how this spacecraft is just a little mote of dust that's barely drifted out of the solar system still," Lee said.

On its current path, Voyager 1 will pass within 1.7 light-years of a dim star called Gliese 445 in about 40,000 years, at which point it will be closer to that star than to our own sun. Farther out, the nearest star system to our own, Proxima Centauri, sits about 4.24 light-years away — more than 1,500 times farther than Voyager 1 will be on Nov. 18.

Meanwhile Voyager 1's twin, Voyager 2, took a different route through the solar system after both probes launched in 1977, in order to swing past Uranus and Neptune after revisiting Jupiter and Saturn. Currently in interstellar space about 13 billion miles (21 million km) from Earth, Voyager 2 will reach its own light-day mark in November 2035, according to NASA.

An illustration of the Voyager probes passing beyond the heliopause, into interstellar space.

Crossing the one-light-day mark doesn't change how NASA communicates with the probe, though it does demand more patience.

NASA talks to the spacecraft using radio signals, which travel at the speed of light. At a distance of one light-day, a signal sent from Earth takes 24 hours to reach Voyager 1, and a reply takes another 24 hours to make the return journey.

"If you want to say 'hello' to Voyager, you send your message and then you go home and you wait two days before you finally get a response," Suzanne Dodd, Voyager project manager at JPL, said in a recent statement.

As the spacecraft continues to cruise deeper into space, that wait will grow longer. Moreover, 50 years of traversing the solar system and the increasing distance from our sun takes a toll on the probe itself. Because sunlight in the outer reaches is far too faint for solar panels, Voyager 1 relies on nuclear batteries that convert heat from the natural decay of plutonium into electricity. That supply is gradually dwindling, prompting NASA to gradually shut down nonessential instruments to conserve what energy remains and extend the mission as much as possible.

Kelly Perry, a data systems engineer on the Voyager program at JPL, told Live Science via email that the mission team's priority remains the same: "keep the spacecraft going as long as possible."

A montage of planets imaged by the twin Voyager probes, showing Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune.

Before the Voyagers launched, the outer solar system was largely a blur of telescopic speculation. The twin probes took advantage of a planetary alignment that comes around only once every 176 years, using the gravity of giant planets to slingshot themselves onward.

Together, they have discovered 23 moons across the outer solar system, revealed faint rings around Jupiter and captured the first detailed atmospheric profiles of Saturn, Uranus and Neptune. They also gave the first detailed, close-up views of Jupiter's moon Europa, transforming our perception of it from a blurry speck into a remarkably smooth, geologically young world — and now one of the prime candidates for finding extraterrestrial life.

We had no idea what they looked like. And all of a sudden they became places we could map, imagine ourselves exploring, landing on…they became places.

Among the more striking finds, Voyager 1 spotted active volcanoes on Jupiter's moon Io in 1979, the first time they had been seen on any world other than Earth.

"We had no idea what they looked like," Lee said. "And all of a sudden they became places we could map, imagine ourselves exploring, landing on…they became places," he added.

"That's what Voyager was for me — a voyage of discovery," he said.

These discoveries laid the groundwork for decades of follow-up exploration, including NASA's Galileo mission to Jupiter and the Cassini mission to Saturn. Decades later, as the only spacecraft to return in situ data from outside the heliosphere, the probes also proved that interstellar space is a dynamic, complex frontier rather than an empty vacuum.

Each Voyager spacecraft launched with 10 science instruments. Today, only two remain active on Voyager 1 and three on Voyager 2, measuring the magnetic fields, plasma and cosmic rays of interstellar space.

NASA began switching off the others one by one decades ago to conserve power, including the camera on Voyager 1 just minutes after it snapped the famous "Pale Blue Dot" portrait of the solar system in 1990. Ongoing power-saving reconfigurations have since helped keep the aging spacecraft operational nearly 50 years into its lifetime.

Voyager's iconic "Pale Blue Dot" image shows Earth as a "mote of dust suspended in a sunbeam," in the words of Carl Sagan.

In one such recent effort, nicknamed the "Big Bang," engineers shut off certain high-power subsystems while switching on lower-power alternatives, which "bought us almost two more years during which we will not need to turn any instrument off," Perry said.

With onboard power steadily dwindling, however, "there's a recognition that it won't be forever," Deana Weibel, an anthropologist at the Grand Valley State University in Michigan who co-authored an upcoming book about the Golden Record aboard the Voyager probes, told Live Science.

Because Voyager is a science mission, its mission will be considered finished when "no science instruments are operational," Perry said. "The Science Team decided that the last remaining instrument will be the magnetometer," she added. "We will never intentionally power off this instrument."

After the science data eventually stops, both probes may still keep beaming back basic engineering updates, such as about their health and power status, until around 2036, according to NASA. Even after the spacecraft finally fall silent, they will keep coasting through interstellar space, and "analysis shows that they should remain intact," Perry said.

Scientists will still be able to calculate their positions based on their last known speed and trajectories, Weibel said. "We'll know intellectually where it is unless it gets intercepted."

An illustration of Voyager shown next to the Golden Record.

Theoretically, yes. But interstellar space is so unfathomably vast that the chances of aliens finding the probes are vanishingly small, Lee said.

That makes it unlikely that aliens will ever find the Voyager Golden Records — twin gold-plated discs meant to portray the diversity of life on Earth. They hold sounds such as wind and animal calls, greetings in 55 languages, images of our planet and a celestial map pinpointing its location — all intended for a hypothetical civilization capable of retrieving and playing them. (The probes also carry visual instructions for spinning the records).

In that sense, the Golden Records are as much an artistic exercise as a scientific one.

"The chances of us going after Voyager 1 and bringing it back for the Smithsonian — not that it's likely — are more believable than any chance of an alien civilization finding it, and then playing the record," Lee said.

Knowing that Voyager will continue its mission long past my lifetime actually gives me comfort

If an extraterrestrial civilization did find the probe after we lost contact with it, "we would have no way of knowing," Weibel added. "It becomes something that's powered entirely by imagination at that point."

So why send a message at all? All three scientists interviewed for this story see the Golden Record as a cosmic time capsule, a symbolic gesture meant to unite humanity around a shared home planet. For all its imperfections, including the omission of some widely spoken languages and a few mislabeled tracks, the disc remains an enduring emblem of human presence on Earth, they said.

"Knowing that Voyager will continue its mission long past my lifetime actually gives me comfort," Perry told Live Science. "Although I won't be able to speak to the Voyager spacecraft any more, I love knowing that I'll always be able to look to the stars and know they're still on their way."

There’s a reason Nashville is known as the bachelorette capital of the world, and it has everything to do with the city’s Southern charm, group-friendly accommodations, and choose-your-own-adventure approach towards night life. No two bachelorette parties are the same, and Nashville gets that more than most cities, where a mix of high-energy Honky Tonks, crave-worthy restaurants, and quaint shopping streets round out its nightly lineup of live music across the city. There are even customizable tours for bachelorettes that celebrate the city’s biggest claims to fame (ahem, Taylor Swift, whiskey, and hot chicken).

Nashville just does bachelorettes right, especially when it comes to places to stay. There’s an Airbnb in Nashville for every group size and vibe, from a spacious loft just off Broadway to a storybook cottage in the trendy 12 South neighborhood. Plus, many of Nashville’s Airbnbs were designed specifically with bachelorette parties in mind, offering spacious rooftops, beauty bars, and plenty of party decor. Neighborhood: Midtown NashvilleThings to do nearby: East Nashville, Germantown, Broadway, Bridgestone Arena, The Parthenon, Music Row

If you feel like staying in, this Airbnb has you covered with endless entertainment options, from a karaoke stage and speakeasy-style lounge to a movie theater, pool table, hot tub, firepit, and more. In the morning, start your day off with an outdoor sauna and yoga session before soaking up some sun in the backyard. Let’s just say your party of 12 will definitely not get bored while sharing this sweet place.

Neighborhood: North NashvilleThings to do nearby: Downtown, The Gulch, Germantown, Broadway, Music Row

The feminine energy of this SoBro (South of Broadway) apartment is strong and 100% bachelorette party–worthy, with chic backdrops and powder pink touches throughout the home. Blush-n-Bloom sleeps up to eight and is part of The Burnham building, which offers you and your crew access to a heated pool, outdoor and indoor lounges, and even a fitness center.

This luxury penthouse sleeps up to 12 and is smack in the center of the city’s nightlife scene in Downtown Nashville, so you can ditch the wheels and head out in heels. The Songbird is just a few steps from Broadway (ahem, easy access to honky-tonks and live music), but the commute to the karaoke stage is even shorter—since this place has its own high-tech system and stage inside.

The most walkable neighborhood in Nashville is also one of its most charming (maybe that’s why Reese Witherspoon chose 12 South for her flagship store, Draper James?). The Cozy Craftsman Escape can accommodate up to 10 and is within walking distance from cute boutiques and local eateries, but it also has its own professional-grade kitchen for whipping up Bushwackers (Nashville’s favorite cocktail) and sipping them from your private patio.

#6295. We know how to stop computer worms. But what if AI helps them persist?

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

AI worms could spread like octopuses or slime molds, exploiting smart devices

Common forms of cyberattack include viruses and worms. Researchers recently added new styles of attack to the twisted menagerie: worms that act more like octopuses or slime molds.

VICTOR HABBICK VISIONS/SCIENCE PHOTO LIBRARY/Getty Images

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

AI is already powering new, more adaptable forms of cyberattack, but hackers typically wield the technology from afar. What if they set the AI models themselves loose to self-replicate and spread in a malicious manner?

Recent experiments have demonstrated two different ways this could happen. Two independent teams showed how a cyberattacker could turn an AI model into a “worm,” a type of malware that, unlike a computer virus, spreads on its own. And AI unlocked a new worm power: adapting attacks to different devices.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The results hint at a new way AI could be used to ramp up cybersecurity threats — not just to computer systems but to smart devices such as security cameras or refrigerators. The good news is that the world still has time to build up defenses as several obstacles remain before this type of malware would work in the real world, says AI researcher Jonas Guan.

AI could indeed make a worm “much harder to stop,” he says, but “there are a lot of kinks to iron out before something like this really works at scale.”

Here is how a worm cyberattack works. A malware worm squirms through the internet, copying itself onto whatever systems it can hijack. Hackers can then mine hijacked systems directly for their data or link them together into a botnet and use its computing power, often to send spam email or overwhelm websites with traffic, knocking them offline.

Historically, computer worms have been small, simple programs preprogrammed to take advantage of specific security weaknesses. So they could only get into devices that had that weakness. When defenders patched a worm’s target, it could no longer spread. With an AI model directing its actions, however, a worm can adapt and learn on the fly, choosing its line of attack depending on the device, says Guan, of the University of Toronto.

That adaptability enables the worm to burrow into many different types of devices, both experiments showed. When hackers unleash AI from afar, they orchestrate what the model does. An AI worm that copies itself widely could hypothetically escape anyone’s control.

Still, there’s a caveat to the experiments’ results, says Michael Alexander Riegler, a cybersecurity researcher at Simula Metropolitan Center for Digital Engineering in Oslo, Norway. Both teams’ test environments made it easier for the AI worm to spread than it would be in the real world, says Riegler, who was not involved in either study.

And there’s another practical obstacle to the unleashing of AI worms. They use more computing power and take up more space than a conventional worm. The Mirai worm, which took down a slew of websites including Reddit and Spotify in 2016, was a few kilobytes in size, while the medium-sized AI models in the experiments were tens of gigabytes. That’s still way smaller than the massive, top-of-the-line models behind the “rogue AI” incidents that made headlines earlier in 2026. (And those weren’t worms, because they didn’t copy themselves and spread.)

Most devices — including typical laptop computers — don’t have enough space or the right kind of chips to run worm-capable AI models, Guan says. But new versions of devices, such as security cameras, are coming out with advanced hardware for running AI, researchers at the AI company Anthropic write. And at the same time, even smaller AI models are becoming more capable of sophisticated cyberattacks. These developments could expand the pool of devices an AI worm could exploit.

“The ingredients are converging” to make AI worms more realistic, Riegler says. How quickly they will converge is up for debate. Anthropic puts the timeline at months into the future, but both Riegler and Guan say it will probably take longer.

The Mirai worm spread itself through smart devices including home routers, security cameras and even baby monitors. It broke into these devices by trying a small set of common default usernames and passwords. “Just using this very simple technique, this Mirai botnet was able to infect hundreds of thousands of devices,” says cybersecurity expert Zane Ma of Oregon State University in Corvallis, who presented an analysis of the attack at a 2017 security symposium. High-profile downed sites such as Reddit were actually collateral damage: A small group of young hackers had created the worm to mess with gaming servers.

Rebooting an infected device cleared Mirai. Changing its default login credentials prevented reinfection through the same route. But an AI-powered worm might make cleaning up this type of cybersecurity breach much more difficult. Why? Because the AI worm acts more like an octopus, Guan says.

Guan and colleagues tested this octopus-worm in a virtual network. Anchored by several powerful computers that each had a chip called a graphics processing unit, or GPU, the faux networks also contained simulations of smart devices, including office printers and security cameras.

The octopus’s AI model head started on a single machine with a GPU. From there it sent out tentacles to take control of smaller devices. Upon encountering a new device, the head would use AI to plan how its tentacle could hack in. Often, a hack wouldn’t work, but the octopus wouldn’t give up. It would use info about how it failed to come up with a new hack to try. That ability is “a new, hypercharged way of attacking systems,” Riegler says. Whenever it found a computer with a large enough GPU, it would copy its head onto that new machine.

An attacker would probably launch an octopus-style AI worm from the cloud. Click through this slideshow to see how it might spread autonomously. First, it takes over and copies itself onto a device with the right kind of hardware (chip icon) to house an AI model (first image). From there, it sends out tentacles (red arrows) to hack into any connected devices, like 3-D printers and security cameras (second image). Devices that don’t have enough space for the AI model become jumping-off points for the octopus-worm to discover new places to copy itself (third image).

J. Hirshfeld; adapted from J. Guan et al/arXiv.org, 2026

J. Hirshfeld; adapted from J. Guan et al/arXiv.org, 2026

J. Hirshfeld; adapted from J. Guan et al/arXiv.org, 2026

The head could also search a simulated internet for information about newly discovered vulnerabilities. (The team didn’t connect it to the real internet for obvious reasons — protection against an AI octopus invasion — and spent considerable effort making sure their creation couldn’t escape the lab, Guan says.)

The octopus-worm even came up with a way to survive a reboot, something Guan says they hadn’t asked it to do. The team posted a preprint of their findings at arXiv.org on June 2, and the paper is now going through peer review.

Meanwhile, at Anthropic, researchers showed another way an AI worm might work by building on Guan and his colleagues’ research. If an octopus-worm wasn’t weird enough, Anthropic dubbed its creation a “digital slime mold”, a name that captures the model’s slow, oozing behavior. Anthropic declined to comment for this story, but Guan says the company’s work shows that “unlike human reasoning, AI reasoning can be distributed.” That means an AI worm wouldn’t necessarily need to hijack a powerful computer to copy and run itself — it could spread its “thinking” out among smaller devices.

And that’s exactly what the slime mold version of an AI worm does. It breaks itself up and runs pieces of the model on multiple smaller devices. In their report posted online October 12, the Anthropic researchers used 15 Android smart TVs that they had networked together.

Anthropic’s chopped-up model processes data thousands of times more slowly than what’s possible with GPUs similar to the ones Guan and colleagues relied on. That’s because the model’s data has to travel over internet connections that could take it all around the world during processing, rather than remaining in one place, within chips optimized for AI processing. That pace was too slow to demonstrate an ability to spread like a computer worm, Guan notes. So the Anthropic team ran a separate experiment with an AI worm running on GPUs that showed it could spread and adapt its attacks to different kinds of devices.

Whether AI worms are coming in months or whether we have longer to prepare, defenders should get ready now, Guan says. And AI worms do have weaknesses.

For one thing, the large size of an AI worm could be its downfall. Even if smaller AI models become more capable, these are still big programs that guzzle computing power. You might not notice if your fridge or microwave suddenly started sending lots of traffic onto the network, but your internet service provider would. They’d realize “there’s something weird going on on these devices,” Ma says. From there, they could quarantine affected devices, disconnecting them from the internet to prevent further spread.

Ma also points out that most smart devices in a person’s home aren’t directly connected to the public internet. Most home networks use a router as a central hub, and that provides a layer of protection against a worm attack.

Strong passwords, regular updates and other normal security measures would also protect against the attacks demonstrated in both experiments, Riegler says.

Guan and some colleagues are now testing specific defenses to stop AI worms, including devising an AI-driven defender. Trying to anticipate emerging threats and protect systems ahead of time is “what I’m passionate about,” Guan says. “We are working on the problem day and night.”

J. Guan et al. AI agents enable adaptive computer worms. arXiv.org. 2026. doi: 10.48550/arXiv.2606.03811

O. Çetin et al. Cleaning up the internet of evil things: real-world evidence on ISP and consumer efforts to remove Mirai. Network and Distributed Systems Security (NDSS) Symposium, San Diego, 2019.

#6294. At the Races: After the deluge

Tuesday’s rout by Democrats has led one group dedicated to electing more Republican women to Congress to warn of a “crisis-level decline” of female GOP members on Capitol Hill.

Danielle Barrow, the president of Women for Women Action Fund, drew parallels between this week’s results and the 2018 blue wave.

“After 2018, when Republicans lost 40 seats and elected only one new Republican woman, the party made a real commitment to recruiting and investing in women – and it worked,” Barrow said in a statement Wednesday, adding that women accounted for 11 of the 15 House seats the GOP picked up in the 2020 election. But she cautioned that the party needs to sustain that focus across election cycles.

“Republicans cannot only make this investment after a wipeout election and abandon it when things improve,” she said. “It is time for party leaders to treat this as a permanent strategy, not a crisis response.”

The ranks of House Republican women won’t plummet to as low as after the 2018 elections, when the caucus had just 13 female members. At least 18 Republican women have won House races so far, according to The Associated Press, and two others are leading as of Thursday afternoon. The conference is likely to see two new female members: Florida’s Sydney Gruters, the wife of RNC Chairman Joe Gruters, and Washington state’s Amanda McKinney, who holds a comfortable lead as votes continue to be counted.

Still, those figures are worlds apart from House Democrats, whose caucus will have more than 100 women next year.

“We have always known that when women run, women win,” Florida Rep. Lois Frankel, chair of the member-led Elect Democratic Women PAC, said in a statement Wednesday.

Those incoming new members span the ideological range of the party, including progressives from New York and California who scored big primary wins this summer, to more moderate Democrats who flipped seats in Virginia and Pennsylvania.

House Democrats had set a public goal this cycle to push their female membership past 100. Former Speaker Nancy Pelosi, who is retiring at the end of the year, said electing Democratic women had been her “passion” since she joined the House in 1987.

“We made a decision to make more room for women at the tables of power – and generations of candidates, organizers and supporters have carried that work forward,” she said.

Blue breakthrough: Democrats flipped the House and Senate this week, giving the party one of its biggest nights in decades. On the Senate side, they wrested seats from Republicans in Texas, South Carolina, Kansas, Iowa, North Carolina and Ohio, while finally flipping Maine. Meanwhile, on the House side, Democrats were on track to not just win every race rated a Toss-up by Inside Elections but also pick up seats in deep-red territory that weren’t considered competitive until late in the cycle. Mary Ellen and Daniela summed up their initial election night takeaways, including how Democratic moderates and progressives both cheered the results and why many of Trump’s picks flopped at the ballot box.

Not going anywhere: The top Senate Democrat, Charles E. Schumer of New York, is confident he will be elected majority leader by his caucus, especially after the party’s resounding midterm wins. Several of his incoming members have promised to support others, our colleague Savannah Behrmann reports, but the reality is there’s no real plausible alternative. Schumer’s own seat is up in 2028.

Redistricting rout: Republicans’ redistricting gambit hasn’t paid off as they’d hoped, the latest election results show, with the GOP appearing poised to flip only a handful of redrawn seats. Democratic incumbents who sought reelection from their reconfigured seats appeared poised to all win, although the race for Rep. Darren Soto’s Central Florida seat remained uncalled as of Thursday afternoon.

Taking the chair: Among the bruising defeats that North Carolina Republicans suffered this week was National Republican Congressional Committee Chairman Richard Hudson’s loss to Democrat Richard Ojeda, a former West Virginia state senator. Hudson is now the second party campaign chief to lose reelection this decade after New York’s Sean Patrick Maloney , who lost in 2022 while serving as the DCCC chair.

New senators: The incoming Senate Democratic class includes a returning senator, a former governor, two lieutenant governors and a congressman, a notable amount of governing experience. Meanwhile, five Republican House members are moving across the Rotunda after winning open Senate seats.

Member-to-governor pipeline grows: Five newly elected governors will be departing Capitol Hill to become the top executive of their state or territory, Savannah reports. Additionally, two former members who also served in the Biden administration were elected governor, though a trio of House Republicans fell short in their gubernatorial bids.

Comeback season: Roll Call’s Nick Eskow reports on the former members who are poised to return to the House or Senate next year, with at least seven winning comeback bids Tuesday.

The firsts: Several candidates made history this week with their elections to Congress or the governorships of their state. Roll Call’s Andrew Menezes rounds up the milestone wins.

D.C. in the House: Robert White, D.C.’s newly elected nonvoting delegate, told our colleague Nina Heller that he plans to lobby fellow Democrats next year to support D.C. statehood. A potential selling point: The party could tackle affordability concerns better with two Democratic senators from the deep-blue District, he said.

Keeping count: As of 4:30 p.m. Thursday, Democrats had flipped 42 seats in the House and seven in the Senate, according to the AP. Republicans have so far picked up two House seats, both through redistricting. Twenty-eight House contests and two Senate races (Alaska and Mississippi) remain uncalled as of publication time. Check out Roll Call’s results tracker for updates as the races are called.

Indie losses: Independent Senate hopefuls running in deep-red states did not find success on Tuesday, even in races without a Democrat on the ballot. In Nebraska, former union leader Dan Osborn came up short in his second Senate bid. In Idaho, former state legislator Todd Achilles failed to dislodge Sen. Jim Risch, while Navy veteran Brian Bengs couldn’t topple South Dakota Sen. Mike Rounds. In Montana, where the Democratic nominee did not drop out, former university president Seth Bodnar lost to Republican Kurt Alme. On the House side, Alaska GOP Rep. Nick Begich comfortably leads commercial fisherman Bill Hill, though below the 50 percent threshold needed to avoid a ranked-choice runoff. With votes still being counted, the AP had yet to call the race at publication time.

Not just Congress: The blue wave that broke Republican majorities on Capitol Hill also washed over state legislatures. Democrats are poised to hold new majorities in 12 legislative chambers, including the North Carolina House and Texas House, according to the Democratic Legislative Campaign Committee, although some results aren’t official yet. The party also won governing trifectas in Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin. Meanwhile, in blue states, Democrats tightened their grip on government: In Rhode Island, Republicans are on track to hold just 10 seats in the entire 113-member legislature, while next door in Connecticut, the 36-seat Senate could have as few as three GOP members.

Blame game: As Republicans take stock of what went wrong for them in the midterms, Vice President JD Vance was quick to point to the Iran conflict as an insurmountable albatross. “The reason we lost is the war,” Vance said in a lengthy X post. “If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. … But everyone knows why we lost.”

But the tariffs: A pair of Republican former senators, Arizona’s Jeff Flake and Pennsylvania’s Patrick J. Toomey, both also urged their party to focus on the impact of Trump’s tariff policies. “Arbitrary and capricious tariffs directly raised costs for all American consumers,” Toomey wrote Wednesday on X. “Many voted for Democrats yesterday.”

Staying put: Pennsylvania Rep. Brendan F. Boyle says he will remain in the House, where he’s poised to become the next Budget Committee chair, rather than launch a Democratic primary challenge to Sen. John Fetterman next cycle.

Bayh Bayh Bayh: A third generation of Indiana’s famed Bayh family won political office this week, with Beau Bayh’s election as secretary of state. Bayh, a Marine Corps veteran, follows in the footsteps of his father, Evan Bayh, who won the same post 40 years ago before going on to serve as governor and senator, and his late grandfather, Birch Bayh, who won three terms in the Senate. Indiana Democrats had a breakthrough election this week, defeating GOP Rep. Victoria Spartz, winning a second statewide office, unseating the speaker and breaking the GOP supermajority in the state House.

A win and a loss: Nebraska Republican Sen. Pete Ricketts won reelection, but his wife, Democrat Susanne Shore, lost a special election for a seat on University of Nebraska Board of Regents, which governs the university system. Shore, who lost to a fellow Democrat in the officially nonpartisan race, was making her first bid for elective office.

Bans on the ballot: Voters in Arizona, Nebraska and Washington state have approved new measures barring transgender athletes from participating in girls sports. A similar proposal in Colorado also appears likely to pass, although the AP had yet to call it as of publication time.

Roll Call elections analyst Nathan L. Gonzales of Inside Elections shares 15 initial lessons from the midterm elections, from the president’s “political mortality” to candidate quality and the power of personal brands. And, Nathan writes, as bad a night as it was for Republicans, it could have been even worse.

As Maine goes: The New York Times caught up with with Republican Sen. Susan Collins, who lost her bid for a sixth term in Maine. Collins, who had survived tough cycles before, spoke of getting “caught up in the Trump tsunami” and how she finally had her “Margaret Chase Smith moment.”

“These are extinction-level numbers”: Texas Monthly sat down for an interview with former state House Speaker Dade Phelan, who anticipated a down-ballot GOP rout but not the full extent of it. “MAGA needs to be dead,’’ said the Republican, who led the push to impeach state Attorney General Ken Paxton in 2023 and then was targeted for defeat by Trump. He opted against reelection this year.

Corruption a top issue: The Associated Press reported that its 2026 voter poll found corruption at the top of the list of concerns for voters who helped sweep Democrats into power on Capitol Hill.

Tar Heeled: Among the states where Republicans suffered their biggest defeats Tuesday, perhaps none was more stunning than North Carolina, where they've so far lost five U.S. House seats and are trailing in one another and lost control of the state House. The (Raleigh) News & Observer looks at how maps “designed to deliver strong Republican majorities [failed] so spectacularly at that goal.”

Support and discord: Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed’s sharply critical views toward Israel roiled the Jewish community in Michigan. But exit polling suggests most Jewish voters backed him, albeit in smaller numbers than they might have had a different Democrat run, Religion News Service reports.

That's how many House districts won by Trump in 2024 have been called for Democratic candidates by the AP as of 4:30 p.m. Eastern time on Thursday.

Twenty-eight additional Trump-won districts remain uncalled at publication time, and Democrats are currently leading in eight of those races.

The figures stand in sharp contrast to the start of the cycle, when there were just 13 House Democrats in districts that backed Trump in 2024.

Since then, several Republican-led states redrew their congressional maps in an effort to increase the number of Trump-won districts and improve their party’s chances of holding the House.

In large part, this effort appears to have backfired in 2026, with the Democratic wave cresting high enough to wash over dozens of Trump-won districts. Twenty-one of the 52 Democratic wins so far have come in states that redrew their congressional lines: Texas (six Trump-won seats), North Carolina (six), Ohio (five), Florida (three) and Alabama (one).

Congressional Republicans are holding leadership elections next week as they transition from the majority to the minority party. Speaker Mike Johnson is not seeking his conference’s top post, setting up a clash to be the next House minority leader. On the Senate side, South Dakota’s John Thune hopes to continue leading his party in the chamber.
