#6258. The 8 Best Shop Vacs for Tackling Tough Messes

From sucking up water to blowing sawdust off your tools, these powerful models have what it takes to get the job done. These are the models we’ve used and recommend.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

You can’t make an omelet without breaking a few eggs, and you can’t complete a project at home or in your workshop without making a mess. These are the laws of the universe. I don’t write them; I just obey them.

But because of this, I also know the importance of a reliable shop vac. Unlike the vacuum you use to clean the floors in your home, a shop vac gobbles up large, chunky messes, including sawdust, screws, bits of wood, and other debris (not to mention spills and other wet messes). So if you’re using woodworking tools like sanders, miter saws, and table saws on a regular basis, you need to have one close by.

When it comes to choosing the right shop vac for your home, there’s a lot to consider. Shop vacs come in both cordless and corded electric models and range in size from small, 1.6-gallon portable vacuums for cleaning out cars to large, 12-gallon shop vacs capable of keeping your entire garage sawdust-free.

All of the products written about below were tested by members of the Popular Mechanics team, including myself (Tony Carrick) and Test Editor Brad Ford.

In an effort to evaluate the performance of the shop vacs on this list, we put them through tests that involved collecting both dry materials and liquid. We conducted three timed tests using only each vacuum’s hose, no attachments. The first test involved vacuuming up 12 cups of sawdust to determine how quickly each vac could collect dry material. We then used each vac to drain 2 gallons of water from a bucket. Lastly, we tested suction power by attempting to use each vac to suck up wood screws and metal bolts.

Along with grading each shop vac’s vacuuming capabilities, we also evaluated how easy each model was to use, based on factors like weight, size, capacity, and cord and hose length. Since every person’s shop vac needs may vary, the list below includes a broad range of sizes.

In the latest update of this guide, we tested and added two new shop vacs. The Vacmaster Professional Beast Series FLT+ is a shop vac with next-level features you won’t find on any other shop vacs. Not only does it connect to the exhaust ports of the large sawdust-producing power tools in your workshop, table saws, miter saws, and the like, but it also syncs with them via a wireless remote. With a vacuum cleaner–like dust collection bag and top-mounted HEPA filter, it’s ideally equipped for collecting sawdust.

The Craftsman CMXEVBE17595 Wet-Dry Shop Vac is our largest pick (with its 16-gallon tank) and also one of our most powerful. With a max airflow of 185 cubic feet per minute (cfm), it sucks up material faster than any other shop vac we tested. It’s also powerful enough to pull in heavier objects, including bolts and small chunks of wood.

The Vacmaster’s impressive power and compact design make it the perfect all-around shop vac. One of our editors owns the previous iteration of this model and has found it to be the ideal shop vac for home use. Its 5.5-hp motor is much more powerful than what you’ll find with most other 5-gallon shop vacs. It also has a small, 18.6-by-13.4-inch footprint, so it’s easy to carry and store, though its smaller capacity may not be enough for busier workshops.

With an 18-foot power cord and 7-foot hose, you won’t need an extension cord to clean up a large two-car garage or reach a car in the driveway. Plus, the newest version of the Vacmaster adds wheels that make it even easier to move around. There are also four attachments, which offer enough versatility to handle different jobs, and all of the Vacmaster’s attachments fit neatly into a storage compartment on the vacuum.

Full Vacmaster Beast Series 5-Gallon Shop Vacuum Review

Stanley’s 6-gallon wet-dry vac is a fraction of the cost of other shop vacs, yet it still packs enough power and capacity to handle most cleanups. Though it lagged behind the top performers we tested, it still completed our sawdust test in a respectable 21 seconds, and it swallowed up 2 gallons of water in just 11 seconds. And with its smaller-diameter hose, it produced enough suction to pick up both screws and bolts.

It’s not too bulky, so it won’t crowd your workshop floor, nor is it so compact that it requires emptying too frequently. It sits on swiveling casters and is relatively light, which made it easy to wheel around our tester’s garage. We also liked its accessories, which include two extensions and three nozzles for both floor and spill cleanup. The crevice tool was particularly impressive in that it reached easily into the tight spaces between the seats of one of our cars.

We did find ourselves wishing the power cord was longer than 10 feet so we could reach all corners of the workshop without having to use an extension cord. Still, with its low price and ample capacity, this Stanley vac is a great value option for any home workshop.

Ridgid's shop vac is powerful and affordable enough to fit most budgets, making it an ideal companion for those bigger and messier home improvement projects.

During testing, it collected a pile of sawdust in just over 16 seconds before proceeding to drain a bucket of water in about 6 seconds. While we liked how quickly it picked up light debris, the Ridgid left a little to be desired with lift power. Its large-diameter hose made quick work of lighter material, but it struggled to pick up larger bolts (though we should note that this was an issue with most other vacs with large 2-1/2-inch-diameter hoses).

The Ridgid also has a sturdy feel to it. The hose resisted cracking or denting, even after mistakenly stepping on it, and the tub is made of thick plastic. There’s also a locking system on the hose, which prevents attachments from falling off when the vacuum is in use.

The vacuum’s long, 7-foot hose made it easy to clean a work area without having to repeatedly reposition the base. Attachments include two extension wands, along with a crevice tool and floor tool, all of which fit onto the shop vac for storage. An included wet filter would make this shop vac a real no-brainer purchase, but it’s not far off from that even without one.

Full Ridgid 12-Gallon 5.0 Peak HP NXT Shop Vacuum Review

The speed and capacity the DeWalt Stealthsonic displayed during my tests makes it a great choice for cleaning up wet messes.

It produced some of the most impressive vacuuming results during our tests. Backed by its 5.5-hp motor and 2.5-inch-diameter hose (about the same size as a fire hose), the Stealthsonic gobbled up our pile of sawdust in just 16 seconds and drained our bucket of water in just 5 seconds, which was among the fastest of any shop vac we tested.

It was also one of the largest of the shop vacs we tested, with a 12-gallon capacity. Thanks to its 20-foot-long cord, it covers an entire two-car garage without the need for an extension cord, and it sits on heavy-duty rubber casters that make it easy to wheel around.

While its larger-diameter hose worked well for the quick collection of lighter materials, it’s not ideal for heavier objects. The Stealthsonic struggled to produce enough lift to suck up wood screws and was unable to collect larger bolts like some shop vacs with smaller-diameter hoses could. It also is a bit too bulky to get into tighter spots, such as the small gaps in and around the seats in a car. But if you’re looking for something that quickly cleans up larger spills and messes at the job site or in a workshop, this vacuum is it.

Milwaukee’s M18 Fuel wet-dry vacuum, which runs off an 18-volt lithium-ion battery, is one of the most powerful shop vac options when there’s no electrical outlet in range. The vac impressed during testing, even matching some of the corded shop vacs we tested. It consumed our sawdust pile in 20 seconds flat and a bucket of water in just 11 seconds, which is saying something given that it has a long, 9-foot hose.

We also loved the design of this wet-dry vac. The accessories, which include a floor utility nozzle and crevice tool, fit nicely inside a compartment on the top of the shop vac, and the tray holds both extensions. The extra-long hose and the small profile of the crevice tool were particularly valuable when we used the M18 Fuel wet-dry vacuum to clean out a car.

The M18 6-gallon vacuum is also easy to maneuver. It sits in a sturdy tray with four casters with rubber wheels that rolled easily over our tester’s garage floor and driveway. The M18’s run time was also impressive. When loaded with a 12.0-ampere-hour (Ah) battery, we got 31 minutes of run time when set to high and a whopping 48 minutes on its lower power setting.

This was the priciest wet-dry vacuum we tested, but it’s worth the investment if you want to cut the cord without compromising power.

If the primary demand for your shop vac is to collect the mountains of sawdust left behind following a carpentry project, then look no further than the recently launched Vacmaster Professional Beast Series FLT+. Not only will this shop vac attach to your power tools’ exhaust ports, but it also synchronizes with them. It comes with a Synchro key remote, which you attach to a power tool via a neoprene strap. The key communicates wirelessly with the shop vac. When it senses the vibration of the tool turning on, the key sends a signal that turns on the vacuum, eliminating the need to walk across the room to turn it on manually. I used it with a table saw, and it worked well, reliably turning on as soon as I fired up the table saw and dutifully sucking up dust as I cut, then turning off when I shut down the saw.

The Vacmaster is designed for collecting dust particles, and it did that extremely well. It sucked up 12 cups of sawdust in under 20 seconds, which is impressive given that it comes equipped with a smaller 1-7/8-inch-diameter hose. The Vacmaster Beast FLT+ also comes with a dust bag similar to a vacuum cleaner and a HEPA filter, making it ideal for trapping fine dust particles.

While most shop vacs have a filter located inside the collection tank, the Vacmaster’s is on top. This frees up space inside the tank for more debris collection while also preventing the filter from becoming inundated with dust. Other notable features you won’t find on most shop vacs include an LED display that shows the vacuum's airflow percentage, so you know when it’s time to clean the filter, and a self-cleaning filter. It’s an excellent workshop shop vac for those who don’t mind springing for it.

With its cordless design, light weight, and compact, box-shaped design, Milwaukee’s M12 Fuel shop vac is made for the road. At just 15 inches long, 13 inches wide, and 12 inches high, and with a weight of just under 10 pounds, Milwaukee’s M12 Fuel shop vac was by far the easiest to carry around of the wet-dry vacuums we tested. Its shape also made it ideal for sitting in the trunk of a car or storing on a set of garage shelves.

Per its name, the M12 Fuel shop vac uses a smaller power source—a 12-volt battery—so it doesn’t have the power of the corded and 18-volt cordless models we tested. Still, it took a respectable 35 seconds for it to complete our sawdust test and was capable of sucking down both bolts and wood screws. Its 1.6-gallon capacity and a max runtime of 26 minutes on low and 14 minutes on high limit it to small cleanup jobs, however.

While it lacks the power of larger shop vacs, it’s hard to overstate how convenient it is to use. We appreciated its compact size and cordless design when we toted it into the car for some detailing, then later up to a second-floor bonus room to clean up drywall dust after mounting a TV.

The M12 Fuel is pricey when you factor in the cost of a battery and charger, but its convenience is unmatched, especially if you’ve already bought into Milwaukee’s 12-volt power tool universe and have a 12-volt Fuel battery to load into it.

Full Milwaukee M12 Fuel 1.6-Gallon Shop Vac Review

The Craftsman 16-gallon wet-dry shop vac was built to clean up large masses fast with a max airflow of 185 cfm, well above the 100 cfm I see on most shop vacs. It vacuumed up 12 cups of sawdust faster than any other shop vac I tested and gulped down 2 gallons of water in 5 seconds flat. Most of the shop vacs I tested with a larger 2-1/2-inch-diameter hose struggled to generate enough lift to pick up heavier debris. That wasn’t the case with the Craftsman, which effortlessly vacuumed up a pile of screws, washers, and large bolts.

The Craftsman sits on four sturdy casters that made it easy to maneuver around when I was using it to clean up my large two-car garage, which I was able to do thanks to its 20-foot-long power cord and 7-foot hose.

With its 16-gallon size, the Craftsman was also the largest shop vac I tested, which made it handy for cleaning up big messes and large open areas. It was less effective for cleaning out a car. The crevice tool and its bulkier hose made it difficult to maneuver around a car interior, and there are no crevice tools for cleaning the gaps between seats and other tight spaces.

While its large size makes the Craftsman capable of cleaning up large messes, it also makes it a bit of a space hog in a garage or shed. You also won’t be carrying it inside the house to clean up messes in the home. But if you’re after a shop vac with the muscle and capacity to handle large postproject messes, this is the one.

The drum capacity of a shop vac determines how much material you can vacuum without having to empty it out. While sizes range from 1.6 to 16 gallons, smaller-capacity shop vacs, like the Milwaukee M12 Fuel 1.6-Gallon Wet-Dry Vacuum, provide more versatility to the average user through easier transport and storage. If you’re short on space, a smaller unit that you have to empty more frequently could be more convenient than a larger-capacity machine cluttering up your garage. Keep in mind that the stated gallon capacity doesn't factor in the space taken up by the filter, so don’t expect a 6-gallon model to suck up exactly 6 gallons of material.

While the majority of shop vacs use corded power, cordless models are becoming more common. These battery-powered options offer more mobility—especially useful for car, boat, or RV cleaning—but they lack the runtime for extended projects. If you prefer the mobility of cordless models (especially if you’re interested in a larger-capacity model that requires a lot of power), choose one from the same brand as your existing power tools. This enables you to extend runtime by using additional batteries you already have on hand.

If you decide to go with a corded model, pay attention to the length of the cord. Models with a longer cord, such as the DeWalt Stealthsonic Wet-Dry Shop Vacuum, give you the freedom to cover larger workshops or reach to your driveway without having to get out an extension cord.

A shop vac’s airflow—measured in cubic feet per minute (cfm)—represents the amount of air a vacuum pulls through its nozzle. Roughly speaking, a shop vac with a higher cfm sucks up material faster than one with a lower cfm, though keep in mind this doesn’t include other factors like nozzle design, motor size, and suction power. As we found during testing, shop vacs with smaller-diameter hoses, such as the Milwaukee M18 Fuel 6-Gallon Wet-Dry Vacuum, often produce greater suction power. So while a larger shop vac with a larger-diameter hose will remove lightweight material, such as sawdust, more quickly than a shop vac with a narrower hose, that smaller vac is better able to pick up heavier objects, such as bolts and coins.

While most shop vacs include several nozzle attachments for the hose, some models offer a more useful variety of accessories. Think about the type and scope of your cleaning tasks, and look for a vacuum with applicable accessories. For example, we’ve found a brush-tip nozzle to be essential for automotive interior cleaning, allowing us to quickly clean dust and pet hair from the dashboard and display screen—areas easily scratched by a hard plastic nozzle. Or, if you want to suck up the cobwebs in the corner of your garage or sawdust deep under your workbench, look for vacs with multiple extension wands to extend the nozzle reach.

#6257. ‘Political malpractice’: Calls grow to delay Senate GOP leadership elections

Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., walks through the Ohio Clock Corridor this summer. Now he’s pushing to delay leadership elections for his conference, urging a discussion of last week’s larger than expected losses. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

After last week’s midterm elections saw them lose at least seven Senate seats and the majority, some Republicans are pushing for a reckoning, saying the conference should stop and think about its future.

“After the stunning defeat [we] just can’t continue on business as usual. That kind of defeat demands change,” Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., said on Monday evening.

Asked if he himself would want to run for Senate minority leader, the Wisconsin Republican responded with a question of his own: “That’s part of our problem. Who’d want the job? Would you want it?”

Though no hopeful had emerged as of Monday afternoon — at least publicly — to challenge current Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., for the top GOP post, the frustration was palpable as Republican senators returned to D.C. and grappled with the election results. Calls grew throughout the day to delay the conference’s leadership elections planned for Tuesday morning.

“Well, I mean, I’m open to hearing what the arguments are for that,” Thune told reporters Monday when asked about the possibility of postponing the leadership votes. “I don’t know if that solves anything, but like I said, it’s going to be a decision that’s ultimately made by Republican senators. We’ll hear them out.”

Johnson told reporters on Monday that if the election is held, he would “leave the room” and walk out. Either way, he seemed certain to at least get a “fulsome” discussion of the topic, as he requested in a letter he sent to Republican Conference Chair Tom Cotton, R-Ark. Four other Republican senators signed on to the letter, hitting the threshold to call a conference meeting under internal GOP rules.

Also signed by Sens. Mike Lee of Utah, Ted Budd of North Carolina, Rick Scott of Florida, and John Kennedy of Louisiana, the letter obtained by CQ Roll Call cites last week’s “stunning defeat” and reads in part: “Holding leadership elections without engaging in a robust discussion and evaluation of how those running for leadership intend to lead would be political malpractice.”

Kennedy said Monday evening that he was asking to postpone the leadership elections because “we need time to talk to each other.”

“We’re like a shop owner who’s losing his customers. It’s not the customer’s job to fix that. It’s the shop owner’s job, and I’m not looking for blame-shifting. I’m looking for self-examination,” he said, adding that he wouldn’t consider running for minority leader himself.

In the letter, the group asked that at the time the leadership elections were set to begin, 9 a.m. on Tuesday, they instead “have a fulsome conference discussion and delay holding leadership elections until we all have a chance to hear from leadership candidates as to what type of collaborative conference governing model we should adopt and what our strategy will be to counter the emboldened Democrats.”

Thune echoed that wording Monday as he spoke to reporters, saying, “I do think that we need to have a very fulsome, robust conversation about where we go from here, and then we’ll see what the consensus of the conference is.”

But Sen. Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va., who serves as chair of the Senate Republican Policy Committee, said she has seen such requests launched in the past and didn’t think it would do much to affect the ultimate outcome. “I think Sen. Thune will be reelected,” she said.

And several Senate GOP aides said that they suspected a “robust” conversation wouldn’t do much to delay the plans and that leadership elections were still expected to take place Tuesday. They noted similar efforts from some of those same senators in previous years to sow discord in the ranks.

That includes Scott, who unsuccessfully challenged Thune in 2024 and then-GOP leader Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., in 2022. But Scott told Fox News over the weekend, “I don’t want to run again. I’ve run twice.”

Republicans “failed. We had a horrible night,” Scott said. “Instead of having an [leadership] election, the first thing you do is you say, ‘OK, what are we going to change? We have to change something.’”

Lee floated the idea of waiting until after the uncalled Senate races in Mississippi and Alaska are officially resolved.

An online pressure campaign was building in some of the same MAGA corners of the internet that have pushed to pass a sweeping voter ID bill, known as the SAVE America Act, that has stalled in the Senate. On Monday morning, influencer Scott Presler in an X post urged constituents to call their senators while praising the lawmakers who have already pushed for the leadership elections to be postponed. “Where is everyone else?” he wrote.

Sens. Jim Banks of Indiana and Dave McCormick of Pennsylvania also called for a delay, though they did not appear on Johnson’s letter.

“A week ago, we had the worst election results in decades,” McCormick said in a post on X, calling Tuesday “too soon” to vote for leaders. “I know it’s been practice to go straight to leadership elections in recent years, but we should not rush it.”

Banks similarly said Tuesday was “too soon,” posting on social media, “Our conference needs to sit down and have a frank conversation about where we fell short, what we stand for, and what we’re going to do for the working families who sent us here.”

One senator speaking out in Thune’s defense was Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, who competed with Thune for the top spot in 2024 but on Monday said the leader isn’t to blame for the midterm results.

“I think the president needs to look in the mirror and look at the flawed candidates that he endorsed, and the kind of environment that we’re in,” said Cornyn, who is still smarting from losing his primary to a challenger backed by President Donald Trump.

Cornyn’s loss means he has no say in the coming conference leadership elections. But he said, “I think Thune’s a good man, and did as well as he could against a president and an environment that was pretty hostile.”

Biologist Gonzalo Quiroga-Artigas lifts the lid on the secret life of tardigrades in stunning detail for the Nikon Small World photography awards.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

It's not often we get to peer into the tiny world of tardigrades (also known as water bears). But through his photography, biologist Gonzalo Quiroga-Artigas is unmasking the secret lives of these creatures in stunning detail.

In one photo, which won Quiroga-Artigas 12th place in Nikon's 2026 Photomicrography Competition, a tardigrade (Hypsibius exemplaris) is seen shedding its tough outer layer, known as a cuticle or an exuvium, while laying an egg in the discarded skin.

"A large part of my research involves imaging, and during the many hours I spend at the confocal microscope, I have come across some incredibly beautiful and unexpected scenes," Quiroga-Artigas, a postdoctoral researcher at the Montpellier Cell Biology Research Center in France, told Live Science in an email.

"An interesting feature of tardigrade reproduction is that some species lay their eggs inside the shed cuticle, or exuvium. The exuvium can therefore provide an additional layer of physical protection for the developing embryos."

In some species, males may place sperm inside the cuticle of a molting female before egg laying, according to National Geographic. In others, the males fertilize the eggs after they have been left inside the cuticle. And some don't even need males to reproduce at all.

"Many species reproduce through parthenogenesis," Quiroga-Artigas said, which is when an embryo develops from an unfertilized egg, also known as a virgin birth. "This means that males are not required for reproduction, and the resulting offspring are genetically very similar to their mothers," he added. The species in the photograph falls into this category.

Molting and egg laying often take place over several hours, but the shedding itself is a relatively fast process. Capturing it on camera is, therefore, no mean feat.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"Once I had collected animals that were laying eggs, I had to fix, stain, and mount the specimens before imaging them," Quiroga-Artigas said. "I then spent a long microscopy session searching for the right specimen and the right orientation to obtain a high-quality image. Finding a specimen at exactly the right stage of molting, and in an orientation that allows the process to be clearly visualized, is largely a matter of patience and luck."

—Tardigrades survive being dried out thanks to proteins found in no other animals on Earth

—Tardigrades may hitchhike on snails ... and then suffocate in their slime

—'Sexy Mantis,' obscene orangutan and prancing sparrowhawk feature in 2026 Nikon Comedy Wildlife Awards

Photographing these animals is also challenging due to their tiny size. "Working with tardigrades in the lab requires a lot of experience with micromanipulation, as they are extremely small," Quiroga-Artigas said. "Hypsibius exemplaris, for example, is only about 250 µm [micrometers] long." That's about twice the width of a human hair.

This particular photo was taken using confocal microscopy, which uses a focused laser beam to light up one section at a time to create a detailed, high-resolution image. Quiroga-Artigas used this technique for a second tardigrade photo that was listed as an Image of Distinction in the same competition.

The second image submitted by Quiroga-Artigas to the Nikon Small World competition of a tardigrade shown from beneath.

He also received an Honorable Mention in the Nikon Small World in Motion Competition for a video of a pregnant tardigrade making contact with another tardigrade, which can then be seen pooping. However, it's not clear whether the contact between the two individuals caused this movement, Quiroga-Artigas said.

Quiroga-Artigas hopes his photography and videos give viewers an idea of just how beautiful and complex the microscopic world really is. "There are tiny animals all around us that we cannot see with the naked eye, yet they live, reproduce, grow, and undergo complex life cycles just like the animals we are more familiar with," he said.

"I will continue capturing images of tardigrades in different contexts related to my future research, without necessarily having a specific photographic goal in mind," he added. "In my experience, some of the best images I have captured were not necessarily the ones I was actively looking for."

Pandora is the trending news editor at Live Science. She is also a science presenter and previously worked as Senior Science and Health Reporter at Newsweek. Pandora holds a Biological Sciences degree from the University of Oxford, where she specialised in biochemistry and molecular biology.

#6255. How I Got My Visa to France

I’ve been in love with France ever since my first trip to Bordeaux in 2010. Friends I had met back in Thailand showed me around the area and introduced me to French culture. It was my first time in France and I loved the food, the wine, and the people.

But that love became an obsession when, after Bordeaux, I stepped out of the Paris metro and onto the Champs-Élysées. The lights, the energy, the mystique! There was magic in the air. I felt like I had known the city my entire life and I was simply returning home.

Since then, Paris has had a firm grip on my heart. Over the years, I spent countless visits exploring France and Paris in particular. I’ve run tours in the city and I spent a few months living there in 2019.

Last August, after yet another sojourn, I thought to myself, “What if I moved back?”

I was growing a bit tired of the NYC dating scene, the rising cost of living, and felt like, creatively, I was in a rut. With AI coming for creators like me and the industry changing, I was a little lost on what, career-wise, would come next.

And Paris seemed like the best place to go.

It’s cheaper than NYC, I had friends there already, I’ve always wanted to learn French, it would make a great base for exploring Europe, and I could start writing my next book there. There’s nothing like a change in scenery to get the creativity flowing!

But the question remained: how do you move to France?

After all, they don’t have a digital nomad visa, and you’re limited to three months if you visit on your regular Schengen tourist visa.

Well, it turns out that it’s not actually that hard. (And while I can only speak for Americans, I suspect the criteria are similar for Canadians, Aussies, Kiwis, and other “developed” nations.)

If you want to move to France, you have four main options:

The student visa is pretty straightforward. You need to enroll in a full-time university program and show you have enough funds to support yourself (around 600 Euros per month). A friend is currently there on this visa, as she is doing a nine-month intensive French program to become fluent. You still have to apply for the visa, but if you’re enrolled in an accredited school, you’ll likely get approved. Another benefit to this visa is that you can work part-time on it!

But this visa is contingent on being in school, so if you leave or quit, it’s voided. However, when you are done, you can change this to a “job seeker” visa, which can give you up to another six months in France (or more depending on how long your program was).

I thought about applying for the entrepreneur visa, but the application process is pretty complex and can take months to be approved. You have to set up your business in France — and that is a lot of paperwork. You have to show that your business makes money, has clients (at least one of them being French), and can support you full-time (you have to make at least the French minimum wage). They will scrutinize your assets and financials a lot and you’ll need to register your business in France and pay French taxes.

Additionally, France offers a talent visa. If you’re an expert in your field (with verifiable accreditations and accolades), this could be a good visa to apply for, especially if you plan to stay in France for a long time and want to physically work there. But, again, you’ll need to have some source of income and plan to do physical business in France. If you’re not an academic but someone in the arts, you have to show how you are going to add to the “culture of France” in some way.

While I would meet the requirements for both those visas, the process for either would have been time-consuming, and, since I’m not sure France is going to be my forever home, I decided not to go through that process.

So I went with the long-term visitor visa, officially called VLS-TS visiteur. This allows me to stay up to 12 months in France and is renewable in the country. It does come with a lot of restrictions, however: I can’t physically work here and I am not allowed into the French social welfare system.

It’s also the visa a lot of Americans (and most retirees) are coming in on. If you have passive income or retirement savings and just want to live in France, this is a good option for you. It allows you to set up a bank account and it can be renewed pretty much indefinitely.

The paperwork for this visa (which I’ll get into in a bit) essentially comes down to whether or not you can support yourself. French authorities want to make sure you won’t be a burden on the system.

My biggest question centered around whether or not I could “work” on this visa. A lot of creators and digital nomads are applying for — and getting — this visa.

But remember: you aren’t allowed to work on this visa so how are you going to work if you can’t work?

So let me take a moment to talk about “work” from a legal standpoint.

As I mentioned, there’s no digital nomad visa that allows you to work in France. And the French tax office said last July that remote work is considered taxable — but there are no official laws that say so. That’s just their opinion and there’s been no progress in codifying that opinion. In fact, my visa doesn’t even come with a tax number, so I can’t be taxed. I couldn’t pay taxes even if I wanted to.

The visa office asks how you’ll support yourself when you are in France and one of the sources of income they accept is “income from work.” I was very open that my means of support would be the income from this blog and my books.

The system there really hasn’t caught up to remote work. It still defines “work” as something you do physically that could take away a job from a French person.

So could I run walking tours in Paris? Nope. Could you work at a café? Nope.

But does writing this blog post count as work? After all, no one is paying for it. It’s a free resource. Does going to a café to work on the next great American novel count? What about my weekly newsletter that has affiliate links (that generate income) in it? Is writing that considered work?

The gray area is considerable, so the best thing to do is to talk to a lawyer. I recommend Daniel Tostado (yes, that’s his real name), one of the biggest American-French immigration lawyers in Paris. He has a huge law firm and regularly meets with government officials to clarify the rules on this. He gave me some solid advice.

For this long-term visitor visa, the application process is pretty easy. You go to the French government website, fill out your application, take the application number to the TLScontact website, and make an appointment. (France outsources the appointment process to this company, which then sends everything to the French consulate for approval.)

The main things you’ll want to demonstrate are that you have accommodation for 90 days on your application and enough income to support yourself. They just want to make sure you aren’t going to be a burden on the system. I went overboard. Here’s what I brought to my appointment:

I didn’t need the second bank account, tax returns, or W-2 (they weren’t required) but the woman at the appointment said the more proof you had the better and it wouldn’t hurt. And another friend who got this visa didn’t bring anything beyond what was asked in the application form. But I wanted to take no chances!

At the appointment, the staff double-checks your paperwork, takes your biometric data, collects the fees, and then sends your passport to the embassy for processing. Officially, it takes up to 15 days to process your visa, but everyone I know seems to get it back within a week.

The worst part was not knowing if you are approved until your passport is returned. While you can track the progress of your application, you don’t know the verdict until your passport is back in your hands. While I was waiting (and anxiously spiraling), I looked on Reddit and found that most denials were for lack of income or issues with their accommodation, which seem to be the two most important things to have perfect on your application.

Once you get your visa back, you can enter France any time after the start date. After you enter, you have 90 days to register your visa with the state (they give you a little QR code with instructions). This allows you to “officially” be on this long-term visa. (It’s a more paperwork kind of thing.)

Once that is done, there’s nothing else to do and you can stay in France (and Europe) until your visa expires!

So, if you’re considering moving to France, these are your options. But, as always, I’m not a lawyer and this is not legal advice. In regard to work and other issues or questions, it’s important that you seek legal counsel and get their expert opinion!

#6254. The 7 Best UPS Battery Backups

Keep your essential devices online and protected from the damaging effects of power outages and surges.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Between a modem, desktop computer, and network-attached storage (NAS), modern computing setups require a reliable power source to function effectively. If you work from home or own a small business, you know that nothing halts your workday and puts you behind like an unexpected power outage. An uninterruptible power supply (UPS) keeps your essential devices temporarily online, which provides a window for you to hit send on that last-minute email.

While a standard power strip or surge protector offers sufficient, albeit basic, protection, a UPS ensures devices are properly shut down and are protected from data loss. Beyond just keeping your devices running, the best UPS battery backups also shield sensitive electronics from potentially damaging power surges and fluctuations throughout the day. Read on to see our recommendations covering a range of needs and budgets.

To find the best uninterruptible power supply, we researched dozens of models from the leading brands in this space. Our selection process focused on several key features, including battery life, automatic voltage regulation (AVR), number of outlets, and other advanced features like power management software. After working from home and testing gear in our home offices for years, we understand the critical need for a reliable power source to keep devices online. Our personal experience and circumstances informed our choices, as we considered the models that could protect devices and provide sufficient battery backup during outages.

The CyberPower CP1500PFCLCD offers a whopping 12 outlets, six of which can pull pure sine wave alternating current (AC) power from the battery. The six secondary outlets give you plenty of surge protection and power for non-essential devices, so you have a full power solution for everyday, and plenty of emergency backup power in an outage.

The battery backed outlets are clearly marked, so there’s no confusion. The shape itself also cleverly makes extra room for bulky power bricks in two spots, in case you have a couple of larger plugs.

The CyberPower model contains two USB ports—one USB-A and one USB-C—on its front, and an LCD display gives you detailed information on battery capacity and current load. An alarm sounds when something is wrong with either the device or your setup (like the battery is low or the UPS capacity is overloaded), plus there’s a button to mute the alarm as needed.

The CP1500PFCLCD also supports data line protection, so your devices stay safe from power surges that travel through Ethernet. The cord is a foot shorter than our top pick, but this model provides slightly more output capacity, so it’s worth checking out if you want a ton of outlets.

The Amazon Basics Standby UPS 600VA provides basic backup on a budget, but it lacks the more advanced features of other options. It has eight outlets total, including four battery-backed outlets to plug in devices like a modem, laptop, or NAS. And with an output of 360 watts, it’s the perfect option for home offices, with space to connect multiple devices simultaneously.

There’s a good amount of space between outlets on the Amazon UPS to easily accommodate two larger power bricks without crowding other nearby outlets. Additionally, it has a user-replaceable battery and supports power management software.

As we said, it lacks more advanced features, including AVR, but it’s still a solid, affordable option.

This CyberPower model offers everything you need in a powerful and reliable UPS. It includes 12 surge-protected outlets, with six of those backed by battery power. This gives you ample space to connect various devices, from your home office setup to more fun devices like your PlayStation 5, smart TV, or gaming desktop. The front of the UPS also features both a USB-A and USB-C port for connecting mobile devices.

An LCD panel displays information about battery and power conditions. If the power goes out, this model’s replaceable battery runs for up to 12 minutes at half load, giving you plenty of time to safely power down. It features simulated AVR, which corrects minor power fluctuations but may not be ideal for sensitive high-end gear.

This APC model features power management software and AVR and comes with an LCD panel, all of which make it another great advanced UPS for home offices and small businesses.

The APC’s power management software boasts several additional features, including the ability to remotely shut down your connected devices during an emergency. This prevents potential corruption or data loss. The device also supports a graceful shutdown feature, which automatically shuts down connected equipment if you’re unable to do it when the connected devices reach a predetermined power level.

The UPS offers both data line and coaxial line safeguards to give you extra peace of mind during power disturbances. An informative LCD screen on the front panel displays crucial information, such as battery capacity, load capacity, the number of power events that have occurred, and any system errors.

For added convenience, the UPS is equipped with both a USB-A and a USB-C port on the front to charge your phone or tablet in the same place as your home office equipment.

Most UPS devices take up a lot of floor or desk space. This one, however, measures approximately 4.1 by 10.8 by 5.5 inches, which is more compact than most for easier integration into your current home office.

Even with its smaller design, this UPS packs a punch with seven total surge-protected outlets, five of which offer battery power. It offers 330 watts of output power—perfectly suitable for a more modest setup.

The UPS automatically switches off from the battery backup when your power comes back on. And when the time comes, you can replace its battery instead of replacing the entire unit.

There are some trade-offs to the more compact design. For instance, more advanced models contain a few more outlets. You also miss out on an LCD screen and AVR. However, these compromises bring the cost down on this space-efficient UPS.

This CyberPower UPS easily integrates into a server setup because of its rack-mounting feature. The design makes it an excellent choice for small businesses that have a data center or server room, keeping the UPS close to the devices it’s protecting. It fits into racks as small as 14 inches in depth.

The device features eight battery-backed outlets and an LCD panel, which displays information on battery and power conditions. The screen also shows alerts about potential issues before they affect your devices.

Like other CyberPower models, this one supports management software for monitoring the UPS remotely. Other features include data line protection and an estimated battery runtime of 10 minutes at half load.

Most UPS models offer limited battery life, even at half load, which isn’t ideal for IT professionals or network administrators. This APC model, however, delivers impressive battery runtime, with up to 23 minutes at half load in the event of an outage. That’s almost double what other top models offer, giving you ample time to save your work and safely shut down your devices.

Beyond excellent battery life, this model comes with a number of advanced features, including cloud-based remote power monitoring, remote diagnostics, and email notifications with recommended actions. It also supports graceful shutdown.

All of these premium features mean this UPS costs more and is noticeably larger than other options on the list. That said, its combination of extended runtime and management features makes it a worthwhile investment, particularly for small businesses that want to protect their hardware and data.

A traditional UPS buys you a few minutes, just enough time to save your work and shut down. If the power's out for hours, you need something bigger. The Anker Solix S2000 is a portable power station that doubles as a UPS: Plug it into the wall, plug your gear into it, and when the power cuts out, it switches to battery power in under 10 milliseconds, fast enough for most home office setups.

And it can keep going for a long time. In our testing, the S2000 ran a refrigerator for just over 24 hours on its 2,010 watt-hours of capacity, and a typical home office draws far less. That's enough to keep a desktop PC and monitor running for several hours, or a modem and router online for more than a day. Its LFP battery is rated for 6,000 cycles before dropping to 80 percent capacity, so it should outlast several lead-acid UPS batteries, and it comes with a five-year warranty.

The trade-off is that it's far pricier than a standard UPS, and at 35.7 pounds, it's not something you'll want to move often. But if you live somewhere with long outages, it's the only pick here that can keep your WiFi running all night.

The UPS you choose should come with enough outlets to accommodate all the devices you need to plug in, with some room for additional devices in the future. Pay attention to the distinction between battery-backed outlets, which offer surge protection and battery power during outages, and surge-protected-only outlets, which, as the name suggests, only offer surge protection.

Every model we write about offers surge protection as a standard feature, even on outlets that don’t offer battery power. Batteries enable a UPS to power your devices once the grid fails. That’s why it’s essential to choose a UPS with enough battery-backed outlets to support the devices you want to keep online.

More advanced UPS models typically offer more outlets (and more that are battery-backed). For example, the more affordable Amazon Basics Standby UPS 600VA has eight outlets, four of which have battery backup, while the more advanced CyberPower CP1500AVRLCD3 has 12 outlets, six of which have battery backup. In addition to AC outlets, some UPS models have USB-A or USB-C ports to connect your smartphone and other devices. These ports easily charge your devices without taking up an outlet.

It’s also important to ensure replacing the battery on the UPS you choose is straightforward and easy. This simplifies maintenance and increases the device’s lifespan. Advanced UPS models typically include battery health monitoring features, so you’ll get a heads up when a battery nears the end of its life.

On average, UPS batteries last three to five years before needing replacement, though this lifespan varies depending on usage. Automatic Voltage Regulation, or AVR, stabilizes inconsistent incoming voltage. It converts fluctuating voltage from the power source into a steady, consistent output for connected devices. This protects sensitive electronics from power irregularities without relying on the UPS battery.

As a bonus, AVR reduces wear and tear on the battery, potentially extending its lifespan. Not all models include this feature, particularly those priced on the lower end.

During an outage, a UPS inverter converts the direct current (DC) stored in its battery into the alternating current (AC) that devices expect. Pure sine wave models output a smooth wave that closely matches utility power. The CyberPower CP1500PFCLCD lists sine wave output on battery and is designed for active PFC power supplies. The APC BR1500MS2 lists sine wave output on battery with a transfer time of as little as eight seconds.

During an outage, a UPS inverter converts the direct current (DC) stored in its battery into the alternating current (AC) that devices expect. Power from the wall doesn’t just switch on and off. Its voltage rises and falls in a smooth, rounded curve called a sine wave, swinging from positive to negative and back 60 times a second.

Pure sine wave models output a smooth wave that closely matches utility power, so your devices run on battery the same way they run on the grid. Some models output a simulated sine wave instead, a stepped signal that switches between positive and negative voltage with brief rests at zero. That output works for basic electronics, but it could cause problems for more sensitive electronics, like audio equipment and desktop PCs.

Desktop PCs are the biggest concern. Most use power supplies with active power factor correction (PFC), a circuit that improves efficiency and helps the unit meet energy standards. On a simulated sine wave, some of these power supplies can shut down unexpectedly or run under extra strain. Most devices without active PFC, including modems and routers, can handle a simulated wave without trouble during a typical short outage.

For a gaming PC, workstation, or home theater system, a pure sine wave UPS is the safer bet. The CyberPower CP1500PFCLCD lists sine wave output on battery and is designed for active PFC power supplies. The APC BR1500MS2 lists sine wave output on battery with a transfer time of as little as 8 milliseconds.

Having a display on a UPS may seem like a luxury, but it’s very helpful to have some kind of indicator to give you insight into battery status. Compact and budget models, like the APC BE600M1, typically stick to a few status lights that tell you whether the unit is running on wall power or battery.

An LCD screen shows measurements such as battery charge, how much power your devices are drawing, input and output voltage, and, most importantly, estimated runtime. That last one comes in clutch during an outage, since it tells you exactly how many minutes you have to save your work and shut down.

The CyberPower CP1500PFCLCD's color screen tilts upward, so it's easier to read when the UPS sits on the floor under your desk, and the APC BR1500MS2 keeps a running count of the power events it has handled. And if your UPS lives in a bedroom, check whether you can dim or turn off the backlight. A glowing screen is useful during an outage, but less so at 2 a.m. when you’re trying to sleep.

A cable that’s at least five feet long offers greater flexibility in terms of where you place your UPS. A five-foot-long cable reaches wall outlets that are farther away and positions the UPS conveniently for your devices. You’ll have the freedom to place the UPS in the best spot for your setup, such as under a desk or in a server rack. Remember, a short cable potentially limits where you place the UPS, so it’s always a good idea to go longer, not shorter.

UPS models that support management software give you greater control over the UPS from a phone or computer to remotely shut down connected devices, and some support “graceful shutdown,” which automatically shuts down connected equipment if you’re unable to do it when the connected devices reach a predetermined power level.

Other features worth considering include an LCD display to monitor a UPS’s status, expandable battery capacity, and an audible alarm during power disturbances.

Setting up a UPS is straightforward: Simply plug the UPS into a wall outlet and connect your devices to the UPS. This plug-and-play simplicity means a UPS device is great for anyone, no matter their level of technical know-how. But be aware of the following safety guidelines before powering on a UPS in your home office.

Companies advise against connecting devices like copiers, laser printers, or space heaters to a UPS, as these can overload the device. Instead, use a separate surge protector.

Additionally, never plug a UPS into a surge protector or vice versa. It’s also important to avoid plugging a UPS into an extension cord because this can potentially overload the cord and create a fire hazard. It’s recommended to always plug your UPS directly into a grounded wall outlet. Doing so will ensure your UPS operates safely while providing the best possible protection for your devices.

Finding the right UPS battery backup largely comes down to the total wattage you need to keep your computer up and running while you save and shut down. Speaking broadly, we'd tell you that most home office setups with a desktop PC, monitor, modem, and router should look for a UPS around 600 to 1500 volt-amperes (VA).

To get a more accurate idea of what you specifically need, add up the wattage of all your connected devices, then look for a backup that can handle 120 to 130 percent of that load. That will give you enough time to shut down safely with some wiggle room in case you need to finish a task (or have something urgent come up before you can finish up).

Every system is different, but we'd expect a UPS in the 1000 to 1500VA range to keep your desktop and monitor running for about 15 minutes, which should be long enough to save and safely shut down. A smaller model can probably keep laptop-based setup for a similar amount of time, or power a modem and router for 30 to 45 minutes.

These are all broad estimates, though, and will vary based on what specific gear you're using. We recommend calculating your own power needs to figure out exactly how much time you'll have to shut down in the event of an emergency.

Yes, a UPS backup easily powers a router and modem, and this is one of the most common uses for a small unit. This type of hardware usually consumes only about 10 to 30 watts combined, which is relatively low when compared to computers or TVs. Because of this low draw, even a compact unit would be able to keep your internet running for 30 minutes or more during a power outage.

Brandon Russell is a freelance writer covering gear and technology. He started his journey as a news writer at a small newspaper and later began reviewing smartphones, movies, and video games. In his free time, he enjoys the slower, more intentional experience of using a 35mm film camera and making short videos about movies he grew up watching.

#6253. New Congress will still be filled with losers

The Capitol Dome is illuminated before dawn on Oct. 13. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call)

OPINION — Once again, the next Congress is going to be filled with losers.

This is not a personal judgment about their character or personality, but a simple recognition that many members have lost races before getting elected. And the incoming class is no different.

I’ve written many versions of this column for more than a decade, and yet the lesson always seems to get lost, no pun intended. Parties routinely attack candidates who enter a race with losses on their record. And, of course, it happened this cycle as well.

“We beat him once. We’ll beat him again,” National Republican Senatorial Committee Chairman Tim Scott declared when Democratic former Sen. Sherrod Brown announced his challenge to appointed GOP Sen. Jon Husted in the summer of 2025.

“Ohioans gladly sent him packing last year, and they’ll not hesitate to toss him aside again,” said a Republican strategist.

Brown lost reelection to Republican Bernie Moreno in 2024 but came back to defeat Husted for the state’s other Senate seat. And Brown is far from the only candidate to avenge a loss with an electoral victory last week.

The fact of the matter is that losing a race doesn’t have to be the end of a political career. Losses can lay the foundation for future success by building name ID or a fundraising network. Or sometimes it takes a change in the political environment or change in circumstances, such as running for an open seat instead of challenging an incumbent.

In addition to Brown, there are more than a dozen losers coming into the next Congress:

In some instances, though, the losses are piling up.

Republican Rep. John James of Michigan now has three statewide losses on his record. He lost Senate contests in 2018 (taking 46 percent of the vote) and 2020 (48 percent) and came up short in his bid for governor this year (44 percent).

Republican former Sen. John E. Sununu of New Hampshire, who lost reelection in 2008 to Democrat Jeanne Shaheen, fell in his comeback attempt for the open seat last week.

But they could take heart from another repeat loser. Charlie Crist, a former Florida governor and congressman, has had a handful of high-profile losses over the years, including for Senate and two gubernatorial comeback bids. He was just elected mayor of St. Petersburg.

So even though I know it’s a futile request, let’s have a bipartisan agreement not to attack candidates for past losses, because losing doesn’t mean they can’t later pull off a win.

#6252. Don’t Visit Ko Lipe

After 19 years, I finally went back to Ko Lipe, the Thai island I spent close to a month on in 2006. Back then, it was one of those super off-the-beaten-path destinations that few but the most intrepid travelers visited, where electricity only ran a few hours a day, basic bungalows right on the beach cost something like $2 USD, and there really was a last boat for the season.

There was much to do here but that was the point. You hung out on the beach, read a book, went snorkeling, went back to the beach, drank beers at the one beach bar on the island, rotated meals between the five restaurants there, and went to bed early.

It was paradise – and a place a lot of people got stuck. Days easily turned into weeks here.

If you asked me what the highlight of all my travels was, I would be the time I spent on Ko Lipe. I made incredible friends, lounged around, got to know the locals, learned a bit of Thai, and, overall, lived that idyllic backpacker life we all dream about.

Over the years, I’ve avoided going back to Ko Lipe because the memory of my time there is so strong that I didn’t want to ruin it. Any re-visit would simply be trying to recreated a magic that couldn’t be recreated because the people that it special wouldn’t be there. I’d be chasing travel ghosts. And, since I know my sleepy paradise has been developed greatly over the years, I was also too afraid seeing that would make me sad.

Tourism in Thailand tends toward the unsustainable. No island really develops in a good way. It’s all build, build, build.

And I didn’t want to see my Ko Lipe like that.

But as I was planning my recent trip through Southeast Asia, returning to Ko Lipe made sense. I was heading down the Indian Ocean side of Thailand on my way into Malaysia and I’d pass by it.

And, since I was looking for a lively place for New Year’s Eve, it seemed liked the best choice. I knew there would be travelers there and there were no other nearby islands that would work, especially since Ko Lipe has a boat to Langkawi, which was my next stop.

And I’m sad to report that Ko Lipe took the Ko Phi Phi model of tourism and is now extremely overdeveloped.

Most of the island is now paved over, the old dirt footpaths having become concrete for the cars and construction trucks. Swaths of palm trees are now the sites of high-end resorts with pools (on an island with no natural water supply). Construction of more resorts continues at a fast pace. The coral around the island is dying, a victim of all the boats, anchors, pollution, and overfishing. Beaches are now lined with boats, their exhaust spilling into the ocean, leaving a shiny film you can see as you swim. And the restaurants cater to tourists looking for bad Western food, not great Thai cuisine.

The island’s boom has displaced many locals, who were forced to sell to mainland developers, and much of the island’s workforce is now from the mainland. They see little of the benefits this tourism boom.

So lies Ko Lipe, another victim of Thailand’s all too common overdevelopment and exploitation of limited resources.

I met lots of people there who loved the island. If it’s your first time, I can see why you would love it. After all, the area is postcard perfect, the water is perfectly an azure blue, the sand is a beautiful white, and since you’re surrounded by a national park, a lot of tours take you to some secluded islands.

And, in comparison to Ko Phi Phi, Krabi, or Phuket, it is less developed so I can’t fault someone stepping here for the first time going “wow!”

But, as I reflect on the island and its overdevelopment, I have come to the same conclusion I have about Ko Phi Phi: people shouldn’t visit.

I’m not against growth, but I’m against this kind of growth. It’s not sustainably managed and going there will only tax the island’s limited resources even further. You can’t put the genie back in the bottle and no local is going to say “sure, I’ll stay broke so you can an idealized vision of the world.”

And, with so many other islands to visit that are well managed (Ko Lanta, Ko Jum, and Ko Mook, to name three nearby), I think you should skip Ko Lipe.

A visit there will only make things worse.

It pains me to say that, because it was such a beautiful place, and my original visit had a huge impact on my life. But if we’re going to be good stewards and travelers, sometimes you just have to say enough is enough.

And Ko Lipe is a place where enough is enough.

Go somewhere else that is better managed.

Riding elephants in Thailand went away when consumers became more conscious of it. Eco lodges got big because of consumers. Overtourism is talked about by consumers as much as it is by locals.

Maybe if enough people start to do something, Ko Lipe will change.

But, at the very least, by not going you are at least no contributing to the problem.

Fossil teeth from two caves in southern China are revealing that at least two lineages of early humans were present in the region around 184,000 years ago.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Homo erectus was adaptable enough to live in rainforests in what is now southern China and may have lived alongside Denisovans there, two new studies hint.

The research is based on the incredibly rare findings of nine fossil teeth from ancient humans — eight from H. erectus and one from a mystery human in the genus Homo. The teeth reveal that H. erectus lived in China much more recently than previously thought and that this population likely devoured tropical food found there.

"I think it's exciting because it means that there are two hominin populations occupying these rainforest conditions there at the same time," study first author Frido Welker, a molecular palaeoanthropologist at the University of Copenhagen in Denmark, told Live Science.

H. erectus is generally seen as the first human species to venture out of Africa, after evolving about 2 million years ago. It spread through eastern Eurasia, reaching China and Indonesia between about 1.6 million and 1.8 million years ago. It is one of the longest-surviving hominin species, and the last known record of it is from 108,000 years ago in river flood plains in Java, Indonesia. However, there was no physical evidence of H. erectus being on the Asian mainland more recently than 400,000 years ago.

But in two caves in Guangxi province in southern China, researchers have found thousands of mammalian fossils, accumulated there by porcupines that scavenged for and collected bones. The Baxian and Naxian caves are about 9 miles (15 kilometers) apart, sitting in a karst landscape of limestone formations that are prone to dissolving to create caves that would have offered crucial shelter for H. erectus.

The entrance to Naxian Cave, as seen by a drone, is the tall and wide opening of a cave that goes back around 330 feet (100 meters) to a fossil chamber.

Researchers found the nine human teeth among more than 18,000 fossils, including from apes, elephants, rhinoceroses and other ancient hoofed animals, Welker and his colleagues reported in a study published Wednesday (Nov. 18) in the journal Nature.

Radiometric dating of the fossils and surrounding sediments by methods including assessing the decay of uranium, pins them to about 324,000 to 184,000 years ago. Eight of the teeth have physical features reminiscent of H. erectus, but the ninth is more elusive. It looks distinct from H. erectus, Neanderthals and modern humans, Welker said.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Welker's team took samples from five teeth ‪—‬ four from the group that seemed to be H. erectus and one from the mysterious tooth ‪—‬ to see which ancient proteins were present, since DNA tends to degrade more easily than the proteins in an organism. (The study of these proteins is known as proteomics.)

The four similar ones had protein signatures that matched what had been seen before in H. erectus.

"The morphology is nicely confirmed by the proteomics," Welker told Live Science. Three of these teeth were from males, and the other was from a female, which the team was able to determine based on the presence or absence of amelogenin-Y, a protein coded for only by the Y chromosome.

Researchers investigating two caves in China have found nine human teeth, eight of which have been confidently identified as belonging to Homo erectus.

However, some parts of the protein signatures differed from what had been seen in other H. erectus remains in China, so the new specimens may be from a previously unknown H. erectus population that perhaps had a slightly different genetic makeup, Welker said.

The finding that H. erectus was present in mainland Asia until at least 184,000 years ago — rather than 400,000 years ago — fills a geographical and chronological gap, helping to explain how H. erectus was on Java 108,000 years ago.

"This brings the history of H. erectus in East Asia closer in age to the late Javanese examples, raising the possibility that these populations were connected through land bridges at times of lowered sea level," Chris Stringer, a paleoanthropologist at the Natural History Museum in London who was not involved in the research, told Live Science in an email.

John Hawks, an anthropologist at the University of Wisconsin-Madison who wasn't involved in the study, previously believed that specimens from the past 400,000 years or so flagged as H. erectus were actually Denisovans ‪—‬ ancient humans who lived in Asia, disappeared around 30,000 years ago and belonged to the Homo longi lineage. But he told Live Science that the new morphological and protein findings provide convincing evidence that H. erectus did survive until relatively recently in some places.

The fifth analyzed tooth, known as PA1796, remains mysterious. The protein analysis revealed it was from a male, but it didn't show a recognizable signature in the protein sequence data. Therefore, Welker's team suggested it could be from another hominin species that was present in the region at the same time.

Welker didn’t want to speculate about which species it might be, but said: "Sequence-wise it doesn't have this Homo erectus substitution and morphologically, it doesn't look like an erectus tooth."

The tooth could be from a previously unknown human species, but many experts suspect it is from a Denisovan.

"With some of the new material probably dating to less than 200,000 years old, this already brings it close in age to known or putative Homo longi/Denisovan samples in southern China and Laos, implying potentially long overlaps between these species," Stringer said. "Tooth PA1796 could represent a longi/Denisovan, though it is relatively small in size, and relevant comparative data for longi/Denisovans is sparse."

The entrance to China's Naxian Cave, which has a small opening and goes back around 164 feet (50 m) to a fossil chamber.

Recent research suggests there was interbreeding between the H. erectus and Denisovan lineages, and the new evidence increases the likelihood that this happened, at least occasionally, Stringer said.

Any firm conclusions of who the tooth is from will have to wait for further finds of similar teeth elsewhere, Welker said.

Hawks agreed that the tooth is most likely from a Denisovan, perhaps from a divergent branch for which we don't have protein data. But it could also be from a novel H. erectus population or someone from the same population as the other teeth who, for developmental or genetic reasons, wasn't typical. "I would have liked to see additional comparisons in the paper to more Denisovan teeth," Hawks said.

In another paper, also published Nov. 18 in the journal Nature, Kira Westaway, a geochronologist at Macquarie University in Sydney, and her colleagues examined trace elements in the same teeth, as well as in animal teeth from the caves, to see what they revealed about the hominins' diet and local habitat.

Their analysis indicated that this H. erectus population found plants and animals to eat in tropical, rainforest-like ecosystems. Previously, it was thought that only our own species, Homo sapiens, was able to adapt to this type of environment.

"Rather than being confined to open woodland and grassland environments, H. erectus was considerably more ecologically adaptable than many of us have assumed," Stringer said.

"Being adaptable and being flexible are not traits that we associate with ancient human species — these are traits that we associate with H. sapiens," Westaway told Live Science. "Suddenly we're seeing H. erectus being able to survive in environments that we didn't think they could possibly survive in."

And given the mysterious tooth, it is possible that two different early human populations were this adaptable, said Welker, who was a co-author of the study.

A view from Naxian Cave in China, where Homo erectus teeth were found.

Westaway and her colleagues also looked at levels of the element strontium in the teeth, which can shed light on where someone grew up based on the unique strontium levels in water and foods they consumed as children. The team matched these strontium levels to another karst landscape about 200 miles (320 km) away, in the Red River valley of northern Vietnam.

"It looks like H. erectus moved across large areas, traversing this karst landscape in the rainforests" ‪—‬ a finding that adds to our understanding of these ancient humans, Westaway said.

It's absurd that people often think of H. erectus as an unsuccessful species, she added. "We think they were the first to leave Africa, the first to use fire. It blows my mind because they survived six times longer than H. sapiens has survived so far, so I don't see them as unsuccessful."

Hawks' big question, however, is linked to modern humans, who were in the Chinese region from at least 45,000 years ago.

"Denisovan DNA is present in the peoples of Island Southeast Asia, so, modern humans must have run into Denisovans at some point," he said. "If H. erectus was enduring in the same area at the same time, might H. sapiens also have encountered late H. erectus?"

#6250. The Best Aluminum Luggage for Travelers, From Iconic Rimowa Suitcases to Sleek Tumi Trunks

The first time I traveled with an aluminum suitcase, I emerged into the airport with a whole new energy. There’s an undeniable allure to rolling through a terminal with a gleaming statement piece, shimmering as it does against a sea of boring black suitcases. There’s no way to travel more smugly.

Commerce writer Charley Ward testing Rimowa's iconic aluminum carry-on in Mallorca

But while the style is an undeniable draw, beyond the immediate hit of glamour, aluminum luggage offers some practical perks too. It offers greater structural protection than polycarbonate and soft-shell options—you can’t really argue with that, given it’s the type of material they make planes out of. And these durable suitcases are typically fitted with secure latch locking mechanisms over temperamental zippers, with steel corners and frames designed to comfortably absorb bumps, drops, and scrapes on the go.

Investing in high-end aluminum luggage is a serious price commitment—especially when considering that there are plenty of excellent soft-sided and hard-shell suitcases on the market. It’s why putting these more expensive suitcases through their paces in real-world scenarios is essential for our testing.

Our editors and contributors took the market's leading aluminum suitcases with us near and far, from long weekends in Milan and Mallorca to extended three-week international journeys, considering wheel smoothness, internal compression systems, weight-to-capacity ratios, and overall durability. Below, the select few of our editors’ favorite aluminum suitcase to travel with for every type of trip.

Carl Friedrik has built a cult following across the globe for its elevated, leather-trimmed luggage. Its venture into all-aluminum suitcases is nothing short of exceptional, with all the same careful design details we know and love from its original Carry-On. This new iteration retains the brand’s signature understated ridged design, super-secure dual lock (no zips to bust here), steel-reinforced corners, leather detailing, and smooth, 360-degree spinner wheels.

I packed comfortably for three nights in Milan and Paris: a couple of outfit changes, pajamas, gym clothes, a toiletry bag, and a spare pair of shoes. For warmer destinations where you'd prioritize packing lighter fabrics, you could likely stretch this to four or five- days’ worth of clothing. I also lent the suitcase to a colleague for a trip to Lisbon, who managed five-days’ worth of packing with ease—and said she could have got in more. Ultimately, capacity will depend on how heavy a packer you are, but it’s ideal for a long weekend during the winter at minimum.

I took this suitcase on a long weekend to Mallorca and immediately understood the hype. While the aesthetics are the real draw here, this hard-shell aluminum carry-on doesn’t scrimp on technical details, gliding smoothly across airport floors and cobbled streets alike, thanks to buttery-smooth wheels and a sturdy handle. What are the benefits of aluminum luggage?

Aluminum luggage offers superior durability and protection compared to fabric or plastic alternatives. Its rigid, crush-proof shell and heavy-duty frame safeguard fragile contents against rough handling and impact during transit. Aluminum suitcases come finished with latches instead of vulnerable zippers, creating an airtight, water-resistant seal that deters theft. Aluminum is built to last a lifetime, developing a distinctive, travel-worn patina over time rather than tearing or cracking. Then there’s that effortlessly sleek aesthetic at the airport, which is another fun perk.

Our editors have personally tested a wide range of bags from leading luggage brands, carefully selecting their favorites based on function, innovation, and design. Each suitcase was thoroughly tested in-office by our editors before being taken on trips by members of the wider team for real-world use. During testing, we assess overall build quality, wheel performance, TSA-approved locks, design features such as external pockets and laptop compartments, and overall value. Weight, size, usability, and visual appeal are also carefully considered.
