#6204. Why This It-Girl Ski Brand Is My Go-To Every Single Winter

If there’s one thing I take almost as seriously as chasing some good snow, it’s having the right wardrobe to go with it. I’m a lifelong snowboarder, a fairly recent convert to skiing, and someone who has spent plenty of winters bouncing between mountains on the east coast and out west. I’ve learned that the best of the best ski gear needs to do a lot more than look good in a lodge photo. It has to hold up through long lift rides, changing conditions, unexpected snowfall, and the occasional unglamorous tumble.

But that doesn’t mean style needs to take a backseat. In fact, I’d argue that the two should go hand in hand. That's a big part of why the popular ski brand, Halfdays, first caught my attention three years ago—and why I keep coming back season after season. Founded in 2020 by former Olympic freestyle aerial skier Kiley McKinnon and Ariana Ferweda, Halfdays came onto the ski scene with a refreshing take: women's ski apparel that actually considers women. Not just smaller versions of men’s gear or the usual boxy, so-called unisex silhouettes, but (finally) thoughtfully designed outerwear that takes fit, function, and fashion all very seriously.

Commerce writer Jessica Chapel is wearing the Halfdays Ashton jacket and Alessandra pant in Stowe, Vermont

The outdoor apparel industry has come a long way, but finding technical pieces that feel just as considered aesthetically as they are functional on the mountain can still be a bit of a treasure hunt. So as someone who has accumulated her fair share of ski and snowboard gear over the years, I immediately fell in love with the brand’s mission, and eventually, the gear itself.

While I’ve come to adore its ski suits, bibs, and winter jackets, Halfdays' assortment has expanded beyond the big-ticket ski uniform. The brand offers sweat-wicking baselayers, cozy fleeces, everyday outdoor staples, and chic accessories that make sense well beyond your stay at a ski resort. My favorite pieces from Halfdays keep me feeling comfortable and put together on harsh winter days in New York City too, from knit headbands that cover my ears to winter leggings and warm socks that aren’t too thick.

Of course, Halfdays isn’t the same brand it was when I first discovered it. What began as a ski-focused label has evolved into an outdoor brand with spring and summer collections spanning hiking, running, and more warm-weather pursuits. Its arrival at major retailers like Nordstrom, REI, and Backcountry, the opening of its Denver flagship (along with plenty of other storefronts), and a string of collaborations have helped solidify it as a functional brand for every outdoor adventurer.

Chapel is wearing the Parks Projects x Halfdays set on the slopes in Park City, Utah

That said, the brand has been having some fun with its fashion credentials, most recently teaming up with Gigi Hadid’s Guest in Residence on an eight-piece winter capsule. The result is a nostalgic take on mountainwear, bringing Guest in Residence’s signature knitwear looks to Halfdays' mountain-ready vibes, with playful retro details that feel just as at home at après-ski as they do on the slopes.

On the performance side, though, I’m excited about the brand’s newest launch: Halfdays has officially joined forces with Gore-Tex for its most technical outerwear collection yet. From down jackets and shells to bibs and mittens, the colorful collection brings together trusted waterproof, windproof, and breathable technology with the fit and design that initially made me fall for Halfdays in the first place.

As another winter of snow chasing commences, I’m giving my cold-weather wardrobe yet another Halfdays refresh. Below, my tried-and-true ski season favorites from Halfdays, along with a few winter staples I’ve got my eye on.

The Lawrence jacket is designed with Primaloft insulation, keeping you warm on the coldest winter days. It features underarm vents and an exterior chest pocket with an attached phone leash. Plus, the hood is adjustable, so you’ll get a perfect fit over your helmet every time. The jacket is best for bluebird days given its cropped length, but it’s also available in a longer version too.

I like to pair the Lawrence jacket with these matching shell pants. With a slim fit, an adjustable waistband, a water-resistant exterior, and zippered hems for snow boots, this pair is just as practical as it is stylish. Pro tip: Try these bad boys on with a pair of your favorite winter leggings underneath before hitting the mountain, just so you know that you’ll be comfortable and warm all day long.

Don’t underestimate the importance of a solid baselayer. The Johnson top features mesh underarms and a sweat-wicking finish, so you don’t have to worry about overheating in your ski gear. The long-sleeve layer also has a silicon grip on the inside hem, preventing it from sliding up as you move.

Pair the Johnson top with these leggings for a stylish, mountain-ready set. They’re sweat-wicking and feature a layer of mesh on the calves for added breathability. Even better, they’re versatile enough to wear off the mountain too, whether you’re shopping at a holiday market or strolling through the park.

Made with 100% merino wool, this chic Jacquard headband will keep your head and ears warm on the slopes—and it tastefully reps the brand too. I have (and love) it in the color Blue Fog, but it’s also available in black and red.

I’m obsessed with these Gore-Tex x Halfdays mittens. Along with the insulated, breathable, and waterproof design, there’s also a leather palm construction for added grip and durability.

I can’t wait to put this three-layer shell jacket to the test on my trip to Stowe, Vermont, this December. It has all the classic Gore-Tex technologies that make the collaboration so enticing in the first place: engineered with durable water- and wind-proof material, and breathable protection without added insulation.

For a matching set, grab this three-layer shell bib constructed with the same Gore-Tex build. With adjustable shoulder straps, a drop-seat construction, thigh vents, and gusseted hems, you’ll be covered and ready for anything, from head to toe.

Ah, one of the early Halfday classics. The tried-and-true Ashton jacket does it all, from ski trips to cabin getaways. With an adjustable (and removable) belt buckle enclosure, a helmet hood, and its many pockets for your phone and ski pass, it offers every bit of function you need for a full day on the mountain.

For those who favor a puffy yet packable one-piece, the Murphy ski suit is another one of Halfdays' original bestsellers. I own this bad boy in red, and wear it when I need extra warmth on the mountain. One thing to note: I’m 5'3", and it’s just a bit long on my legs when I’m not in snow boots—but it’s not very often that I wear the suit without them.

While I haven’t shopped the new Guest in Residence collection yet, I’m eyeing this chic ski sweater that looks straight out of a ’70s après-ski scene. I can already picture myself wearing it post-slopes, sipping on a spiked cider at the ski lodge.

For another vintage-inspired piece from the Guest in Residence collection, this cable knit inspired down jacket is all about staying warm in style. (And I’ve already added it to my cart.)

Get your hands on one of the Parks Project x Halfdays ski jackets while you still can. This gorgeous print is inspired by the Rocky Mountains—and I always receive compliments from other shredders when I wear it out on the slopes. Not to mention, it keeps me warm and comfy while doing so!

Situated halfway between San Francisco and the Oregon border, California's Mendocino Coast has managed to remain a relatively hidden gem, of sorts. While it's certainly not a secret, its remote location has kept it from getting overrun with tourists — but new direct flights and millions of dollars in roadwork funding are making it more accessible than ever. And that's just one reason the coastal town of Mendocino made our list of top destinations to visit in 2027.

Nestled between rugged cliffs, redwood forests and rich wine terroirs, Mendocino has it all. No matter what you get up to out here — and there’s more to do than you might expect — it’s virtually impossible not to feel your blood pressure drop. The area’s relaxed pace of life is infectious, and during a recent two-day trip, this type-A traveler found herself hopping on the slow travel train.

From how to get there and where to stay to the best things to do and eat, here’s how to spend a long weekend (or longer!) on the Mendocino Coast. I dare you not to fall in love.

Travelers have several airports to choose from when flying to Mendocino.

The closest, albeit smallest, option is Charles M. Schulz–Sonoma County Airport (STS), which puts you only a two-to-three-hour drive from Mendocino. Alaska Airlines, Delta and Southwest have all launched new routes to STS this year from Austin, Phoenix, Salt Lake City and more.

You’ll have more options if you fly into San Francisco International Airport (SFO), Oakland San Francisco Bay Airport (OAK) or Sacramento International Airport (SAC). All are roughly the same distance from Mendocino — three to four hours depending on traffic — and offer plenty of direct flights from around the country through various airlines. A local I spoke to recommended SAC, saying that the drive is less stressful because it doesn’t go through a city.

No matter where your flight lands, you’ll need to rent a car. The drive can be tiring, especially as the roads get windier approaching the coast. Thankfully, there are plenty of wineries and cideries along the way where you can stop for a restroom break (and maybe a drink or two, if you’re not the driver).

One of the many facets of Mendocino’s appeal is the charming, walkable downtown — complete with views of Mendocino Bay.

You’ll find no shortage of souvenirs here, from bookshops and toy stores to clothing and home decor. Art lovers will enjoy perusing the handful of galleries. Coffeeshops, bakeries and chocolate shops abound, so you needn't worry about finding caffeine or snacks to sustain you during your wanderings.

If you wear jewelry (or are in the market for a unique gift that will fit in your suitcase), you won’t want to miss Mendocino Sandpiper, which offers a wide variety of work by local artists.

And that’s just the town of Mendocino. Its slightly larger neighbor, Fort Bragg, located about a 15-minute drive north along the coast, has even more boutiques to browse.

Related: 9 tertiary cities in the US that are both charming and affordable

You will need a car to get around the Mendocino Coast area, but you won’t have to spend much time in the car once you arrive. That’s because the area’s best outdoors activities are within easy reach of Mendocino and Fort Bragg.

The expansive Mendocino Coast Botanical Gardens were a highlight for me, and would probably be stunning in the spring and summer when most of the flowers are in bloom.

Mendocino Headlands State Park is literally steps from downtown, and there are several other state parks under 20 minutes away, including Jug Handle State Natural Reserve and Russian Gulch State Park. To commune with the area’s famous redwoods, head to Otis R. Johnson Wilderness Park, a glorious corner of green tucked away on the edge of Fort Bragg. Or head to MacKerricher State Park for a stroll along a black-sand beach and views of the aptly named Seal Rocks.

February to March is peak whale-watching season due to the gray whale migration, but this area gets visits from various whale species year-round, so keep your eyes peeled. I didn’t spot any whales, but I did see some seals and sea lions bobbing in the waves, as well as flocks of pelicans and other waterbirds.

You may also hear about a place called Glass Beach, which served as a community garbage dump at the beginning of the 20th century; over several decades, the waves tumbled some of the debris into colorful sea glass. Locals warned me that most of the glass is gone now, snatched up by tourists over the years. You’re better off going to the International Sea Glass Museum in Fort Bragg — with over 3,000 pieces on display, it boasts the world’s largest permanent sea glass exhibit.

Related: 7 warm-weather expedition cruises that will wow nature and adventure lovers

Both Mendocino and Fort Bragg have surprisingly varied food scenes, from the casual organic Good Life Cafe & Bakery and elevated all-vegan Fog Eater to the Irish-inspired Patterson’s Pub and Asian fusion Gnar Bar. And foodies won’t want to miss the local farmers’ markets, held on summer Fridays in Mendocino and Wednesdays year-round in Fort Bragg.

However, the main draws for foodies are, of course, the seafood — I heard Fort Bragg’s Sea Pals described as “the best fish ‘n’ chips outside of the U.K.” — and the thriving beverage scene.

Oenophiles will want to take the Highway 128 Wine Road to sample the fruits of the nearby Anderson Valley and Yorkville Highlands wine regions. But you’ll get plenty of opportunities to sample local wines in town as well. My hotel even offered a lobby wine machine where you can get wine samples with the press a button and tap of a keycard.

If wine isn’t your thing, don’t worry, there are plenty more local beverages to try. Gowan’s Cider Garden, which brews both alcoholic and non-alcoholic varieties, bills itself as California's first-ever cider tasting orchard. Meanwhile, the zero-waste, solar-powered North Coast Brewing Co. has been brewing unique beers (and winning awards for them) since 1988.

Related: The best credit cards for dining

The Mendocino Coast is also home to some fascinating history, and it has an array of museums and other attractions where visitors can learn more.

Fort Bragg’s Guest House Museum is a great starting point to learn about local history, from the logging industry to the Great 1906 Earthquake. Or visit during Labor Day weekend to experience lumberjack games at the annual Paul Bunyan Days festival.

If you have young travelers in tow, check out Fort Bragg’s Noyo Center for Marine Science, which offers interactive exhibits like tide pools and a full orca skeleton. Or climb to the top of a lighthouse and see a real Fresnel lens at either Point Cabrillo Light Station State Historic Park or the 156-year-old Point Arena Lighthouse.

Train enthusiasts won’t want to miss the historic Skunk Train, which started carrying timber in the late 1800s and now carries passengers through scenic redwood forests. While the train’s traditional 35-mile route has a reputation for jaw-dropping scenery, a tunnel collapse in recent years has shortened the route to a sliver of its former glory. However, I still enjoyed the nostalgic vibes of the Redwood Presidential Class, which made me feel like I had been dropped into one of my favorite Agatha Christie murder mysteries.

Related: The world's most scenic train rides

The Mendocino Coast has been leaning into slow and wellness travel, and for obvious reasons. With ancient redwoods on one side and windswept cliffs on the other — and blessedly few tourists crowding the trails — the landscape itself is therapeutic.

If you want something more structured, there are plenty of wellness activities if you know where to look. Many are offered by locals hotels but open to the public.

A few examples include yoga classes at Stanford Inn by the Sea, redwood hot tub and sauna sessions at Sweet Water Inn & Spa, sound healing in a geodesic dome at Mendocino Grove, and guided shinrin-yoku (forest bathing) walks at Brewery Gulch Inn & Spa.

Related: 9 wellness trends and where to experience them

Summer is Mendocino’s most popular season. It will also be the most expensive and busiest time to go — though I don’t expect the area to get too packed at any time of year, given its remoteness.

For adventure seekers looking to make the most of the area’s hiking, water sports and more, it’s probably worth planning your trip in summer for longer days and maximum sunshine. And with average highs topping out in the mid-70s Fahrenheit, Mendo could make a nice coolcation spot.

However, you can save money and all but guarantee a quiet vacation by traveling in the shoulder seasons from mid-October to November and April to early June. During these times, you can still expect warm enough weather for outdoor exploits, though temperatures will drop at night and more frequent rains may wash out hiking trails occasionally.

The hotel scene in Mendocino is characterized by quiet luxury. Its neighbor, Fort Bragg, has more variety and more budget-friendly options.

I spent three nights in the new Hill House at Trailborn Mendocino, a half-century-old property that was recently renovated before joining the Trailborn nature lodge collection and Marriott Bonvoy program. Other points options include Holiday Inn Express Fort Bragg by IHG and Baymont by Wyndham Fort Bragg.

If, like me, you love a good independent or boutique hotel, Mendocino is full of them. For instance, you could book a seaside cottage at Agate Cove Inn through Amex Travel or Capital One Travel, earning 5 points per dollar with your or 10 miles per dollar with your Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card, respectively.

Or consider staying at SCP Mendocino Inn and Farm, a 19th-century manor turned B&B where guests can enjoy complimentary breakfast sourced from the onsite farm. Even better, you can redeem your points for more than 1 cent apiece via Chase Points Boost.

Overall, one of the things I loved most about the Mendocino Coast was its manageable size. From the downtown areas to the state parks, everything I visited was small but high-quality.

So instead of running around a city trying to cram in as much as possible, you can spend a leisurely weekend (or longer) exploring charming boutiques, quirky museums, local dining or natural wonders. You won’t run out of things to do, but the close proximity between attractions and “island time” mentality will help you savor the activities you choose.

That’s what slow travel is all about, right?

#6201. Air India Cuts Up To Five Hours From New York Flights By Flying Over Iraq

Air India has eliminated fuel stops in Rome on its flights from Delhi and Mumbai to New York, cutting some journeys by five hours. The surprising key to restoring nonstop service was not Russian airspace, but the reopening of a shorter corridor over Iraq.

Air India has restored nonstop service on all four of its routes linking Delhi and Mumbai with New York JFK and Newark.

Flights that had taken approximately 22 hours with a technical stop in Rome are once again operating in about 17 hours.

The Delhi flights are operated with Airbus A350-900 aircraft featuring business class suites, premium economy, and economy class. The Mumbai routes use refurbished Boeing 777-300ERs with first class, business class, premium economy, and economy class.

Removing five hours from an already very long journey represents the difference between a difficult nonstop flight and a 22-hour saga involving an annoying fuel stop.

Pakistan closed its airspace to Indian-operated aircraft, eliminating the most direct westbound corridor from India toward Europe and North America.

The conflict involving Iran then created further restrictions across the Middle East. Air India was forced to operate a much longer route through Jordan and Egypt before continuing across Europe and the Atlantic. That routing pushed the limits of what the aircraft could operate with a commercially useful payload. Air India consequently added a technical stop in Rome to refuel before continuing to New York.

The reopening of Iraqi airspace changed the calculation. Air India can now fly a shorter route across Iraq and Turkey before continuing through Europe and across the Atlantic.

The airline says this has reduced total journey time by as much as five hours. Additionally, the shorter route will reduce fuel consumption by approximately 10% and also ease crew scheduling pressures associated with flight-duty limits. Considering the cost of operating a fully loaded Airbus A350 or Boeing 777 for several additional hours, this is a substantial operational improvement for Air India as well as a welcome one for passengers.

Air India remains permitted to use Russian airspace and has done so on certain North American routes, particularly services connecting India with the West Coast of the United States.

That has given Air India an advantage over U.S. and European airlines that avoid or are prohibited from using Russian airspace. But it would be incorrect to assume that Air India routinely flies over Russia when traveling between India and New York.

The available flight-tracking data suggests otherwise.

Recorded routes displayed by FlightPaths.com for Delhi–JFK show no use of Russian airspace in its sample of 20 flights. Among seven recorded Mumbai–JFK flights, just one crossed Russia. The pattern is even clearer in the opposite direction. Russia did not appear in the displayed samples of 20 JFK–Delhi flights or 10 JFK–Mumbai flights.

(Those samples are not a comprehensive record of every Air India flight, and routings can change based on winds, restrictions, and operational requirements. But they demonstrate that Russian airspace is not the normal solution for Air India’s New York service).

These flights generally travel westward through the Middle East and Europe, which why access to Iraqi airspace has such a large effect.

Air India has restored nonstop flights from Delhi and Mumbai to New York JFK and Newark, cutting journey times by as much as five hours.

The change was made possible by renewed access to Iraqi airspace, not by shifting these flights over Russia. Although Air India uses Russian airspace on some routes, flight-tracking data indicates that it is not routinely used for New York service.

A 17-hour flight remains very long, but it is much better than a 22-hour journey with an unwanted fuel stop in Rome. For passengers traveling between India and the New York area, this is a genuine and substantial improvement…and ironically might allow Air India to charge a higher premium for its nonstop service, despite the fuel and labor savings this shorter flight time will produce.

#6200. What’s Your Airport Dwell Time? A Metric Businesses Think A Lot About

Dwell time, simply, is how long you spend in an airport, or airport space, before a flight. For most people, it’s not something they’ve ever actively really thought about.

For businesses in air travel and airports, like lounge operators, credit card companies or airlines, it’s one of the main things they think about. So what’s yours and what does it say about you?

Well, a lot. More importantly, the tracking of that dwell time has contributed to quite a lot of innovation in lounges and airports, with hopefully much more to come.

Build it and they will come. Who knew Kevin Costner knew so much about lounges?! In truth, if someone builds a lounge, everyone will come and ensuring it’s a good experience is an art form requiring math. Crowds can be hard to predict and most lounges are “too” full these days.

Knowing the average dwell time of a customer, and even a specific customer profile is one of the best tools lounges have to predict the flows of customers, including how much they’ll need to stock in food and drinks and everything else during peak times.

Even outside of lounges, knowing how long an air traveler spends in the airport is vital to understanding what kind of businesses, restaurants or concessions to offer. There’s a reason grab and go places do really, really well and get away with charging $12 for water.

Surprisingly to some, top tier frequent flyers typically have a really low dwell time compared to lower ranks or leisure travelers.

If an airline knows their lounge is full of top tiers that day, they can expect many people who won’t stay long. Whereas, if it’s a day with full flights and mostly leisure travel passengers, you can predict people will dwell far longer.

It makes sense. If you’re not used to the delights of a great airport lounge you come earlier, stay longer and take advantage of more. You also have less confidence in timings of the check in and security process, so you pad time in, in addition to the natural, “treat yourself” vibes.

If you do it all the time, every minute not in the airport is often seen as the win, so lounges are just a place to quickly reset and refresh before carrying on.

The first time I experienced a true first class lounge I think I got to the airport at the earliest possible interval. I had hours in there and of course, tried everything.

But I’ve been very lucky, I’ve experienced most lounges many times, been spoiled by the best many times, and unless there’s a real wow factor moment, I’m happiest spending as little time waiting in an airport as possible. Don’t get me wrong, I still indulge from time to time, but I’ve seen a huge dip in my own dwell average.

As I strolled through T2 at Heathrow this week en route to the United Club, it occurred to me that most of my recent lounge visits averaged about 30 minutes in total. In that 30 minutes I’d say I have a maximum of one drink, often little or no food, and mostly take advantage of the wifi and nice calm facilities.

I’ve gotten my time from curb to security at Heathrow down to a decent science and I like it that way. At other airports with even more predictable security and check in patterns, I’ll shave even more time off, often leaving no time for lounges at all.

And this raises a fair question: if everyone could truly model out their time from curb to airside, would they spend as long? Things like TSA PreCheck and CLEAR have been monumental in adding a layer of certainty to this process and I’d expect we’ll see more of it. Will more passengers change habits as they have better confidence in making their flight while cutting it fine?

Now of course, all bets are off when I travel with my kids. And that’s kind of the point. We think we’re very unique in our travel habits, but there are many variables of our travels which drop us into a fairly predictable pattern … and dwell time.

When lounge access is a marquee benefit of being a frequent flyer, but most top frequent flyers hardly leave any time for lounge dwelling, is that a real selling point?

In response, we’ve seen really clever pivots lately, including from Air Canada and Capital One. Each brand has created curated “grab and go” offerings in their lounges or lounge-like areas to offer passengers complimentary things which have tangible value — a nitro cold brew latte, or a nice pastry — for “free”, which they’re totally able to take on the road with them.

That’s a huge departure from the days of lounges with signs everywhere saying no outside food and drinks and no removing food or drinks from the lounge. People never paid attention anyway, and this now just creates a formalized and better thought out approach to catering to all traveler needs.

The big question is: what’s next for adding value to a travelers airport journey? Be sure to share your lounge and travel habits as well.

#6199. The Best Resorts in Turks and Caicos: Readers’ Choice Awards 2026

Trends come and go, but here at Condé Nast Traveler, one thing never changes: your insatiable appetite for seeing the world. This year our readers cast an almighty 798,867 votes in our 39th Readers’ Choice Awards to tell us about the planet’s best travel experiences: You fell hard for palace hotels in Morocco, cruised down the Amazon, and got swept up in New York City’s exhilarating energy. Now, read on to find out where your favorites fall among the winners—and get inspired for where to go next, whether it's to a top-rated hotel or resort, or centered around a worthy cruise, spa, or island. These are the best hotels in the world as voted by you, our readers.

View all of the Readers’ Choice Awards winners for 2026 here, and the best resorts in the Caribbean here.

Turks and Caicos’s bustling yet beautiful island of Providenciales (affectionately dubbed “Provo”) has had its moment in the proverbial sun. Consider venturing southeast to South Caicos for a more intimate and undeveloped look at what are arguably the Caribbean’s most jaw-dropping beaches. The first property to put down literal roots with nearly 800 acres of primarily local vegetation is Sailrock South Caicos: a stunning, 40-unit property on the southeastern island’s northern tip where the Atlantic Ocean and Caicos Bank converge to house the area’s latest and greatest escape. Travel to South Caicos is also more convenient than ever with two direct flights from Miami on Wednesdays and Sundays via American Airlines. This means guests can now bypass a layover in Providenciales and reach paradise in less than two hours.

At the Ritz-Carlton Turks and Caicos, guests can sandwich sun-soaked days of lounging in a private cabana or on Grace Bay’s idyllic slice of beach with plenty of on-site experiences. A favorite for its white-sand beachfront and unrivaled centrality on famed Grace Bay, there’s no shortage of pursuits here—it’s a choose-your-own-adventure property with great amenities for young kids. 147 luxury ocean-view rooms and suites—with the Ritz-Carlton standard—awe and delight. There’s also a collection of luxury residences and penthouses for longer stays, each, of course, with stunning floor-to-ceiling views of Grace Bay’s turquoise waters. Interiors are all creams and whites with gentle pops of beachy colors, large windows, and pristine linens. As the most central property in Grace Bay, everything is within walking distance: the best restaurants, shops, and even a grocery store. For families with little ones, the Ritz Kids club is the place to be for guests ages 4–12. Drop the kids off and embark on the resort’s luxury sailing catamaran, the Lady Grace.

Basking on a coveted stretch of Grace Bay, this well-appointed resort is as lax as it is luxe. While there’s plenty of opportunities for R&R at the blissful on-site spa and for romance to blossom over candlelit dinners, the Sands at Grace Bay also know a thing or two about picking up speed. It wouldn’t be a proper Turks and Caicos vacation without hitting the water, and the resort provides complimentary access to a variety of water sport equipment ranging from sea kayaks to snorkeling gear to explore the mirror-clear seas. If you’re traveling with little ones who aren’t quite ready for the open ocean yet, there’s also kid-friendly pools and sprawling perfect for their next adventure. If you’re looking for a resort that grows up alongside your family, look no further.

Wymara Resort + Villas sits on the western curve of Grace Bay in Providenciales, just a 10-minute drive from the airport. It’s a place for travelers who like their luxury understated and favor the clean lines of minimalist design. Rooms and suites open to sea views and sun-washed balconies, while the villas—set apart from the main resort on a 15-acre peninsula—offer private pools, over-water decks, and personal hosts. The food is sustainably sourced: Indigo serves refined Caribbean dishes, and the Pink Bar is a magnet for sunset watchers. The spa, using island-grown botanicals and 111SKIN products, is intimate and calm. Service is polished yet relaxed, with staff who are friendly and will remember your preferences. Eco credentials are strong, from solar-powered electricity to refillable amenities. Complimentary wellness activities include yoga, pilates, HIIT, and sound baths, while evening entertainment leans local and cultural.

This mega-resort sets itself apart from other all-inclusive properties throughout the region with its family-friendly activities. There is a 45,000-square-foot waterpark and kids clubs for different ages, including one with Caribbean-ified Sesame Street characters, the Xbox Play Lounge, and a teen disco. For the rest of the family, there are 10 swimming pools, 21 restaurants, 15 bars (some of them swim-up), and access to the 12-mile Grace Bay Beach. The 758 rooms and suites are spread across five themed villages, with architecture that represents different regions: France, Italy, the Caribbean, and Key West. With 43 room categories, the resort truly offers something for everyone.

Grace Bay Club offers not one, but three distinct accommodations to its discerning guests: the adults-only Hotel building, the family-friendly Villas Suites, and the Estate, a resort within a resort, with exclusive access to dedicated amenities, such as a separate pool, cabanas, and more. Despite catering to different crowds, they do have a few common features, including spectacular oceanfront views and personal concierge service. Head to the oceanfront Infiniti Restaurant & Bar for bites of such fresh local fare as a warm South Caicos lobster salad, garnished with shaved carrots and crispy basil, or the Mahi Mahi carpaccio, with a kick of jalapeño, served to the sound of breaking waves. Looking to stake your umbrella in the sand a little while longer? Rent one of the homes in the Private Villa Collection, a cluster of five freestanding private beachfront residences that come with all the amenities and services of a superior hotel stay, including roundtrip airport transfers, daily housekeeping, and complimentary breakfast.

A fan-shaped trio of seven-story buildings curve around a beachfront pool and patio at this Grace Bay resort, close to Providenciales's shopping district. Enormous rooms in soft colors have marble baths and soaking tubs, proving that bigger can mean better. Staff members always serve with a smile and make a point of remembering names. The restaurant Seven dishes up Caribbean-inspired cuisine, with entrees like house-made stone crab ravioli, or you can opt for private beachfront dining, complete with a personal butler and a playlist of your choosing. If you're traveling with the family, the kids camp provides diversions such as lizard hunting and sand-castle building—or you can all go for a dip in the island's only heated saltwater pool.

#6198. Thune will lead Republicans through the minority

Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., leaves a meeting in the Capitol on Tuesday, before his election as incoming minority leader later in the day. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

Senate Majority Leader John Thune was reelected as the Republican leader on Tuesday and will steer the conference through their time in the minority.

The South Dakotan ran uncontested despite a push from some of his colleagues to delay the leadership elections following Republicans’ stunning defeats last week in the midterms, which saw them lose at least seven seats and the majority.

“Obviously, the election result was not what we hoped for,” Thune told reporters, referring to the midterms. “But I think it’s important that we take the lessons from that and internalize the message the American people were sending to us.”

While he and the rest of the leadership slate sailed through the conference contests by voice vote, it wasn’t without drama.

Before the leadership elections began in the Old Supreme Court Chamber early Tuesday morning, the conference held a meeting at the request of a group of GOP five senators, led by Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis.

The conversation, which several senators described as “frank,” ended up pushing back the leadership elections by a few hours. But they were not postponed to another day as some had hoped.

“This has never been anything against John Thune,” said Johnson, as he made good on his commitment to leave the room early if the conference proceeded with its election. “What I didn’t agree with was holding the election right away, giving nobody an opportunity to really challenge any leadership position.”

“Part of the issue here is who wants the job? God bless him for serving,” Johnson added.

The conference conversation Tuesday morning turned into an “open-mic” with both conservatives and those who lost their elections speaking, according to senators.

Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., told reporters, “To rush into this and to just ratify all the same leadership — I mean, what message does that send?”

But no contender to Thune emerged despite the angst, and a motion to proceed to the election, introduced by Thune’s fellow South Dakotan Sen. Mike Rounds, was accepted.

Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., said voters who rejected Republicans last week were reacting to high gas prices, the war in Iran and the cost of living, not to how Senate leaders were running the conference.

“I don’t think anybody in Texas who voted for the Democrat governor was voting against John Thune. If you diagnose that as a problem, you’re misdiagnosing the problem,” Paul said.

Whip John Barrasso, R-Wyo., was reelected to his position, as was the chairman of the Senate Republican Conference, Tom Cotton of Arkansas. Sen. James Lankford of Oklahoma was again selected as vice chair of the conference, while Sen. Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia was reelected as Republican Policy Committee chair.

“Our first step is to make sure the American people know that we heard what they said, and the American people’s priorities are our priorities. That’s the way we regain their trust,” Barrasso said afterward.

Sen. Bernie Moreno of Ohio got the nod to chair the National Republican Senatorial Committee, meaning he will helm the campaign arm as the party looks ahead to the uncertain waters of 2028.

Moreno said, “I was in the retail automobile business, so when you don’t listen to your customers, your customers punish you. I think we have to own it, and I think we have to learn from it.”

Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., said on Monday evening, “What we as a conference right now need is honesty. We need focus. We need to try to reach a consensus on what we need to change.”

Kennedy was among those pushing to delay the leadership elections and told reporters on Tuesday he voted present instead of yes on whether to proceed to them.

Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., who ran for GOP leader twice — once in 2022 against Sen. Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., and in 2024 against Thune — declined to run again to challenge Thune. But in a Dear Colleague letter on Monday, he detailed what he’d like to see in the lame-duck session before Democrats take power, including confirming every nominee President Donald Trump has sent to the Senate, funding the government without an omnibus, banning stock trading, passing the permitting bill that is advancing this week in the Senate, passing the National Defense Authorization Act, balancing the budget and pushing through a sweeping voter ID bill known as the SAVE America Act.

Senate Republicans on Tuesday also voted on a resolution on their path forward that was spurred by a motion from Scott, aides said.

“It is the sense of the GOP Conference that we will maximize the 54 days we have with congressional majorities, to confirm every judicial nominee and every executive nominee that the conference approves of, to pass our core Republican priorities, and to do everything humanly possible to pass a reconciliation bill before Jan. 3,” the resolution reads in part.

That long list of goals highlights the expectations Thune has faced as leader, where he led one-third of Republicans’ trifecta in Washington. In the next Congress, Democrats will hold the majority in both chambers of Congress after their larger-than-expected wins, while Trump finishes out his term as president.

Thune said he told his conference: “As I look back on the last couple of years, my question is, what would you have me do differently?”

“Given the constraints we had to deal with, all the stuff that was coming at us on a daily basis, a narrow margin in the House, the White House, the Democrats over here who were obstructing two long government shutdowns — I think we came out of it as well as could have been expected, and got a lot of stuff done,” Thune told reporters.

“If you believe the exit polls, it was the war, it was the economy, it was inflation, it was fuel prices,” Thune added. “So no, I wasn’t apologizing for anything that we did. And I think on the political side, I don’t know what else I could have done.”

Yes, Serbia requires U.S. citizens to have a passport to enter.

Small tips are customary at restaurants and hotels.

Taxis are cheap and plentiful, but public transport within the city is free.

Yes, Serbia is generally considered safe for travelers. The U.S. State Department currently lists it as Level 2, so travelers should exercise increased caution, but no severe threats are present.

September-October offers long days with plentiful sunshine, while April-May is when the city starts to warm up before the full heat of summer.

The historic city center is compact, so you can easily see most of it even on a short, two-day trip.

You might have seen Serbia in the news lately. The country’s recent national elections enacted a political sea change spearheaded by student groups seeking greater freedoms and opportunities.

The jubilant energy unleashed, combined with the Serbian capital’s soon-to-shine spotlight as it prepares to host the 2027 World Expo make now the perfect time to plan your visit to Belgrade. That’s why the city made our list of top destinations for next year.

Sleepier than some other European capitals, yet vibrant and buzzing with a construction boom, Belgrade is coming into its own. It’s also easier than ever to get there, thanks to plentiful airline connections not only to other European hubs but also to the U.S. via the country’s national carrier, Air Serbia.

So start your points planning and make Belgrade a part of your next transatlantic trip.

The fastest way to get to Belgrade’s Nikola Tesla Airport (BEG) from the U.S. is aboard Air Serbia from Chicago’s O’Hare International Airport (ORD) or New York’s John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK). The airline also recently announced that it will launch twice-weekly service to Miami International Airport (MIA) in May 2027.

Air Serbia’s main major airline partner is Etihad, so your best bet for booking award tickets is to use Etihad Guest miles. The program is a transfer partner of:

That said, award availability is hard to come by since these flights only operate a few times a week. Instead, you might want to consider redeeming Flying Blue miles for flights on Air France via Paris-Charles de Gaulle Airport (CDG) or via Amsterdam Airport Schiphol (AMS) on KLM.

For Star Alliance flyers, award availability between the U.S. and Belgrade is plentiful on carriers like LOT via Warsaw Chopin Airport (WAW) and Lufthansa via Frankfurt Airport (FRA) or Munich International Airport (MUC) and Swiss via Zurich Airport (ZRH), starting at 42,500 Aeroplan points each way in economy and 75,000 Aeroplan points each way in business class. Taxes and fees range from about $100 to $150 in each direction.

Belgrade is expecting to see its first Intercontinental open in early 2027, just in time for the World Expo. Until then, there are plenty of other hotels where your points will come in handy.

Located in the new riverside Belgrade Waterfront District, which is home to a sprawling luxury mall, a promenade with tons of bars, cafes and restaurants, and more than a few high-rise apartment buildings, the St. Regis Belgrade opened in November 2024 in a striking glass-and-steel tower. The hotel has just 119 spacious rooms and suites with floor-to-ceiling windows, a beautiful spa with an indoor pool, a cafe-patisserie, a continental restaurant and an outpost of the brand’s signature St. Regis Bar. Rates start at $290 or 43,000 Marriott Bonvoy points per night.

The Hyatt Regency Belgrade is a comfortable, modern hotel in Novi Beograd, the city’s main business district, across the Sava River from the historic core, so it’s not the best for leisure travelers. That said, you can’t beat nightly rates that start at $148 or 6,000 World of Hyatt points per night.

The Hilton Belgrade is centrally located near Slavija Square, within walking distance of attractions like the Nikola Tesla Museum and the Church of Saint Sava. It has 242 rooms and suites and a restaurant that serves contemporary Serbian cuisine. Rates start at $170 or 50,000 Hilton Honors points per night.

You won’t find Uber in Serbia, but taxis are plentiful and can be hailed via apps like Yandex, Pink Taxi Nova and Car:Go. The apps make it easy to pay with a credit card. Just be sure to use a credit card that earns bonus points on ride-hailing services or on travel charges in general.

Sometimes drivers will not accept rides unless you are paying cash, though, which you can also book through the app and then take a metered ride. So be sure to pull some cash out at the ATM at the airport before heading into the city.

Once in Belgrade, it’s easy to get around by public trams and buses, which are free to use within the city center.

Related: The best credit cards for commuting expenses

For a city of its size, Belgrade’s restaurant scene is surprisingly diverse. Of course, you should make it a priority to try typical Serbian dishes like grilled cevapi sausages with fluffy bread and ajvar red pepper sauce, and sarma, which is pickled cabbage stuffed with spiced meat and rice, not to mention the plethora of cured meats and mountain cheeses. Bela Reka is a great place to try a smattering of Serbian specialties, many of them sourced from the restaurant’s own farm in the Homolje Mountains.

Perched on the riverbank, Suvenir serves traditional dishes like roasted lamb and bacon-wrapped prunes in a beautiful setting.

For a contemporary take on Balkan cuisine, Iva is a sophisticated hideaway tucked into a courtyard near Saint Sava church where age-old dishes are reinterpreted through a modern lens. The piping-hot burek pastries stuffed with cheese, baked peach, hot pepper and honey are not to miss ($12), as is the confit river pike-perch with gnocchi and charred Swiss chard in a white wine sauce ($20). A glass of crisp Deuric Severna Morava white wine from the Fruska Gora region is the perfect accompaniment ($7).

Be sure to book ahead for a table at S5 by Angie, a fine-dining bolthole hidden in an otherwise unremarkable apartment building in the city’s quiet Zemun district. Spend a while enjoying a cocktail in the living-room-like parlor, complete with a vinyl record collection, then settle in for a multicourse feast prepared by chef "Angie" Risimic that might include dishes like creamy labneh with tart tomatoes, fluffy ravioli with mild ricotta-style cheese doused in a green herb and blackberry sauce with trout roe, and tender pork in a rosehip demi-glace with end-of-summer morels. Prix-fixe menu prices vary but range from $75-$150, though a la carte ordering is also possible.

For something more casual, spend an evening strolling cobblestones of Skadarska Street in the bohemian neighborhood of Skadarlija, just a short walk from Republic Square, where you will find over a dozen traditional kafane, or taverns, serving similar menus of hearty dishes along with plenty of plum-flavored rakija spirits.

Tri Sesira, or the Three Hats, was a favorite of the Serbian Romantic poet and painter Dura Jaksic, a statue of whom sits outside his humble former house nearby.

Belgrade has a handful of worthwhile museums, but not so many as to commandeer your entire timeline.

The National Museum has exhibits ranging from prehistoric artifacts to medieval Balkan icons, Italian Renaissance and Flemish masters, French Impressionists and modern artists, including pieces by well-known Yugoslav painters like Sava Sumanovic. Entrance is $3 for adults.

It’s free to stroll the grounds of Belgrade Fortress and Kalemegdan Park, which overlook the confluence of the Danube and Sava Rivers and are popular places for sunset meetups.

Some of the museums at the fortress have their own entrance fees and operating hours. The citadel dates to the third century B.C.E., though it has seen hundreds of battles and been destroyed, rebuilt and expanded dozens of times in the ensuing millennia.

Even if churches aren’t your thing, no visit to Belgrade would be complete without a stop at the brilliant white, copper-domed Church of Saint Sava, which is one of the largest Eastern Orthodox churches in the world.

The interior mosaics gleam with gold and are utterly breathtaking. Entrance is free.

Nearby the Nikola Tesla Museum is a fun, interactive affair. It offers guided tours every 45 minutes, but they fill up fast, so get there at least half an hour before the next one to line up. Entrance costs $7.50 and includes a short film, then demonstrations using Tesla coils before a small exhibit spanning the inventor’s life and some of his personal effects.

Sitting in a small park of its own, the Museum of Yugoslavia is a memorial to the former country’s late strongman, Josip Broz Tito, who rose to prominence in the resistance to the Nazi occupation of World War II and eventually oversaw every aspect of life in Yugoslavia until his death in 1980.

The complex includes his mausoleum — the so-called “House of Flowers” — an older building with some of his personal belongings and displays about daily life in Yugoslavia and a larger wing with temporary exhibits including a recent one on themes of propaganda in wartime. Admission is $7.50 for adults.

The pedestrian shopping street of Knez Mihailova is also well worth a wander, if only for unique souvenirs produced by Serbian craftspeople at the Belgrade Window boutique.

It might not have been on your radar before, but Belgrade is well worth a visit, especially with all the events on the calendar for 2027, including hosting the World Expo. Along with some luxurious new hotels and a growing crop of exciting new restaurants, plus a small but impressive cadre of museums and galleries, it might just become one of your favorite European capitals.

#6196. Guide: United Airlines Has Starlink On More Than Half Its Flights, But These Aircraft Offer The Best Odds

United Airlines has reached an impressive milestone: Starlink is now available on more than half of its daily flights. I increasingly choose United when I know Starlink will be onboard, but customers generally cannot determine that when booking. Here is what United should change and which aircraft currently offer your best chance of getting Starlink.

United announced last week that Starlink had crossed the 50% threshold across its daily schedule. The airline expects that number to approach 64% by the end of 2026 and plans to complete fleetwide installations by the end of 2027.

That is an extraordinarily fast rollout for an airline with more than 1,000 mainline aircraft plus a large regional fleet.

The announcement was packaged around Thanksgiving travel, with United expecting to carry more than 6.6 million passengers between November 19 and December 1. But the more consequential development is that Starlink is no longer a novelty you might encounter on a regional jet. Instead, it is becoming a defining part of the United experience.

I have used just about every major inflight internet system, and Starlink is clearly the best.

The connection is fast, latency is low, and it works well enough that I can complete almost everything onboard that I would ordinarily do from my office. Large files load quickly, video calls are possible (but thankfully not allowed on United), and the service supports multiple devices. It is also free for MileagePlus members.

If two departures are similarly priced and one has Starlink, I will choose the Starlink flight. I may even accept a slightly less convenient departure time because several productive hours in the air are worth far more to me than leaving an hour earlier.

That is precisely the sort of customer behavior United wants. Scott Kirby has repeatedly suggested that Starlink will persuade customers loyal to other airlines to try United, after which the rest of the experience will convince them to stay.

I understand his confidence. Once you experience internet that works almost like it does on the ground, returning to a slow or unreliable connection is painful.

Here is the problem: United generally does not confirm Starlink availability until three days before departure.

The airline offers a useful Starlink tracker, but it is designed to check an upcoming flight rather than help someone choose among flights several weeks or months in advance. By the time the tracker confirms the aircraft, most passengers have already purchased their tickets.

Aircraft substitutions will always occur, and no airline can guarantee that a particular tail number will operate a flight. But that does not prevent United from displaying the expected connectivity during booking.

United already identifies many onboard features in the reservation process. It could add a Starlink indicator based on the scheduled aircraft, accompanied by a clear disclaimer that equipment may change. Even an imperfect forecast would be useful.

United carefully says Starlink is available on more than half of its daily flights, which is not the same as saying more than half of its aircraft or passenger seats have Starlink. Regional jets and narrowbody aircraft generally operate more flights per day than widebody aircraft, allowing each installation to influence a larger number of departures.

United’s entire two-cabin regional fleet now has Starlink. If you want the best chance of getting it, book a flight operated by a Bombardier CRJ-550 or Embraer E175.

If you are traveling on a mainline aircraft, the Airbus A321neo is most likely to have Starlink, with 88% of that fleet equipped. The Boeing 737-800 follows at 77%, while 67% of the Boeing 737-900 fleet has it.

Avoid the Airbus A319, Airbus A320, and Boeing 757-300 if connectivity is important to you. None currently have Starlink, and the aging Panasonic systems installed on some of those aircraft are most likely not to work at all.

Personally, I avoid 757-300s and go out of my way to fly on A321neos. You should too if onboard connectivity is important to you.

Progress on the widebody fleet remains slow. Only 2% of United’s Boeing 787 fleet and 5% of its Boeing 777 fleet currently have Starlink, while none of its Boeing 767s are equipped.

Delta Air Lines has selected Amazon Leo for its next-generation internet, with installations scheduled to begin in 2028. As I discussed yesterday, a rocket failure that destroyed 40 Amazon satellites illustrates the risk of selecting a network that is still being constructed.

Delta already offers free Wi-Fi on most of its fleet, and I have found it perfectly usable on many flights. This is not a choice between internet and no internet. But in terms of functionality, Starlink is better. It is not even a contest.

United may complete its fleetwide rollout before Delta installs Amazon Leo on its first aircraft. That gives United time to turn a technical advantage into a behavioral one: customers try Starlink, discover they can be more productive in the air, and begin considering connectivity when selecting future flights.

That is why displaying Starlink during booking would be valuable. If the product is strong enough to influence purchasing decisions, United should make it easier for customers to find before purchasing.

It would also help reduce disappointments. I was recently on a Boeing 777-200 with old-school Panasonic Wi-Fi, and a business class passenger across the aisle from me was fuming that there was no Starlink. Better to underpromise and overdeliver than the other way around.

Starlink is now available on more than half of United Airlines flights and should reach nearly 64% by the end of the year. That is impressive progress and gives United a genuine advantage over its domestic competitors.

I increasingly choose flights based on whether Starlink will be onboard. The frustration is that United generally cannot confirm it until three days before departure, long after the booking decision has been made.

A Starlink indicator during booking would not need to be a guarantee. It could simply tell customers what United reasonably expects to offer. In the meantime, regional jets, Airbus A321neos, and Boeing 737-800s give you the best shot at Starlink on United.

What customers consider to be “premium” is an ever changing thing. What exactly is so premium about Delta as compared to others? On time performance? It’s surely not the food. FAs are as much of a mixed bag as at UA/AA.

Even if DL wifi is usable, it’s certainly not thought of as premium. Starlink is simply excellent and is thought of as premium. Therefore, it would make sense for a brand that wants to be associated with the word premium to actually associate themselves with a brand that stands for premium and excellence.

The fact that DL did not do so is completely indefensible. Full stop. We know this to be the case because (other than B6, which barely counts) literally every other major airline in the world has signed on with Starlink. I think it’s around 50 of them at this point?

So DL is going to be an outlier… why? Because it’s CEO didn’t like having to bend the knee to Elon Musk? I mean, sure, personally, that’s a hard ask. But as a business matter? Not a close call.

So DL’s plan is to wait a few more years for Amazon to come online? Amazon may be many things, but it is not thought of as premium. It’s utilitarian. So even once that happens, they will have associated themselves with a non-premium brand. Why?

If DL wants folks to think of them as utilitarian, and wants to switch places with AA, that’s up to them I guess. But one would think the folks at Amex would be ringing alarm bells over this, and that someone at Amex is making some well placed phone calls to try and stop this madness.

Now, @TD will tell us that there’s no data anyone can point to, blah blah blah. What that has to do with brand perception is beyond me. And brand perception that translates into credit card spend is literally the entire ballgame!

@TD will also say that DL has more wifi throughout its fleet today or whatever and UA still doesn’t have Starlink on the widebodies, blah blah blah. How you can criticize a company for rapidly installing an excellent service throughout its fleet is beyond me. UA will be done installing Starlink in 2027, well before DL installs anything relating to Amazon – and does anyone seriously believe 2028 is achievable for more than a handful of installations just to say that they install something in 2028?

In sum, @Matthew is 100% correct that Starlink will absolutely drive consumer behavior here. And corporate behavior – shockingly corporations want their employees to have access at all times to internet that is high speed and works! DL’s actions here are borderline insane.

Is DL suddenly going to be unprofitable because of this? Of course not. Inertia is a powerful thing. But why DL would surrender an inch of premium association is beyond me. And that ultimately may have an impact on the bottom line – maybe not tomorrow, but in the weeks, months and years to come.

Finally, spare me the morality play. Competition is a good thing of course, and it’s good that Amazon is trying to be a viable competitor. But corporations have a responsibility to make sensible business decisions that enhance their profits, not to ensure competition. Amazon is simply not a competitor today. The airlines do everything possible to reduce competition at their hubs, they know the playbooks well. DL gets exactly zero moral brownie points for going with Amazon.

thank you for confirming how few UA flights actually have Starlink. After years of hyping Starlink, UA has created enormous dissatisfaction by not delivering what it has been hyping.

this statement is absolutely key to the debate and at least you have accurately stated your experience w DL WiFi which mirrors what the majority of people see. “Delta already offers free Wi-Fi on most of its fleet, and I have found it perfectly usable on many flights. This is not a choice between internet and no internet. But in terms of functionality, Starlink is better. It is not even a contest.”

Nobody has ever debated that Starlink is faster. The question is what speed advantage is necessary for passengers to move from a slower platform (including B6 and DL and most legacy AA and WN systems) to a Starlink carrier. The simple fact is that there is NO data to show that people are moving just to get faster WiFi. You are already highly loyal to UA -and that is true w/ the vast majority of business passengers. WiFi speed is simply nowhere even in the top 10 purchase drivers even for customers that are truly “up for grabs”

DL has high speed WiFi in service now on 95% of its fleet covering its entire global network and is expecting to install Hughes hybrid WiFi on the remaining couple dozen 717s and RJs in the next few weeks. #6195. New Credit Card Sets Annual Fee Dynamically, Based On Benefit Usage

Among savvy Redditors and credit card blogs, there’s a common thread with many recent credit card changes. “It feels like a coupon book” is often the consumer reaction, particularly as annual fees rise as justification for an increasing number of partner offer benefits, which if consumed in entirety could lead to more value.

Since many people simply won’t use all the benefits and partner offers being baked into the card, people increasingly feel like the annual fee rises are getting too steep. In a bold move, a new card launched today which offers a flexible annual fee, based only on the benefits you actually use.

Signed up for a card named after a precious or semi precious metal and shocked by the $450-$695 fee? You’re not alone.

To get your money back from such a fee, you’d need to take advantage of regular lounge access at airports, utilize your TSA PreCheck/Global Entry credit, maximize every monthly dining or entertainment credit and sign up for every other fee credit, which often requires a purchase.

To quell this issue, the new card is effectively a build your own card, card.

Despite the innovation, the card draws on the historical concept of the coupon book, where you only pay for the offers you tear out and redeem. The annual fee starts at zero, but as you actually redeem the cards benefits, you get billed accordingly. Your fee can be zero, or as high as $10,000 per year.

Done right, you can end up paying $650 in annual fees for about $800 worth of stuff, some of which you wanted and most of which, about $700 worth, you didn’t really want or need, but felt compelled to get, just because it’s there.

This model allows you to really dive into the classic coupon book, feeling like you’re really tearing offers out of the page, and simply leaving the ones you’re not using in the book. You’re only paying for the ones you rip out, but when there’s so many offers to choose from, the book just feels so compelling.

Obviously, it’s April 1st and no such card is coming to the market (yet, lol), but hopefully this light hearted amusement has been a helpful exercise in framing the true value you’re really extracting from your premium credit card, or conversely, the lack thereof.

Consider the things you’d actually purchase without the “offer” prompt and if that number still adds up to be more than the annual fee, you’re doing it right. If it doesn’t…

Laura Burns is a frequent traveller with an affinity for fine coffee, delicious food and the world's most beautiful sights. If she's writing about it, it's worth exploring. Happiest in Tokyo, Melbourne,... More by Laura Burns

#6194. At Our Annual Points of View Summit, Experts Make Their 2027 Travel Predictions

When planning our 2026 Points of View Summit, we wanted to be sure to set time aside to hear directly from our travel specialists—the behind-the-scenes experts who work tirelessly work to curate ambitious and deeply personal itineraries around the world. Spliced between compelling panels on Lowcountry heritage, summer travel trends, and the evolving appeal of all-inclusive stays, the breakouts allowed for extended discussions with Traveler editors on a range of themes. From culinary experiences inspired by Hilton Head Island's Gullah cuisine, to the evolving dynamics of multigenerational travel and a new guard of ultra-luxe globetrotters, we got the inside scoop on where travelers are going and how they're getting there.

Jim Berkeley, founder and CEO of Destinations and Adventures International, speaks on culinary moments.

Inspired by Hilton Head Island's rich tapestry of culinary traditions, senior features editor Megan Spurrell and editorial assistant Skyli Alvarez led a discussion on traveling for taste—from the rising interest in foraging over traditional cooking classes to the draw of big-name chefs contrasted with harder-to-find local gems, and the hotspots that deserve to be on our food maps.

Our specialists all agreed that travelers yearn for “authentic” food moments, though defining authenticity—and actually finding it—often becomes tricky. To Omolola Campbell, sixth-gen Gullah descendant and executive producer of Gullah short documentary The Spirit We Move With, it's about who provides the experience. “Taking a cooking class is much different than getting it from a local chef who can tell stories about why a dish means so much to this locality,” she said, explaining how so many of South Carolina's Gullah dishes contain okra because its seeds were sown into the hair of West Africans who were brought to the South for slavery. The plant has come to represent resilience, and it's that integral context, according to her, that gives a meal its soul. “That's how you differentiate the person who really knows why they're cooking what they're cooking,” Campbell concluded.

Dana Kravis, Madison Flager, and our travel specialists explore multigenerational travel trends.

When it comes to multigenerational trips, the grandchildren are choosing the destinations and the grandparents are paying—it's their way of leaving a legacy amongst those dearest to them. During a discussion led by global executive director of video Dana Kravis and commerce director Madison Flager, our travel specialists observed that, because people today tend to wait longer to have children, grandparents are older than they used to be. Travelers in their 80s and 90s are increasingly joining trips, shifting the multigenerational travel dynamic away from the traditional picture of grandparents in their 70s. To trip designers, this means there must be layers of options catering to different activity and exertion levels.

Many in this session agreed the most successful family trips provide opportunities for separating and coming back together. Three itinerary choices in one day are ideal, so younger folks can be out and about, with the whole family reuniting for mealtimes and perhaps an afternoon activity. Boat and yacht experiences were especially recommended as spaces where the family is forced to be together—grandkids cannot simply run off and do their own thing.

What's luxury to one traveler might seem the furthest from it to another; some long for jam-packed, once-in-a-lifetime itineraries, while others want total disconnection and the privilege to do absolutely nothing for a week. Features director Rebecca Misner and commerce writer Jessica Sulima led this breakout, as specialists debated the definition of luxury itself. “Luxury is being able to pass on meaning to kids [and] exposing families to the broader world and its cultures,” Virgi Schiffino Kennedy, managing partner at Lux Voyage, said of its intangible appeal. To Ruchi Harnal, founder of Harnal Travel, true luxury “is not about the resort or the villa but the personalization of the trip.” As for who’s spending money on trips? Thomas Robinson, MR at Dehouche, has observed that Gen Z and Millennials are more inclined to spend but want to know where that money goes. Additionally, the specialists largely agreed they’re seeing a shift away from parents taking their children on trips, and towards 30- and 40-somethings treating their parents to a vacation. In Harnal's experience, milestone birthdays and anniversaries are driving clients to book a trip.

Between rising temperatures and overtourism, our specialists discuss the factors impacting European summer destinations.

What is the impact of overtourism, price inflation, and rising temperatures on our Euro summers? Director of special projects Lale Arikoglu and commerce editor Meaghan Kenny opened the floor for our specialists. “If you’re thinking of traveling to the Dolomites, consider Switzerland instead. There’s history and beautiful scenery with fewer crowds,” Brian Dore, owner of CIU Travel, said. For the hiking curious, some added that Switzerland offers plenty of one-day hiking trails or “soft adventure” travel—three-to-four days combined with a lake or city destination. Others agreed that traveling to the Alps offers a significant advantage—higher elevations means cooler temperatures—and that Slovenia is a great alternative to Italy. To dodge the crowds, travelers might also consider Belgium, Denmark, or Norway (where ocean ships and river cruises are opening earlier in March). For families, consider Umbria (hot tip: plenty of festival and craft opportunities for kids), Austria, Ireland, or Croatia.

For those who want to stick with more tried-and-tested European itineraries next summer, consider going as early as possible, for instance, in May instead of August. When it comes to traveling to France specifically, folks advised flying into Paris or Nice, then venturing out to the countryside or oft-overlooked Atlantic Coast. And our specialists could not stress it enough: Always, always check the temperatures in advance of your trip.

As discussed by Mei Zhang, chairman and founder at WildChina, during the panel on summer travel, the demand for travel to Asia is only increasing. Global features director Erin Florio and editorial assistant Kat Chen continued the conversation with travel specialists on the destinations and experiences driving this growth. For Silk Road Treasure Tours president Zulya Rajabova and her clients, it's the destinations with indispensable craft identities, such as Samarkand in Uzbekistan with its millennia-old design traditions, that make the continent so varied yet distinct. Meanwhile, Marigold Wood, travel designer at Blonde Atlas, explained that she's been recommending routes going through China, such as Yunnan's tea trails, which offer trekking and hiking opportunities. For Ethan Crowley, lead trip designer at Asia Desk Ltd, educating his travelers on navigating countries like Cambodia, beyond their most-visited landmarks, is key.

If 2026 was the year of the fan, 2027 is ushering in even more reasons to travel for entertainment. Associate editor Charlie Hobbs and commerce writer Jessica Chapel helmed this breakout on the sporting events, music festivals, and art fairs that specialists are seeing people travel for (and the subsequent hurdles they must overcome to). From Pink at the Sphere, where access requires a Venetian hotel package to the Ryder Cup at Adare Manor, where full-house and package buyouts, high-demand events are increasingly forcing bundled purchases.

The specialists also highlighted how limited legal protections in the States enables extreme ticket scalping for stadium concerts and makes domestic events increasingly unaffordable. Stephanie Malakie, founder of Empress Travel Club pointed to a related challenge: With so many events and providers, travel advisors find it hard to filter the options and identify the right fit for clients. Rather than just acquiring a ticket, specialists agreed the focus should be on curating the surrounding experience or tapping into evergreen and niche experiential travel, with events like the Jets playing in London or F1 in Shanghai. Cultural milestones like Vatican City trips featuring Papal Blessings or European Christmas markets pair well with entertainment, too. To Zhang, set-jetting to filming locations also offers value, minus the headache of peak-event ticketing.

Hannah Towey co-leads the breakout session on outdoor travel.

Everyone is hiking, or so it seems. Helmed by Jamie Spain, travel bookings commerce editor, and Hannah Towey, news editor, this breakout explored nature as wellness and why it is we're increasingly longing for all things outdoorsy. However, our specialists offered a frank reality check on our dumbphone fantasies. “Guests all want to have access [to Wi-Fi] for emergency reasons at a minimum… I don’t have a single guest who wants to [fully] digital detox," Kate Doty, trip designer at Geographic Expeditions, said. It seems that many travelers want to be disconnected until the time comes for true disconnection, and Lou Lagrange, trip consultant at Luxury Travel Advisor, added, “Even planning for national park trips, [you have to] warn them there won’t be Wi-Fi.” However, the group observed that services such as having photographers on small ships, helps reduce a traveler's dependency on their phones.

There's still a real demand for glamping, as guests want access to nature but with a side of luxury. And when it comes to extreme weather events, instead of having travelers write off entire regions or countries, Doty has figured out collaborative ways to shelve them for potential future trips. In Travel Studio founder Kerri Lisa's case, it's a matter of reframing the perks of a destination and its seasons; the rainy season, for example, might be exceptionally lush and green. There's always something to be learned in welcoming a bit of playful unpredictability into our itineraries.

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.
