#6182. Wander.com: Best Luxury Take On Airbnb (With Real Value Too?)

At first, the big hotel chains of the world laughed off Airbnb and vacation rentals. No seriously, they did. Now, they all compete in the vacation rental business and act like it was always the plan.

The problem for the traveler, is that almost all of the newer entrants just plug into a massive pipeline of already existing vacation homes and apartments and pop them on their own branded website with no added luxury, differentiation, amenity or expertise in curation.

There’s no huge unlock of new places or highly curated places that you could virtually always stamp as worth recommending to a friend, the way you’d rate an Aman, St. Regis, or Four Seasons hotel.

This is precisely where Wander.com comes in, and it’s by far my favorite luxe vacation rental platform to date. The fact that it’s boutique and limited is what makes it, at least for me. And, the $350 off Wander promo code doesn’t hurt either.

Wander is a vacation rental company which truly hand picks every property that it lists, and has the exclusive listing on. Crucially, each of the vacation properties undergoes a sort of ‘Wander’ transformation to conform with brand standards for wifi, amenity, style and vibe.

It’s above my pay-grade as a blogger on this topic, but it seems like Wander co-invests in the real estate portfolio’s, or partners with owners in a unique way that’s far more integrated than others.

Where are they? Most Wander.com properties are scattered across the US, from the shores of Malibu to the great National Parks in Wyoming and all along the Eastern seaboard too. Hawaii is also a recent addition. New destinations keep popping up!

Each of their properties feels uniquely wonderful and aspirational, and I’d say all have a very modern and contemporary slant to luxury. Grandma’s cabinets are not in any of these homes, but Tesla chargers are. One nice touch: each Wander offers a dedicated workspace with desk, chair, monitors and lightning fast wifi.

I completely respect that all tastes are individual, but the interiors and setups of these homes much more reflect my personal tastes, more minimalist chic, than many less curated vacation rental options.

Most Wander properties are around $1000 a night. Some will be half that, some will be double. On its face, that’s intimidating to many, but when you factor in the number of bedrooms and features it’s really reasonable. Families, or multi-family get togethers… amazing.

All Wander.com properties are at least two bedrooms and many are four, five or even twelve. One is an entire island with multiple residential complexes. For me, I love these sort of getaways for catching up with family or friends, and I never mind when other people are contributing too.

We’ve had some of our best ever vacations renting a house in Palm Springs for weeks or months at a time. Often, family or friends want in too, so we split the house and end up with two bedrooms each for under $500 per night.

We’ve used these bonus rooms and features to socialize or catch up with people in the serenity of the home, not annoyed by service, crowded pools or tight room setups. For a longer stay, I absolutely hate having to rely on a hotel kitchen for every meal. I love to hit a local market and grill with family or guests.

Wander is offering $350 off first bookings, which is a great way to get started. To browse the homes, you simply download the Wander app and start doom scrolling. When you find one you’re ready to book, the process is very self explanatory and easy to share with others.

I’m personally a fan of virtually California vacation and the properties offered on the platform cover everything from Palm Springs to Napa and all in between in stunning form. The $350 off is a solid discount and combined with new property discounts, which are frequent, there is a lot to love. You can browse Wander and download the app here.

If you don’t see the Wander.com discount in your account, you can add promo code AKFVDFD7 once the app is downloaded.

#6181. Republicans tap Moreno and Jack to lead Senate and House campaign arms

Ohio Sen. Bernie Moreno will chair the National Republican Senatorial Committee during the 2028 cycle. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call file photo)

House and Senate Republicans picked their new campaign chiefs Tuesday, tasking Ohio Sen. Bernie Moreno and Georgia Rep. Brian Jack with leading the GOP campaign arms for the 2028 election cycle.

In their new positions, both will spearhead Republicans’ push to win back majorities on Capitol Hill after Democrats seized control of both chambers of Congress by flipping more than 40 House seats and at least seven Senate seats in last week’s midterm elections.

Republicans returned to Capitol Hill this week still reeling from their losses but resisted calls to delay Tuesday’s leadership elections. In the Senate, South Dakota’s John Thune was reelected Republican leader without any opposition, while Ohio Rep. Jim Jordan defeated Louisiana Rep. Steve Scalise in a closed-door, secret-ballot election to lead House Republicans next year.

Moreno will succeed South Carolina Sen. Tim Scott as chair of the National Republican Senatorial Committee.

“Republicans must enter this next election clear-eyed: the road ahead back to a Republican Senate majority will by no means be easy but the fight has never been so important,” the Ohio senator said in a statement.

Speaking to reporters on Capitol Hill, Moreno described his new role as “a hell of a job.” He said Republicans would be “absolute savages” on ending government corruption and continuing “to work for the American people.”

“I suspect the best tailwind we’ll have is that the Democrats will learn all the wrong lessons,” he told reporters.

Moreno, a close ally of President Donald Trump, is currently serving his first term. He first ran for Senate during the 2022 cycle but dropped out of a crowded GOP primary eventually won by JD Vance. Two years later, buoyed by an endorsement from Trump, he won a contested primary for the state’s other Senate seat and went on to oust Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown that fall.

Brown is poised to return to the Senate after defeating appointed Republican Sen. Jon Husted last week in a special election for the remaining Senate term of Vice President Vance. While Ohio has swung heavily toward Republicans over the past decade, Democrats scored big wins in the Buckeye State last week, winning several statewide offices and flipping three seats in the U.S. House.

But assuming he runs again for a full term, Brown will be on the ballot in 2028, setting up what’s likely to be a tense home-state fight.

In an apparent reference to the returning Brown, Moreno offered some Washington advice Tuesday: “Make sure you rent. Do not buy.”

The 2028 Senate map gives Republican pickup opportunities in a handful of swing states, including Arizona, Georgia, Nevada, New Hampshire and Pennsylvania. The party will also be defending battleground seats in Alaska, Iowa, North Carolina and Wisconsin. Also on the Senate ballot are races for Republican-held seats in Kansas and South Carolina, where Democrats scored surprise wins last week.

On the House side, Jack defeated Indiana Rep. Rudy Yakym III to become the next chairman of the National Republican Congressional Committee. He takes office after one of the worst elections for the GOP in recent decades and will succeed outgoing NRCC Chair Richard Hudson, who lost his own North Carolina seat last week.

House Republicans face the tough task of cutting into Democrats’ 40-plus-seat majority next cycle. But the party will have a slew of pickup opportunities, given the sheer number of seats Democrats won in historically red territory this year.

Like Moreno, Jack was first elected to Congress 2024, leveraging a close relationship with Trump to win an open seat outside Atlanta. He previously was White House director of political affairs during Trump’s first term and was a senior adviser to the president’s 2024 campaign. Over the past two years, he served as the NRCC’s recruitment chair.

Savannah Behrmann contributed to this report.

#6180. The 40 Best Resorts in Mexico: 2026 Readers’ Choice Awards

Trends come and go, but here at Condé Nast Traveler, one thing never changes: your insatiable appetite for seeing the world. This year, our readers cast an almighty 798,867 votes in our 39th Readers’ Choice Awards to tell us about the planet’s best travel experiences: You fell hard for palace hotels in Morocco, cruised down the Amazon, and got swept up in New York City’s exhilarating energy. Now, read on to find out where your favorites fall among the winners—and get inspired for where to go next, whether it's to a top-rated hotel or resort, or a TK centered around a worthy cruise, spa, or island. These are the best resorts in the world as voted by you, our readers.

View all of the Readers’ Choice Awards winners for 2026 here.

The most distinctive part of Hilton’s luxury debut on Mexico’s Riviera Maya is its chameleon-like approach to hospitality. Yes, with its 349 rooms, acres of pools, 11 restaurants, and kids’ and teens’ clubs, the Conrad is the type of resort whose (large bronze) gates a traveler would be content to pass through only twice: right before check-in and right after checkout. Spiritually, though, it aligns more closely with the smaller-scale properties 30 minutes north in Tulum that seek to connect guests with the surrounding destination. Honoring the Mayan cultures that have occupied this stretch of Caribbean coast for centuries, a traditional sacbe, or “white road”—the name of the ancient roadways Mayans created to travel by moonlight—cuts through the jungled grounds. In the lobby, a soaring art installation takes a cue from Mayan macramé. And at the cenote-inspired spa, a traditional four-hands massage is second only to a jalapeño margarita in the open-air bar as a way to immediately shed any lingering real-life stress remaining after a dip in the sea.

Beaches with sand as soft as silk and water as pure as a turquoise gem sound like a dream, and the balmy surroundings of the Hyatt Zilara Riviera Maya make that vision a reality. An adult-only resort just a 30-minute drive away from Cancun International Airport (CUN), this Hyatt outpost makes booking in some much-needed R&R more convenient than ever. The beach is truly at your fingertips at this reader-favorite hideaway with swim-up suites, bars right on the shore, and the Zen Spa which perches right above it all. You may be parked at this bolthole in the Caribbean, but when it comes to your dining options, the world comes to you. The property houses seven bars and restaurants that cater to every palette, whether you're looking for coastal Italian one night or sushi the next.

Along a palm-studded stretch of coast in the Yucatán Peninsula is the recently opened SLS Playa Mujeres, a 498-room resort offering an array of suites, some with a private balcony, terrace, or a garden with a swim-out pool. The opening of SLS Playa Mujeres also marks the debut of SLS Elite, a selection of rooms offering benefits, including private lounge access, preferred dining reservations, and entry to an exclusive beach. Available to all guests on an all-inclusive basis are 18 restaurant and bar concepts, including Mediterranean-inspired dining at Fi’lia and Cleo, fresh catch at Caracol, and classic steakhouse fare at Union. At the heart of the resort is the 20,000-square-foot Ciel Spa, a wellness destination with thermal baths and an outdoor tranquility pool.

Here, the first cocktail arrives before you do, served aboard the open-bar catamaran that carries you from Cancún to this adult-only retreat on Isla Mujeres. Joining Hyatt’s Unbound Collection in November 2026, Impression lives up to its name, with terraces cascading toward a sheltered beach and rooftop infinity pools that give you every reason to admire the water without venturing down to it. Each of the 125 suites comes with dedicated butler service and all-inclusive coverage, including gourmet à la carte dining. At Spezia, decadent Italian cooking offers a reason to dress for dinner, though your butler can arrange a quieter evening in, should you desire.

Opened in February 2022, this Costa Mujeres gem has become a winner for its stand-out dining (including a food truck and on-site Japanese restaurant) as well as a beachfront pool deck complete with a glass-sided infinity pool. The modern amenities and standout service make it clear this is a five-star property, and guests love the poolside sushi and steak as much as the vast beachfront and unending views.

Etéreo, Auberge Collection is only a 30-minute drive from the Cancún airport, but this slice of heaven on the Riviera Maya feels light-years away from the chaos. The resort is incredibly family-friendly, but not in a way that sacrifices any of its sophistication. It’s the type of place where you stay put and enjoy everything it has to offer, like luxurious spa treatments, unique culinary experiences, and pool and beachside lounging, unless you’re going on one of the excursions organized by the hotel, which range from water activities, like cenote exploration and sailing to a tour of the local archaeological zones. Every single one of the 75 rooms is ocean-facing, with floor to ceiling sliding glass doors framing the view, and leading to private terraces perched above the mangroves. Couples and families with young kids looking for an easy, peaceful escape would do well to book a stay at this intimate property.

Staying at the Viceroy Riviera Maya is a vacation in the truest sense of the word: Palapa villas with lots of wood and rattan (many with private pools and outdoor showers) are connected by meandering pathways that fan out to lush, fragrant gardens. And it’s all fronted by seven miles of glorious, white sand beaches. Just remember that you are in the jungle, so be sure to keep your eye out for wily spider monkeys.

This palm-studded resort has been one of the most beloved destinations on the Riviera Maya since it opened in 1995. But a complete reimagining of the 72-room hotel has given it a renewed edge over its neighbors—without losing any of its soul. Arriving at Maroma involves driving through thick mangroves where spider monkeys swing from the trees (the property sits on 200 acres of jungle) before reaching its signature whitewashed architecture and thatched roofs. The design still leans heavily on the region’s Mayan vernacular—the curved stucco buildings are based on ancient geometric principles—and wider Mexican craftsmanship. In fact, almost every detail of the restoration, overseen by interior designer Tara Bernerd, prioritized Mexican makers and artisans (80 percent of the property’s furnishings and objects were made in the country), from the hand-painted Saltillo floor tiles and woven wall hangings to the cotton “manta” caftans left in rooms for guests to slip into. Rooms overlook the palm tree-lined pool, the Caribbean Sea, or both, and feature more of those beautiful tiles, along with whitewashed walls hung with regional textiles. Every detail is designed to keep guests rooted in the Yucatán Peninsula: Even the in-room bar, which is far from mini, is stocked with local spirits like pox, a Mayan liquor made of corn, sugarcane, and wheat, and Mayalen Guerrero mezcal in a beau­tiful bottle. Of the two restaurants on site, the pick is Casa Mayor from Mexican chef Daniel Camacho, which does mind-blowing tomato salads. (The chef also teaches a predictably delicious tortilla-making class.) While the property is spectacular, you shouldn’t miss the chance to explore the surroundings, which include a network of cenotes reached through underground caves. A swim in the pools, bats swooping overhead, is the stuff memories are made of. From $845. —Lale Arikoglu

Done up in a relaxing palette of Caribbean Sea blues, sandy beiges, and cumulus-cloud whites, the 371 rooms at this adults-only, all-inclusive resort are designed to set minds at ease at every turn. The hotel occupies an enviable strip of real estate on the Zona Hotelera waterfront, but guests won’t need to wander far to occupy time during their stays: The 11 bars, restaurants, and cafés include such standouts as Sea Corner for ceviches and tropical cocktails, while spa treatments draw on the aromas and ingredients of the region, including avocado, cocoa, and coffee.

At this all-inclusive, adults-only resort along the Riveria Maya, the food, spa treatments, and stellar views are the main attractions. Rooms and suites come with perks like private swim-up pools, outdoor spa tubs, and panoramic views, while the airy interiors feature wooden accents, hand-crafted furniture, and works made by local artists. Guests can opt for “local host” service: They will help arrange everything from a pillow menu request to an insider’s guide to the local food scene. Alternatively, take your pick from the five onsite restaurants—spanning Mediterranean, Mexican, Japanese, and European cuisines—including Cueva Siete, overseen by celebrity chef Xavier Perez Stone.

After its recent $50 million expansion, this is the star of the Mayakoba development in Playa del Carmen, with 34 private beachfront pool suites and a brand-new beach club with an infinity pool overlooking the ocean.  Beneath wooden pergolas and linen umbrellas of the Sands Beach Club, city dwellers on a seaside escape bask in the balmy Yucatán air before the languid Caribbean waters of Riviera Maya.  The development includes a waterway lined with mangroves perfect for kayaking excursions, over two miles of biking and walking trails, and a Greg Norman-designed, 18-hole golf course. The resort has its very own turtle field since, where four of the seven species worldwide come to nest on the beaches of the complex.

#6179. Delta Air Lines Cuts JFK–Dulles Route After More Than 30 Years

Delta Air Lines will end nonstop service between Washington Dulles and New York JFK in February, leaving the two airports without a direct link. The cut removes another connection to Delta’s JFK hub and follows similar exits by United and JetBlue.

Delta will operate its final flight between Washington Dulles (IAD) and New York Kennedy (JFK) on February 10, 2027. The move eliminates the only nonstop link between the two airports (JetBlue cut the route in 2019 and United in 2014). Delta is not leaving Dulles, nor will this route cut eliminate flights between Dulles and the New York metropolitan area. United serves Newark and LaGuardia from its Washington hub.

But passengers who specifically want to connect at JFK on Delta or its partners will lose an option.

This route has run for over 30 years, so the route cut is certainly newsworthy. Without seeing Delta’s route economics, I’m not going to speculate how much money this service made or lost. But I struggle to see a large number of passengers who need this particular connection and cannot reasonably be accommodated elsewhere. I’m frankly surprised Delta operated a route like this for so long, which sounds like the sort of slot-squatting United does by scheulding so many flights between Washington National and Newark.

The case for this route has always been onward connections at JFK, particularly to international flights. But even there, Delta has alternatives. Washington-area passengers can begin at Reagan National (DCA), while travelers who prefer Dulles can connect through another Delta hub, such as Atlanta or Detroit, depending on their destination. I cannot imagine that there is so connecting traffic from Northern Virginia and the broader Washington area that Delta cannot handle it through DCA or another hub.

While I’m sure there will be “regulars” who are greatly inconvenienced by this route cut, that’s no justification to keep any route going and we do know the load factor was lower on this route than its network average.

This brought back memories of my coverage of United ending JFK–Dulles service in October 2014.

“Two-thirds of traffic on the route is connecting traffic that does not generate sufficient yields.”

United’s circumstances were somewhat similar. Dulles was its hub, while JFK had become a small station focused on flights to Los Angeles and San Francisco. Today, Delta operates a substantial hub at JFK, but it only flies to its hubs, now less JFK, from IAD.

In both cases the underlying question is similar: does the connecting revenue justify using an aircraft and scarce airport access on a short route when passengers have other ways to reach the network?

United decided it did not. Delta is now removing the same airport pair from its schedule.

More than 12 years later, I still find United’s explanation brutally honest as to why it cut that route (and eventually pulled out of JFK altogether).

I have written about Delta becoming more selective at JFK, including cuts to domestic feeder routes and international destinations. With air traffic control congestion and slot restrictions still in place, it makes sense to me that Delta would want to funnel less travel through JFK and more throughout other hubs: the focus must be on local traffic or at least costal traffic that can command a higher premium.

Meanwhile, United is preparing to return to JFK through its partnership with JetBlue. Does this create an opening for United to restore Dulles service? Perhaps, but I would think it would be difficult to work now just like it was then and has been for Delta. United already has extensive Washington–New York connectivity through Newark, and its initial JFK access will be limited. Each available slot will have more compelling uses via transcon traffic.

I do not think the disappearance of Delta from this route will make starting that route attractive to United, especially since United previously abandoned it.

Delta will end JFK–Dulles flights after February 10, 2027, removing a useful option for some Washington-area passengers connecting through Kennedy. Even so, the decision makes sense to me. Delta can accommodate much of that traffic through Reagan National or other hubs, and local Washington–New York travelers have several alternatives…so no, this isn’t a sign that Delta is continuing to lose ground in New York.

United cut this route in 2014 because connecting traffic did not produce sufficient revenue. Delta has not publicly supplied the same explanation, but the commercial question remains much the same. A “useful connection” for many passengers does not necessarily mean a profitable or smart one for the airline.

#6178. My First “New” Chase Sapphire Reserve Travel Redemption Blew My Mind

There’s… a lot… of coverage surrounding the revamped Chase Sapphire Reserve Card. As per usual these days, the hot takes are plentiful and people are fired up. It’s either the apocalypse or the beginning of something great, depending on which attention seeker you read. As a long time cardholder, I’m really intrigued by the new changes.

The changes really fit my profile and sure, the card will cost more, but I won’t have to introduce any behavior change to get more, unlike some other cards. I’ll do most of my spending on this card. I’m a keeper just from the fee credit and earning multipliers.

Well, if my first Chase Sapphire Reserve redemption is any indicator, this card may single handedly change the redemption game and just about everyone should take note — including airline and hotel transfer partners. It’s already a huge win.

Chase Travel’s ‘The Edit’ is a curated selection of nice hotels, which offer benefits similar to those provided by a travel agent or other luxury credit card booking platform. When booking a ‘The Edit’ property, you can expect breakfast for two, a $100 F&B credit, late check out and an upgrade subject to availability.

Which leads me to the important bit! With the revamped Sapphire Reserve Card, there’s a new “Points Boost” feature, which offers up to two cents per point (25,000 points would cover $500, etc) for some flight or hotel purchases.

This can be amazing value, with flights of $3,000 being grabbed for just 150,000 points, with no taxes and fees and the ability to still earn frequent flyer miles and elite status points, since the airline treats it like a cash ticket.

Previously, the Sapphire Reserve card offered a steady point redemption opportunity directly on Chase Travel at 1.5 cents per point (100,000 points would cover $1500, etc). But with the new version, some travel purchases you want to redeem for will either offer less value than before, the same, or more, with this new ‘Points Boost’ at 2 cents per point. We like more!

I am in New York and wanted to do a little staycation, so I fired up Chase Travel and found one of my more reliable upper mid-scale hotels, The Thompson Central Park was on as part of ‘The Edit’. My two options became a very clear singular, third option.

Typically, I’d consider paying cash or transferring my points from Chase to Hyatt to pay for a stay like this. Hyatt has “fixed” points rates, meaning the points price is largely irrespective of the cash price and only changes by seasonal dates. For this season, it was 25,000 points per night for the Thompson Central Park.

If I were to transfer my points, I’d get a free night (the cash rate was around $500) and have a really solid points redemption at exactly two cents per point. I’m not loyal to any hotel chain really, so I wouldn’t get any breakfast or “elite” benefits, but a free night is a free night.

BUT — Chase Travel had a ‘Points Boost’ option to book the hotel directly on their platform and not transfer points to Hyatt. Chase Travel was offering this property for circa 25,000 points and that would cover the $500 cash rate, but unlike transferring points to Hyatt, because I was redeeming a ‘The Edit’ property on Chase Travel, I’d receive…

Yep, by NOT transferring my points (and dealing with the fractured transfer journey) I was able to get myself basically $200 in additional value added to my stay with the breakfast and $100 property credit, not factoring in the value of late check out or a category room upgrade. In addition, I’ll be able to earn elite nights and Hyatt Points on the stay.

A mere 25,000 Chase Ultimate Rewards Points got me a “free” $500 hotel night, breakfast for two, and $100 to spend at the hotel. That’s a pretty stunning redemption, giving more than two cents per point of value and still allowing me to earn on the stay, unlike when you transfer your points to a loyalty program. I wish I could’ve stayed longer.

For the first time I can remember, transferring points to Hyatt was not the best option here and that’s something to stand up and take notice of.

If Chase can keep up this Points Boost game, it can really send ripples through rewards. For the first time, people can easily receive tremendous value for their points through a credit card portal while still earning elite status and points with the hotel or airline of their choosing.

You can check out the new 100,000 point + 500 travel credit offer for the Sapphire Reserve. It’s 200,000 points for Sapphire Reserve Business Cards.

#6177. A total solar eclipse, the real-life Tatooine and crowd-free Roman ruins: The ultimate 7-day Tunisia road trip

All responses are submitted by individual contributors, and neither the bank advertiser, our partners, nor TPG are responsible for ensuring that all posts and/or questions are answered.... Read more

American citizens do not need a visa to visit Tunisia for stays of 90 days or less, just a valid passport with at least six months’ validity and one blank page.

Tipping is appreciated but not expected, unlike in many neighboring countries such as Egypt. I generally added 10% to restaurant bills and rounded up taxi fares. For my tours, I tipped between 20 and 50 dinars, depending on the length and whether there was a separate driver.

Tunisia is essentially bilingual, with most people speaking Arabic and French fluently. In most tourist destinations and hotels, people spoke English, but the French I remembered from high school did help me in a few situations.

Ride-hailing apps like Uber are not available in Tunisia. Taxis are available, but ask for the fare upfront or confirm the meter is turned on before getting in. I pre-booked airport transfers through my hotels to avoid negotiating prices on the spot.

For my road trip, I found it easy to rent and drive a car throughout Tunisia. There is a major highway with toll booths running north to south through the country. In more rural parts of the south, roads are still well maintained — just watch out for sneaky speed bumps. All my hotels featured easy parking, but keep in mind that hotels inside medinas may not be accessible by car or might require navigating very narrow streets. Driving behavior is more erratic in Tunis, but generally, I found the rest of the country easy to drive in.

To visit mosques, you’ll need to cover your knees and shoulders — as well as hair if you’re a woman — but coverings are provided free of charge at most. To adapt to the heat and sun, wear loose layers of light-colored linen and be sure to bring a hat.

The U.S. Department of State lists Tunisia as a Level 2: Exercise Increased Caution, which contains areas with a higher security risk, the same as Turkey and Egypt. Save for a few curious stares from men and one overzealous self-appointed medina guide who demanded a tip, I felt perfectly safe as a solo female traveler. It is best to avoid wandering around medinas after dark since most shops and restaurants are closed anyway. I felt most comfortable with pre-arranged guides, but more because they knew exactly where to go, and I didn’t have to navigate things solo.

For the most comfortable weather with a low chance of rain, visit Tunisia between March and May or between October and November. If you do decide to visit for the Aug. 2, 2027 solar eclipse, keep in mind it can get up to 120 degrees Fahrenheit in the middle of the day out in the desert. During my visit in August, I also experienced rolling blackouts and bottled water shortages.

Tunisia is about to have a big year. On the morning of Aug. 2, 2027, a total solar eclipse will cut a path across the central part of the North African nation, bringing several minutes of darkness to sites like the ancient Roman amphitheater in El Jem, the Great Mosque of Kairouan and the dramatic Sahara Desert dunes and canyons surrounding Tozeur.

The latter will also draw “Star Wars” fans to many of the Tatooine filming locations to mark the franchise’s 50th anniversary of the movie’s release in 2027. The capital of Tunis isn’t in the path of totality, but any trip in 2027 should also include a stop in the picturesque cliffside village of Sidi Bou Said, which UNESCO recently added to its World Heritage list, joining other culturally significant sites like the Medina of Tunis and the Archaeological Site of Carthage.

This 7-day itinerary covers a tour of Tunisia’s most important cultural and historic landmarks in a road trip from Tunis to Tozeur and back, plus tips for where to be during the 2027 eclipse and how to maximize the perks and benefits of the Chase Sapphire Reserve® (see rates and fees) along the way.

Currently, there are no nonstop flights between the United States and Tunisia, so you’ll need to plan for at least one layover before connecting to Tunis-Carthage International Airport (TUN), the country’s largest airport.

I flew to TUN on Air France via Paris-Charles de Gaulle Airport (CDG), since I’m loyal to the SkyTeam alliance and it offered the most frequent connections. However, if you’re loyal to another airline alliance, you can also find connections to TUN on Lufthansa via Frankfurt, ITA via Rome, Royal Air Maroc via Casablanca and Turkish Airlines via Istanbul.

Chase Sapphire Reserve editor tip: When booking flights, check the Chase Travel℠ portal to see what routes and airlines are available to book using the Points Boost feature. I found several business-class fares offering the maximum Points Boost value of 2 cents per point. I ultimately transferred 142,000 Chase Ultimate Rewards points to Air France-KLM Flying Blue after finding an amazing round-trip business-class fare directly on the Air France website, yielding a value of 5.83 cents per mile.

I landed in Tunis around 5 p.m. after a red-eye flight from New York and a relaxed connection in Paris.

A pre-arranged car transfer whisked me to the Four Seasons Hotel Tunis, a luxury beachfront resort in the suburb of Gammarth, about 30 minutes from the airport. Upon arrival, staff greeted me warmly and took me directly to my upgraded Deluxe Sea-View Room for an in-room check-in. The spacious room had a balcony overlooking the Mediterranean, a walk-in closet and a marble bathroom with a separate tub and a shower.

After a quick rinse, I wandered down to Blu, the hotel’s alfresco poolside restaurant, where I enjoyed a refreshing salad of a soft local cheese, tomatoes, onions and peppers served with a glass of Tunisian rosé. Since it was my first day in the country, the friendly staff made sure I tried some spicy Tunisian harissa, a smoky chili paste drizzled in olive oil that I sopped up with fluffy squares of focaccia.

Chase Sapphire Reserve editor tip: Book the Four Seasons Hotel Tunis through The Edit to use one of the twice-annual, up-to-$250 credits toward prepaid hotel stays of two or more nights reserved through Chase Travel. By booking through The Edit, I also received other perks like complimentary hotel breakfast for two and up to $100 property credit, which I used for meals but could have used toward spa treatments like the ceremonial hammam experience, which comes out to approximately $100.

Since I only had one full day in Tunis, I headed out bright and early for a private tour of the capital’s major sites, booked through Chase Travel with Didon Tours. My guide, Baligh, and a private driver picked me up for a full 8-hour day that included lunch and fascinating storytelling about the city’s ancient and modern history and politics.

To beat the cruise groups and midday heat, we visited the ancient ruins of Carthage first, taking in the views from Byrsa Hill before heading down to the circular Punic port and the massive seaside complex of the Baths of Antoninus.

From there, we drove to the charming blue-and-white village of Sidi Bou Said, Tunisia’s newest UNESCO World Heritage site, for fresh juice and almond cakes at Cafe des Delices and iconic views of the beach below. While we didn’t have much time to browse the cliffside town’s shops, I did pick up some handmade souvenirs at the ceramic store at 16 Rue Habib Thameur.

For lunch, we stopped in the coastal suburb of Le Goulette at Restaurant La Victoire for a traditional Tunisian meal of brick à l’oeuf, a deep-fried pastry stuffed with egg, tuna and onion and a freshly grilled dorade fish served with rice and carrots.

Next, we turned inland toward the western side of the city to visit the Bardo Museum, set in a former palace and home to the world’s largest collection of Roman mosaics. (Don’t miss the mosaic of the Roman poet Virgil, flanked by the muses of history and tragedy, as it’s considered to be the Mona Lisa of Tunisia.)

Finally, we hit the medina of Tunis, where we visited the courtyard of the Zitouna Mosque and made a quick pass through the souk's meandering lanes before returning to the hotel for a much-deserved swim in the indoor pool and a nap before a quiet room-service dinner.

Chase Sapphire Reserve editor tip: Earn 8 points per dollar spent on Chase Travel purchases, including activities and tours like the one I booked. Those with more time can add another day in Tunis and split this itinerary into two for a more relaxed pace in each location.

Around midday, I returned to the airport to pick up a rental car from Avis and set the GPS to drive two hours south to Kairouan, a UNESCO-recognized city famous for its picturesque medina and Great Mosque, which dates to the 9th century AD. While Kairouan is considered one of the holy cities of Islam, film buffs may recognize it from “Raiders of the Lost Ark,” where it stood in for 1930s Cairo. It lies along the northern boundary of the 2027 solar eclipse’s path of totality.

La Kasbah Hotel, booked via Chase Travel, provided a soft landing with its private parking lot, pool and strong air conditioning. The shops and sites in the medina tend to close in the late afternoon, so if you arrive after then, plan on a quiet night in the hotel, cooling off in the pool or lounging on woven rugs in its vintage café, drinking mint tea.

Chase Sapphire Reserve editor tip: Pay for car rentals with Chase Sapphire Reserve to receive primary auto rental coverage (just be sure to decline the agency's collision insurance). Though I didn’t end up needing it, I had peace of mind knowing I was covered for up to $75,000 of theft or collision damage to the rental car.

Having arrived the previous afternoon after the mosque closed, I went first thing the next morning to admire the column-lined courtyard and three-tiered minaret before the tour groups arrived. The ticket to the mosque also included admission to the nearby Sidi Abid el Ghariani Mausoleum, built in the Moorish style with black and white marble arches. A few doors down, I stopped by the former home of the governor of Kairouan, an ornately decorated mansion that now serves as a rug shop. While I wasn’t in the market for a carpet, I enjoyed the architecture and left with a handwoven scarf for 40 dinars ($14).

After checking out, I hit the road again for the 4.5-hour drive south to Tozeur, a city in the heart of the Sahara Desert. Though I drove straight through, making brief stops at gas stations along the way, it’s also possible to break up the drive with stops at either the well-preserved archaeological site of Sbeitla or the Roman baths of Gafsa.

Just be mindful of timing: I wouldn’t recommend driving at night. Though the roads are well-maintained, speed bumps are common and harder to spot after dark.

Once in Tozeur, I checked into Dar Saida Beya, a traditional Tunisian guesthouse, booked through Chase Travel. After a long drive, I had a quiet evening to walk around and explore the nearby old town center.

Chase Sapphire Reserve editor tip: Though the upscale Mora Sahara Tozeur resort west of town isn’t bookable via Chase Travel currently, it’s still possible to earn 4 points per dollar spent on direct hotel bookings made with the Chase Sapphire Reserve.

The Atlas Mountains meet the salt flats and sands of the Sahara Desert in Tozeur, creating an otherworldly landscape that inspired many film directors. Most notably, the canyons and dunes around Tozeur served as the filming location for the desert planet of Tatooine in the “Star Wars” movies. The epic sci-fi series is celebrating the 50th anniversary of its release in 2027, and fans can experience the eclipse from here, since Tozeur falls along the southern boundary of the path of totality.

I booked a 7-hour tour with Attractive Discoveries via Chase Travel to see everything the area had to offer. Before diving into the area’s cinematic legacy, my driver and guide, Firas, began the day at Chebika Oasis, where a 45-minute hike wound through the ruins of a former Berber village and down to the oasis and its waterfall.

Our next stop was the Grand Canyon of Tunisia, Mides Canyon, roughly a mile from the Algerian border and featured in films like “The English Patient.” During the 30-minute hike along the dry riverbed, I spotted no fewer than six falcons diving in and out of the cliff face while hunting.

To avoid the worst heat of the day, the tour included a break from 1 to 5 p.m., during which we stopped to pick some dates from my guide’s family’s oasis of palm trees. I also tried a makloub sandwich filled with chicken, cheese and harissa and took a short nap.

At 5 p.m. on the dot, Firas picked me up again in his 4x4 to head out into the desert to watch the sunset over the dunes. Along our drive, we spotted a herd of camels, stopped to climb the Ong Jmal or “Camel’s Neck” rock formation and did some adrenaline-inducing 4x4 driving. We arrived at the remaining film sets that served as the desert trading post of Mos Espa in “The Phantom Menace” just before sunset.

To cap off the day, we drank fresh mint tea with almonds — a local treat — and watched the sun set behind the dunes before heading back into town.

Chase Sapphire Reserve editor tip: Put the card's up to $300 annual credit to work on travel purchases like the tour I booked. The credit is applied automatically to eligible purchases each account anniversary year.

The biggest Star Wars fans may want to stay another day to visit other nearby filming locations, such as Sidi Bouhlel Canyon and the Lars family homestead exterior near the town of Nefta.

Since I had another 4.5-hour drive ahead of me that day, I left around 11 a.m. to drive back north to the city of El Jem via Chott el Djerid. Before heading off across the massive salt lake, I filled up my gas tank and packed snacks for the long drive since there aren’t many places to stop in the first couple of hours.

Built about 1,800 years ago, the Roman amphitheater of El Jem is roughly 70% the size of Rome’s amphitheater but has significantly fewer crowds and offers wide-open access to each level — even the underground level where animals were kept before they fought gladiators.

After checking into Hotel Julius, booked through Chase Travel, I dropped my bags and took the five-minute walk to the amphitheater before it closed. The 20 dinar ($7) ticket includes entrance to both the amphitheater and the nearby El Jem Archaeological Museum on the same day. Since I arrived a little later in the afternoon, I went to the museum first thing the next morning and justified the extra $7 by spending a leisurely morning taking in the incredibly detailed mosaics without being rushed.

El Jem falls within the path of totality for the 2027 solar eclipse, so history buffs may want to make this city their home base for the celestial event.

Chase Sapphire Reserve editor tip: Tunisia is still a predominantly cash-based society, so it may be hard to find restaurants that accept cards. I couldn’t earn 3 points per dollar spent on dining worldwide with my Chase Sapphire Reserve in El Jem, but the two fricassee (fried dough buns stuffed with egg, tuna, potato and harissa) I ordered at a street food stall on the way back from the amphitheater only cost 7 cents total (yes, really), so I wasn’t worried about missing out on too many points.

After checking out the museum, I loaded up my rental car one last time for the two-hour drive back to Tunis. Those with more time and desire to sit on the beach than I did could easily add a day or two in the coastal town of Hammamet, which sits about two-thirds of the way back to Tunis from El Jem.

Once I handed off my rental car keys at the airport, I met the taxi driver I had prearranged with my final hotel, Dar Ben Gacem, a traditional guesthouse in the Tunis medina. Since my tour of Tunis at the beginning of the trip only included a brief visit to the medina, I was glad to have the rest of the afternoon and evening to poke around the shops and alleys of the historic city center and do some final souvenir shopping before flying home the next day.

Keep in mind that most stalls in the medina are open from around 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., with more closed on Fridays and Sundays, so plan your visit accordingly. (Plus, many restaurants are closed for dinner on Sunday nights as well.)

Though some flights depart in the evening, I opted to take a connecting flight back to Paris in the morning and stay an extra night to avoid a rushed final day.

During my week-long road trip, I explored Tunisia’s ancient ruins, UNESCO-recognized Islamic architecture and otherworldly desert landscapes, many of which lie in the path of totality of the 2027 solar eclipse. Booking through Chase Travel maximized my Ultimate Rewards earnings, while the card benefits helped offset travel expenses along the way, like the $300 annual travel credit on tours, The Edit perks and $250 statement credit at the Four Seasons and primary rental car coverage through Avis. When I returned to New York, I was glad I had enrolled in Global Entry before my trip. The Sapphire Reserve's $120 Global Entry application fee statement credit helped offset the cost, and the program made reentering the U.S. much easier.

#6176. Independents decide the election, again!

A group of new senators-elect gather for a photo in Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer’s office in Washington on Monday. The large class of incoming Democratic senators was propelled by votes from independents, Winston writes. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

Once more, independents were the decisive factor in what amounts to the Republicans’ midterm disaster that was both broad and deep. No one who reads this column should have been surprised that this growing segment of the electorate became the equivalent of the “deciders-in-chief” who used their vote to send a tough message to the president and his party.

“We hired you to fix the Biden economy and you failed.” Pretty simple.

According to the exit polls, Democrats won independents by an astonishing 22 points. If this holds, it will be the largest margin in the history of exit polling, beating the Republican margin in 2010 of 19 points. For Republicans, this is the fifth consecutive election losing independents.

It was the size of the GOP defeat with independents that put the number of states and congressional districts into play, districts that President Donald Trump won in 2024, many by double digits.

Independents made up 33 percent of the electorate; Democrats were at 35 percent and Republicans at 32 percent. This is the second consecutive election where independents were a larger part of the electorate than one of the major parties. It also shows that while independents may not have been enthused about voting, they showed up.

Looking at the 13 battleground Senate races, which now include Mississippi, Democrats won independents in all of them by double digits, and 10 of them by 20 points or more. The independent vote allowed Democrats to overwhelm significant Republican Party ID advantages in many red states and districts.

For example, in Kansas (exit poll not final), Republicans had a 17-point party advantage, but lost independents by 33. Incumbent Sen. Roger Marshall went down with a 5-point loss. In South Carolina, Republicans had a 14-point party advantage, but lost independents by 31 points. A liberal activist Democrat beat a neophyte Republican candidate, appointed Sen. Darline Graham, by 4 points.

Despite Texas Republicans’ 5-point party ID advantage, Ken Paxton lost independents by 31 points and lost the Senate race by a huge 12 points. It goes without saying that voters in Texas shocked Republicans by not only rejecting the president’s primary choice for Senate, but taking down all Republicans in statewide races.

Overall, Republicans lost six states with key Senate races where Trump won by double digits in 2024, with Mississippi being a potential seventh. In the House (with 7 races yet to be called at the time of this writing), Democrats have won 56 congressional districts that Trump carried in 2024, along with carrying all 201 districts that Harris won.

Clearly, Republican operatives, consultants and the media missed the boat when it came to evaluating the viability of House races. Using the 2024 Trump-Harris race results to assess the safety or vulnerability of a particular seat proved to be the wrong context.

In the spring, I was beginning to see some danger signals in our polling and in public surveys that raised questions for me about just how many House seats were actually in play, fearing perhaps far more than anyone was predicting. By early summer, I decided to undertake a different analysis on the state of current races using the 2020 Trump-Biden results by congressional district. The research found a much larger number of GOP seats could be vulnerable. In the end, the analysis proved to be right. Democrats won all of the 220 districts that Biden carried, and at least 37 seats that Trump won.

According to the exit polls, the independent vote, not surprisingly, was largely driven by the economy, their top issue concern. Much to the detriment of Trump and the Republicans, 80 percent of independents thought the economy was not good/poor, versus 20 percent who thought the economy was excellent/good. In terms of inflation, 82 percent said it had been a severe or moderate hardship for them, and 89 percent said the cost of living was a crucial or major factor in how they voted for Congress.

The president and his party got the blame. Looking at specific policies, 71 percent of independents thought that Trump’s tariff policies had hurt the national economy, and more broadly, 72 percent said his policies had worsened economic conditions in the country. As a result, Trump’s overall job approval among these voters was 29 percent approve with 71 disapproving; 59 percent strongly disapproving. These extraordinarily bad numbers topped even Biden’s worst job approval numbers.

Trump’s decision to ask voters to “pretend I’m on the ballot,” was, in retrospect, a strategic miscalculation. It was a mistake to tell voters that the economy was in great shape when it was clear the majority of people were very unhappy when it came to inflation — the rising cost of gas and groceries.

A little empathy on economic issues and a lot better explanation of why the Iran conflict was crucial to national security and worth the economic sacrifice would have gone a long way to minimizing the size of the GOP defeat.

Neither happened, and Republicans were overwhelmed by a blue tsunami almost nobody saw coming. Still, despite the size of the Democrats’ win, they would be wrong to see this as an ideological mandate of any sort. The exit polls showed that the electorate remains center-right. Moderates are the largest component at 41 percent, but conservatives still outnumber liberals by a 33-26 margin.

Independents have a negative view of both parties. Their view of Republicans is 32 percent favorable and 68 percent unfavorable. However, Democrats are not far behind, at 42 percent favorable and 58 percent unfavorable.

At a policy level when independents were asked which party was better able to handle the economy, 41 percent said the Democratic Party, 28 percent said the Republican Party, and 30 percent said neither. Both parties are well short of a majority. This reflects the fact that the electorate still negatively remembers the Biden economy, but also believes that Republicans didn’t fix it as they promised two years ago.

Democrats would be wise to moderate and not continue down the increasingly extreme progressive path. Republicans and the president need to take a hard look at their own failings and understand that when it comes to voters, especially independents, all the money in the world is no substitute for good candidates with real solutions.

David Winston is the president of The Winston Group and a longtime adviser to congressional Republicans. He previously served as the director of planning for Speaker Newt Gingrich. He advises Fortune 100 companies, foundations and nonprofit organizations on strategic planning and public policy issues, as well as serving as an election analyst for CBS News.

#6175. How to Plan a Trip to the World’s Largest Ski Resort, Les Trois Vallées

Standing at the top of a steep gully, I looked down at the line ahead. A handful of tracks cut through 10 inches of powder to my left, telling the story of the skiers who arrived before me. But I couldn’t help but notice untouched snow under an overhanging cliff face to my right.

Before I dropped in, I looked out at the view ahead. I could make out tiny chairlift towers on the snow-capped peaks and ridgelines on the horizon. It felt as if the entire mountain range belonged to the Les Trois Vallées Ski Resort, one of the best—and the biggest—ski destinations in Europe.

Les Trois Vallées (also known as Les 3 Vallées, or the 3 Valleys) began with the construction of a 19-passenger open-air “chairlift” in 1938 in the small town of Méribel. But it wasn’t until 1971, with the creation of the joint ski pass that offers access to the seven resorts that make up Les Trois Vallées, that the ski area took its current form.

Today, the resort spans three main valleys and has 169 chairlifts accessing nearly 26,000 acres of skiable terrain (for comparison, Park City has 7,300 acres of skiable terrain). That makes it the world’s largest interconnected ski area—and it’s all accessible via a single ski ticket. Lift tickets for each of the seven resorts are available, but the cost savings don’t make it worthwhile—for a couple of extra euros, you can buy a pass that gives you access to the entire resort. Les Trois Vallées is also a convenient destination for Epic Pass holders, who get seven days of skiing at Les Trois Vallées.

Given the destination is so vast, here are some tips for navigating the expansive terrain and various villages that make up Les Trois Vallées, based on my most recent trip in 2026.

An aerial view of the skiing area of Les Trois Vallees, also known as The 3 Valleys.

“We need to ski over there today,” our guide and former ski racer, Timothée “Timy” Theaux, says as he pointed toward a distant ridgeline. “The wind is coming from Italy, so that side of the ridge is where we’ll find the best snow.”

We skied seamlessly from lift to lift until we reached an open bowl with untouched powder. Theaux knew exactly where to go given the current conditions, and how to get there.

Les Trois Vallées isn’t like a typical US resort. The terrain is so vast and complex that skiing it without a guide can be more of a chore than skiing with one. Guides—which you can hire through each resort’s ski school, like ESF Val Thorens—not only know how to navigate the resort and keep you safe off-piste, but also know exactly where to go to score skiers the best possible conditions and overall experience.

I pictured myself without a guide at the resort, spending day after day staring at trail maps, hopping on lifts that dropped me a mile from where I thought they would. Thankfully, our guide’s expertise spared us from what could’ve been a logistical nightmare.

On our third day at the resort, low visibility made it hard to see more than 15 feet ahead. As we impatiently waited for the fog to lift, lapping groomed runs outside of our hotel, Theaux decided to head toward Courchevel.

“Courchevel and Méribel are good to ski when visibility is low,” he told us, explaining that they’re both at a lower elevation and have more tree skiing.

Even if it’s just for a day or two, hiring a guide at the beginning of the trip will help skiers and riders get a feel for Les Trois Vallées and each individual resort. While all seven resorts offer a good mix of terrain for every ability level, some, like Val Thorens, sit at a higher elevation and have more alpine terrain than resorts like Courchevel, which are lower and have more tree skiing.

The terrain is also so vast that it’s not hard to avoid crowds—which typically stick to the pistes at each resort (Courchevel, Val Thorens, and Méribel are some of the more popular ones). Focusing on one resort per day, rather than spending an entire day riding lifts from one side of the resort to the other, is a stellar way to maximize time on snow.

Backcountry skiers can enjoy the vast off-piste areas beyond the resort's groomed runs.

Unlike many US ski areas, there aren’t dedicated off-piste areas marked on a map—everything within (and really, outside of) the resort’s boundaries is fair game. But leaving the pistes requires a guide, or at the very least, knowledge of how to navigate backcountry terrain. A low-angle, mellow backcountry slope can quickly steepen enough to raise avalanche concerns, and skiers who leave the pistes should be able to recognize and manage backcountry hazards. And while not all off-piste terrain at Les Trois Vallées requires the chops of an expert skier, it doesn’t take much to get yourself in trouble. When it came to navigating the resort, keeping us out of trouble, and scoring the best conditions away from the crowds, Theaux took out all of the guesswork.

After several lift rides and traverses, we finally found ourselves in Courchevel, on the opposite side of the resort from where we were staying in Val Thorens. We immediately left the groomed runs and headed for the trees, leaving the crowded pistes behind.

As a New Englander, I feel at home in tight, scrappy tree runs. But leaving the pistes to explore the vast terrain and big lines encompassed by Les Trois Vallées was special. Unlike the runs I’ve grown accustomed to at my local ski areas, pistes at Les Trois Vallées don’t have a hard line defined by thick trees and icy trail edges; almost everything is skiable.

“Dropping into an off-piste line alone, with just your guide, is one of the most special feelings in the world,” says Dan Egan, a pro skier who has been spending winters in France for nearly three decades. He was skiing with us for the week. “You really get to connect with the place in a way you never would on a groomed run filled with people.”

At the top of nearly every chairlift, I spotted about a dozen distant backcountry lines I wanted to explore. Saw-toothed peaks gave way to steep chutes and couloirs, many of which funneled into open powder fields. “I need to come back and ski that,” I found myself thinking about a dozen times per day.

Courchevel is perhaps the spiffiest resort at The Three Valleys—but there are budget-friendly villages nearby.

Each resort town has its own feel, so it’s important to know your priorities before booking. Courchevel, for example, is the most luxurious destination, while Col de la Chambre is perfect for skiers who want to spend their evenings partying. Budget-conscious skiers should consider Brides-les-Bains or Orelle; whereas Les Menuires might be better for families. Saint-Martin and Méribel both have a cozy European village vibe, but Méribel might have the slight advantage for off-piste skiers.

Val Thorens is known for its vibrant aprés-ski scene.

When we first arrived at the Fahrenheit Seven hotel in Val Thorens, I felt like I was in an early 2000s ski movie. The back deck was packed shoulder to shoulder, and the DJ knew just what to play to keep the crowd going. It was the middle of the afternoon on a random Sunday.

While there is plenty of partying to be done all over Les Trois Vallées (the parties at La Folie Douce Val Thorens and La Folie Douce Méribel are not to be missed), there are also more laid-back places to stay. Of the seven resorts and villages, each has its own unique feel and caters to different types of skiers. And all of them offer lift access to the pistes.

“Courchevel is my favorite place to ski because it has a lot of luxury restaurants and accommodations, so hardcore skiers think it’s not for them,” Theaux told us during our low-visibility day. “The off-piste terrain is always empty.”

But if you’re heading to Courchevel for the accommodations over the skiing, Les Airelles Courchevel is about as luxurious as it gets.

Saint-Martin-de-Belleville, slightly below Val Thorens in the Belleville Valley, has the quiet feel of a quaint European hamlet. Like Val Thorens (and most villages around the resort), it’s very walkable, but it's better for skiers who value history and culture over parties. Orelle, made up of 10 hamlets and less popular than other villages, and Brides-les-Bains, known for its thermal waters and spa culture, are also quiet options; the latter is great for budget-conscious travelers.

Méribel, next to Courchevel's high-end restaurants and parties, is known as a family-friendly resort village with plenty of restaurants, bars, shops, and easy lift access. Similarly, Les Menuires is also known as a family destination, but is ideal for skiers looking to explore some of Les Trois Vallées’ bigger off-piste terrain.

Food across the resort is locally sourced, even at on-hill dining options, like Caron 3200.

No matter which village you stay in, good food is never more than a couple of steps or a chairlift ride away.

“I really love the jamon because it requires patience,” says Vincent Suchet, the cheesemaker and grandson of Pépé Nicolas at family-owned, Michelin-starred Chez Pépé Nicolas—located just below Val Thorens in the Belleville Valley. He told us as we sipped wine and tasted local cheeses in a cool, stone-walled cellar: “And I favor the cheeses because you have to wait two years; the flavor is the best when you have to wait.”

The culinary experience stood in stark contrast to what I was used to at US ski areas—fast service, overpriced, yet mediocre cheeseburgers and pizza, and ingredients sourced hundreds, if not thousands, of miles away. At Les Trois Vallées, home to ten Michelin-starred restaurants like Hotel La Bouitte, the food is just as important as the skiing.

During my week at the resort, I couldn’t find a single fast-food or chain restaurant in any of the seven villages. Restaurants are all family-owned, and thought goes into where ingredients are sourced. It’s not uncommon for cheeses to be made by a local farmer whose family has been doing it for generations.

Caron 3200, perched above Val Thorens, is the highest wine bar in Europe.

Even on-hill dining options, like Caron 3200, perched above Val Thorens at 10,500 feet (making it the highest wine bar in Europe), emphasize the culinary experience.

“We have 150 different wines, and most are French,” Eric Bonnel, managing director of Val Thorens Tours, told us as we sipped wine and admired the views of Mont Blanc and the surrounding Alps through the oversized windows. “And we store them at three different altitudes. The reds are aged at a higher altitude because there’s less oxygen.”

On our last evening at Les Trois Vallées, it finally started snowing. I momentarily felt a slight sense of disappointment about leaving ahead of a huge storm. But as I sipped my post-meal Génépi with new and old friends, I realized it didn’t matter. The skiing was only a small part of the Les Trois Vallées experience.

Les Trois Vallées is accessible via train, plane, or car.

For international travelers, the most convenient airport to fly into is Geneva, which is located just a couple of hours from the resort (depending on where you’re staying). While the Swiss airport has the most international flight options, it’s also possible to fly into Lyon, Chambéry, and Grenoble.

Companies like Alpine Fleet offer shuttle transfers from the airports to the resorts in Les Trois Vallées. You can also rent a car, but with the lifts and shuttles available in each resort town, you don’t really need one once you arrive.

Those traveling within Europe or from one of the area’s international airports can access Les Trois Vallées by train, with the Moûtiers﻿ train station serving major cities like London, Paris, Geneva, and Lyon. From the train station, travelers can get to each resort by taxi or bus.

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#6174. Aer Lingus Unveils Business Class Suites With Doors And Its First Premium Economy Cabin On A330s

Aer Lingus has announced a cabin overhaul for 10 Airbus A330 aircraft, with the first refurbished jet scheduled to enter service on October 1, 2027. The initial route will be Dublin–New York JFK, on select EI104/EI105 services. Additional North American routes will follow as more aircraft are refurbished.

This is an A330-only project for now: there will be no corresponding cabin overhaul for the Airbus A321LR or A321XLR.

The refurbished aircraft will feature 28 Collins Elevation business class suites in a 1-2-1 layout. Every passenger will have direct aisle access and a closing door, with each seat converting into a 78-inch flat bed. Improved bedding and amenity kits are also planned.

The renderings look attractive to me. Green upholstery and lighter finishes give the cabin an Irish identity and a premium feel (hello Singapore Airlines). More importantly, the layout addresses a weakness I encountered on my Aer Lingus A330-200 flight from Dublin to Los Angeles. I had a window seat with a passenger beside me and no direct aisle access. Storage was limited too.

I slept well, but the seat was behind what many competitors offered. The lovely crew helped redeem that flight, though warm service should complement a competitive seat rather than compensate for one. Doors are fine, but giving every passenger access to the aisle is the more consequential improvement.

Aer Lingus also plans refreshed dining and a self-service business class snack and refreshment bar, much like SAS offers its on its A330 aircraft:

The new premium economy cabin will have four rows of Recaro R4 seats:

Passengers will receive an upgraded three-course meal, complimentary drinks, bedding, an amenity kit, and noise-reducing headphones. It’s a hardly a unique or transformative hard product compared to its peers, but it’s an increasingly important middle way providing a noticeably more comfortable seat at a price that makes sense relative to economy and business class.

This fills an obvious gap for Aer Lingus. Someone who wants more room than economy offers but cannot justify a business class fare currently has limited options within the airline’s own cabin lineup. A genuine premium economy product gives that passenger another reason to stay with Aer Lingus.

Economy will retain the A330’s appealing 2-4-2 layout, with new seats and adjustable headrests. A self-service snack station is coming to this cabin too.

If I fly economy class, I prefer the A330 or 767. Two seats together by the window remain a compelling reason to choose an A330 when traveling as a couple, especially compared with being part of a block of three on most other widebody aircraft.

Aer Lingus promises more personal space, but we will wait for the final seat pitch and total economy seat count before drawing conclusions about legroom. A redesigned seatback can improve knee clearance without increasing the distance between rows, but padding is also essential.

The refurbished A330s will receive Panasonic Astrova entertainment systems, with 4K screens, Bluetooth headphone pairing, and USB-C charging.

Free Starlink Wi-Fi will also be available, though Aer Lingus says that service is already offered across its transatlantic routes. Passengers do not need to wait for the new cabins to benefit from it. My previous A330 flight featured an entertainment system with missing graphics and internet that was slow but stable. Working screens and fast connectivity would improve the experience considerably.

For a daytime transatlantic flight, I place enormous value on reliable internet. A better seat may help me sleep on the overnight journey to Dublin, but Starlink makes the flight home a far more useful part of my day.

The first aircraft is still almost a year away, and the announcement does not provide a completion date for all 10 retrofits.

An October 1 launch on select JFK flights should not be confused with every Aer Lingus A330 having the new cabins from that date, even to JFK. During the transition, you’ll be able to tell which aircraft have the new business class because that aircraft will also be selling premium economy seats.

I hope Aer Lingus makes the differences clear during booking and handles aircraft substitutions sensibly…

Aer Lingus is giving 10 A330s new business class suites, adding premium economy, and refreshing economy class, with the first aircraft scheduled to debut between Dublin and New York JFK in October 2027.

My last longhaul flight on Aer Lingus left me impressed by the crew but disappointed by parts of the onboard product. This overhaul addresses the seat and technology shortcomings that made me reluctant to seek out the airline. I look forward to trying it. Aer Lingus already showed me how pleasant its service can be. Pair that with a competitive seat and better catering, and I might go out of my way to book it again.

#6173. A Flight Only Bookable With Points Offers Amazing Winter Sun

I often tell people that the best unkept secret with Avios is, in fact, the Avios app. Separate to the British Airways app, the Avios app allows users to set flight alerts and goals, but also gives a heads up about opportunities before they appear anywhere else.

Case in point: before a press release had even hit my inbox, the Avios app alerted me that an ‘Avios only’ flight had just launched. This isn’t the first time Avios has launched a flight only bookable with points, but it is the first time they’ve done one to CAPE TOWN, during peak winter break time.

British Airways and Avios have collaborated on a flight only bookable with Avios, where every seat on the plane is available for sale with points. First, business, premium and economy, all available using Avios. The flights depart as follows…

As noted, these flights are now bookable and if history repeats itself, they won’t be available for long. This plane only has 8 seats in first, so get in quick! One amazing thing about Avios is that they aren’t just the currency of one airline, but a whopping seven. If you have any points with Finnair, Iberia, Qatar, Aer Lingus, Logainair, Vueling or British Airways you can pool points together to book these flights.

Avios is also a transfer partner of Amex, Bilt, Capital One, Chase and plenty of other global financial institutions, so there should be ample opportunity to convert bank points into Avios and get these booked. Hot tip though, ensure there are seats available before you make your transfer, since this will be a hot commodity.

I love any airline rewarding members with flights entirely bookable with points. What makes this one different is that it’s not some off peak, off season destination. It’s Cape Town, easily one of the toughest tickets with any currency, during peak time, perfect for people looking to ditch the weather for the holidays and catch NYE in one of the best cities on earth.

Yes, Cape Town is by far one of my favorites and for any oenophiles, a trip to nearby Stellenbosch or Franschoek is a must. Standard luggage limits apply, so definitely bring enough suitcases to haul back wine. Fin. Head to British Airways website to book.

#6172. Hyatt Adds Stackable Awards, But Globalists Lose Free Parking Benefit

World of Hyatt is adding new Milestone Rewards and allowing members to combine awards starting in 2027. There is plenty to like, particularly the ability to apply a suite upgrade to a free night certificate. But Globalists will lose automatic free parking on award stays, and a uniform one-year expiration will make some awards harder to use.

Hyatt has announced changes beginning January 1, 2027, that will give members more ways to earn and redeem rewards. But there are concessions here too, especially for frequent guests who already make good use of the existing benefits.

Globalists currently receive complimentary parking on eligible award nights at participating hotels where parking can be charged to the room. That can be a substantial benefit, particularly at city hotels and resorts with expensive parking.

Hyatt is replacing that status benefit with a selectable Free Parking Award, first available at 60 qualifying nights or 100,000 Base Points. Each award will cover one qualifying stay of up to seven nights and can be gifted. The improvement is that the award will work on eligible paid stays too. The drawback is that members must select it instead of another reward.

“This decision was made as 70% of Globalists did not use the free parking benefit in 2025; 95% used it 4 times or less, and moving this to a choice allowed the program to retain it for members who value it and introduce other exciting new awards like the $200 Thompson Hotels Credit and the $500 Premium Suite Credit.”

After that, Globalist status alone will not provide free parking.

I appreciate the advance notice, but this is a devaluation for members who regularly drive to Hyatt properties and redeem points, a benefit I used regularly when I was still Globalist and still use on Guest of Honor awards today.

The ability to stack eligible awards is the most appealing part of this announcement and is a very positive change. Starting in 2027, members can combine a Suite Upgrade Award with a free night certificate, including Category 1–4, Category 1–7, Ultimate Free Night, and other eligible promotional certificates.

That addresses a frustrating restriction and having both a free night and a suite upgrade in your account should make it easier to plan a special stay. Other eligible combinations will include Suite Upgrade Awards, Guest of Honor Awards, and Free Parking Awards on the same reservation.

For someone without Globalist status, combining a confirmed suite with Guest of Honor benefits could make for a very nice stay. For a Globalist, being able to confirm a suite while using a free night certificate is also very useful.

There are still restrictions. For example, the new Thompson Hotels and Premium Suite credits cannot be combined with a Free Night Award (I address the new milestone awards below). Hyatt has published the details on its 2027 updates page.

Awards issued beginning January 1, 2027, will expire 365 days after issuance.

That makes the rules easier to remember, but whether it helps depends on the award.

Some milestone free night certificates currently expire after 180 days. Doubling that window is welcome…six months can pass very quickly when you are trying to find the right opportunity to use a certificate.

But Suite Upgrade Awards, Club Access Awards, and Guest of Honor Awards currently can remain valid considerably longer, through the end of February of the second calendar year after they are earned. Reducing those to one year is a loss. Even today as I look to book stays in January and February of next year, I’ll be using those “older” Guest of Honor Awards.

That said, I would not call this change unreasonable and for most people it will be a net positive.

Milestone Rewards will begin at 10 qualifying nights or 20,000 Base Points, with additional milestones every 10 nights through 150.

Here are some notable new choices (which are in addition to the existing choices):

The $500 Premium Suite Credit awarded at 100 nights requires an eligible paid stay of at least two nights. I would evaluate that against what I would otherwise spend…a discount on an expensive suite is only useful if you would not otherwise get the upgrade anyway as a Globalist.

At 50 nights, the suite upgrade choice drops from two awards to one.

At 60 nights, My Hyatt Concierge becomes a selection rather than an automatic benefit (a worthless benefit, in my opinion). Members will choose two rewards from a menu that also includes suite upgrades, parking, points, and a skimpy Delta eCertificate.

If you value your concierge and want to retain the suite upgrades, that leaves no selection for parking…

The new Delta partnership adds eCertificates at milestones from 20–60 nights, two single-visit Sky Club passes at 70, 80, and 90 nights, and Medallion status options at higher thresholds. Of course the Delta Air Lines awards replace the American Airlines awards.

Members will need to link their Hyatt and Delta accounts. Hyatt is also enhancing “Pay My Way” so members can choose awards, points, cash, or Points + Cash for individual nights within a stay.

Hyatt’s technology has long lagged, but this is a nice new update.

The ability to combine free night certificates with suite upgrades is an excellent change. Earlier milestones and additional reward choices should also give members more opportunities to find something useful.

But the parking change is a loss for Globalists who regularly use that benefit. Shorter validity for some awards, fewer suite upgrades at 50 nights, and making concierge access a choice deserve attention too, as much I always loathed my own concierge agents.

I appreciate that Hyatt is providing notice and protecting existing parking benefits during the transition. All in all, I’d say these changes are positive, but will hurt some travelers a lot more than others.

Matthew is an avid traveler who calls Los Angeles home. Each year he travels more than 200,000 miles by air and has visited more than 135 countries. Working both in the aviation industry and as a travel consultant, Matthew has been featured in major media outlets around the world and uses his Live and Let's Fly blog to share the latest news in the airline industry, commentary on frequent flyer programs, and detailed reports of his worldwide travel.

Going to respectfully disagree here on the parking. And no, I am not some defensive fan boy.

As a many year Lifetime Globalist I have taken advantage of the free parking perhaps twice total on redemptions. I would say most are like me and that Hyatt is correct on those numbers they cited. The reality is that aspirational properties, the ones a Globalist would likely be wanting to use points at (I hope!) are rarely going to result in the need for parking. Maldives, Paris, London, New York, Milan, Tokyo, Any SE Asia property are all examples of Park Hyatts (which comprise the most percentage of aspirational hotels) and for which I imagine Hyatt’s number is conservative – betting parking comprises less than 5% of total check-ins on points. In fact, the only Park Hyatt I have ever redeemed points and used parking was in Sydney. And I have stayed at most all of them across the world. Properties like in Chicago are usually priced such as to not justify using points anyway.

I am actually much happier with the 7 day free parking milestone which I can use somewhere like in Chicago where I never redeem points.

Hyatt’s concierge service for globalists is generally useless.

So while having to choose concierge service over other benefits is a devaluation of globalist, it’s, practically speaking, not a huge loss for most members.

The loss of free parking on award-redemption stays is somewhat similar. On paper, it’s a significant devaluation. However, how many guests actually use it? If I’m going to a resort, I’m not arriving with a car. Same for if I’m redeeming points to stay at the Park Hyatt in Paris or wherever. So, practically speaking, it may not be a huge loss for many elites.

What I don’t understand is why wouldn’t you come up with better offerings for globalists who do 100, 120 or 150+ nights?

I wish they would have created a benefit to compensate for the growing number of Hyatt Regency and Grand Hyatt properties WITHOUT an open or operational club lounge.

I personally wish they’d get rid of the club passes since it seems that most properties I’ve been to sinve covid have closed them. I’d prefer free breakfast vouchers for the years I come up short of globalist.
