#6150. Deadline looms for post-9/11 FirstNet reauthorization

In an aerial view, a fire truck sits parked in a neighborhood destroyed by a wildfire on Aug. 11, 2023 in Lahaina, Hawaii. The performance of the FirstNet network during the Maui fires has partially led to calls for a revamp of its structure. (Justin Sullivan/Getty Images)

Supporters of the FirstNet program that provides emergency communications for first-responders still see hope for reauthorization this year, despite continued disagreements over what changes, if any, should be made to how the program is governed.

A House-passed reauthorization bill would shift authority toward the Commerce Department’s National Telecommunications and Information Administration and away from the FirstNet board, which is made up in part by first-responders.

The potential change is opposed by the influential Fraternal Order of Police, but any new bill or amendment would require floor votes in both the House and Senate, a potentially tall order as the 119th Congress draws to a close.

Authority for FirstNet, a program developed in the wake of 9/11, is set to expire in February of 2027 unless lawmakers pass an extension.

The program’s governing entity, the First Responder Network Authority, was created in 2012 in response to recommendations after the terrorist attacks, during which public safety agencies using different radio systems and overloaded phone lines struggled to adequately communicate.

The House passed its bipartisan reauthorization bill in April via voice vote. Senators have not yet taken up that legislation or introduced their own. In January, the Senate Commerce Committee’s Telecommunications and Media Subcommittee held a hearing on the program.

Related: First-responder network reauthorization advances

Craig Wheeler, a spokesman for subcommittee Chair Deb Fischer, R-Neb., said in a statement this week that reauthorization is still a priority.

“Sen. Fischer has been working closely with Chair Cruz on a bill and is having bipartisan discussions with Ranking Member Cantwell,” Wheeler said, referring to Sens. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, and Maria Cantwell, D-Wash.

“Moving a bill as soon as possible remains a top priority for Sen. Fischer, including getting it through both chambers and signed into law by President Trump.”

The House bill would extend authority for FirstNet through fiscal 2037, stagger terms on the authority’s board and require five members of the board with public safety backgrounds, rather than three as needed under current law.

At issue in the reauthorization debate, in part, is control of the First Responder Network Authority.

The House bill would eliminate language in current law that established FirstNet as an “independent” authority within the Commerce Department’s National Telecommunications and Information Administration and would require the administration’s approval for most non-planning or emergency actions, though the bill was amended to include a list of actions the network can take without NTIA approval.

The changes are meant to respond to reports from the Commerce Department's Office of Inspector General that found that the AT&T-run service was not sufficiently available during the Maui wildfires in 2023 and that senior officials of the FirstNet Authority attempted to interfere with audits.

The Maui report noted the small number of FirstNet subscriptions among state and local first responders in the area and in an op-ed earlier this year, Maui Fire Chief Brad Ventura said his department was “not using FirstNet devices” at the time of the fires but is now adopting them. He also supported reauthorization in the op-ed.

Related: First-responders network faced with calls for change

But the shifting of control drew opposition from the Fraternal Order of Police, which prior to the bill’s committee markup urged its members to instead support a “clean reauthorization” of the program.

Jim Pasco, executive director of the FOP, emphasized his group’s desire to see decisions made by the FirstNet board, rather than by NTIA. He said that moving authority away from a group that is required to include first-responders would be “a threat to officer and public safety.”

Yucel Ors, legislative director for public safety and crime prevention at the National League of Cities, said that his group, along with the International Association of Fire Chiefs and other state and local government and public safety groups, worked closely with the House, including on the changes to put some “everyday controls and functions” back directly under the board’s control.

He said the National League of Cities supported the House bill, but that they hope that any changes made to FirstNet’s governance are “not going to impact the day-to-day operations that public safety depend on, rely on, and expect.”

Ors said he expects the Senate would make changes to the House-passed bill, but he doesn’t know if those changes would come in the form of an amendment or an entirely new bill.

No proposed Senate amendment to the House bill, or alternative Senate bill, has yet to emerge.

He expressed concern over the timeline for reauthorization, especially if the Senate doesn’t take up the House bill as is.

A new Senate bill or amendment would require votes in both the House and Senate, with floor time dwindling as both chambers work through must-pass legislation before the end of the year.

Congress could potentially pass a short-term reauthorization of FirstNet. Ors expressed worry that option could jeopardize the public-private relationship with contractor AT&T.

Pasco said he would prefer a short reauthorization over the House-passed bill, but said he hopes a full reauthorization could still pass this Congress.

The House bill has strong bipartisan support and the Senate’s negotiations are also bipartisan. Both Ors and Pasco expressed confidence that if time runs out this year for a reauthorization bill, a new version of the legislation would still have strong prospects under a Democratic Congress.

Additional context regarding the role of FirstNet during the Maui fires was added to this report.

#6149. 3,400+ Miles: Air Canada's Longest Ever Boeing 737 MAX Flights Launch In 4 Weeks

Air Canada is preparing to launch its longest-ever Boeing 737 MAX 8 route in less than four weeks. Beginning December 13, the Canadian flag carrier will connect Vancouver International Airport (YVR) with Liberia International Airport (LIR) in Costa Rica, covering 3,425 miles (5,512 km). The new service will surpass Montreal-Nantes as the airline's longest MAX route by distance, while the return journey will have a scheduled block time of up to eight hours and 55 minutes.

The route will be operated by Air Canada Rouge, the airline's leisure subsidiary, which is undergoing a significant transformation. Air Canada is transferring its 737 MAX fleet to Rouge, while moving older Airbus narrowbodies to mainline operations or retiring them. The result will be a substantially larger Rouge fleet, with nearly 70% more installed seats than at the end of 2025.

Air Canada's new Vancouver-Liberia service will launch on December 13, operating twice-weekly until April 12, 2027, with three weekly departures during selected periods. Flights will use Rouge's 177-seat 737 MAX 8, configured with 12 business-class, 18 preferred economy and 147 standard economy seats. The route is part of Air Canada's expanded winter sun network.

The route will provide another nonstop option for Canadians visiting Costa Rica's Guanacaste region, known for its Pacific beaches and resorts. Air Canada will compete directly with WestJet, which already operates Vancouver-Liberia flights using the MAX 8. The additional service also strengthens Vancouver's position as a departure point for winter leisure travel to Central America.

The new route follows the opening of Rouge's Vancouver crew base in March this year, supporting the airline's Western Canada expansion amidst the ongoing fleet transformation. The updated Rouge cabin includes seatback entertainment, reclining seats, and complimentary Wi-Fi for Aeroplan members, making it better suited for longer leisure flights.

Air Canada's COO Mark Nasr emphasized the importance of a consistent passenger experience across the airline's network.

“When customers step onto our aircraft, they should instantly feel a sense of comfort, care, and pride. This renewal program is about delivering that feeling consistently, across every flight. Every update is designed with our customers in mind, as we introduce an entirely new Air Canada Rouge product.”

Air Canada's 737 MAX 8 has operated some remarkably long routes, including transatlantic flights to Ireland, France, Belgium, and the United Kingdom, as well as services to Hawaii and the Caribbean. However, the new Vancouver-Liberia route will take the top spot at 3,425 miles (5,512 km), exceeding Montreal-Nantes by 98 miles (158 km).

Historical MAX service; A321XLR/787 in 2026

The ranking illustrates how Air Canada has used the MAX to support thinner transatlantic markets. Halifax to London Heathrow Airport (LHR) is particularly significant, recording nearly 2,000 departures since the variant was introduced, while Montreal–Nantes and Toronto–Shannon demonstrate the aircraft's ability to serve secondary European destinations. Several of these routes are now transitioning to the longer-range Airbus A321XLR.

Beyond Europe, the MAX has also supported long leisure routes from Western Canada, including Calgary-Honolulu and Calgary-Kahului. But the aircraft's future is increasingly tied to Rouge's leisure strategy, with Edmonton-Montego Bay joining Vancouver-Liberia in December 2026. These additions illustrate how Air Canada is redirecting its MAX fleet toward vacation destinations while deploying the A321XLR on selected longer international routes.

The list is dominated by leisure destinations across Europe and the Caribbean.

Rouge's transformation involves more than replacing aging Airbus aircraft. At the end of 2025, the subsidiary operated 33 aircraft, comprising 15 A319s, five A320s and 13 A321s. Air Canada's fleet plans envisage an eventual all-MAX fleet of 52 aircraft, representing a 58% increase. The A320s and A321s are being transferred to mainline following refurbishment, while the A319s are being retired.

The capacity implications are substantial. Rouge's fleet will grow from 33 to 52 aircraft, but with the average aircraft capacity also increasing from 164 to 177 seats, the installed fleet seats will increase from 5,428 to 9,204, a gain of 3,776 seats, or 70%. Standardizing around the MAX should simplify training, maintenance and scheduling while providing newer aircraft with improved fuel efficiency.

The larger fleet also gives Air Canada more flexibility to expand leisure flying from Western Canada, supported by Rouge's new Vancouver base. New services to Liberia, Mazatlán and Puerto Escondido illustrate that strategy, while mainline receives refurbished Airbus aircraft and introduces the A321XLR for longer international operations. Vancouver-Liberia is therefore more than a distance record: it represents the emerging role of a substantially larger Rouge operation within Air Canada's network.

#6148. Update: United Resolves System Outage

United said it has resolved a system outage that delayed flights across its network late Monday afternoon.

“We have resolved a technology issue that delayed flight departures,” the airline said in a statement. “While some flights were delayed, there was no impact on flights in progress, or on United Express flights. There is no indication that this was a cybersecurity-related issue.”

Between 4 p.m. and 6 p.m. Eastern time, crews at multiple airports reported they could not get the final weight-and-balance figures required for departure.

United acknowledged a “widespread system outage” in a post on X. In a separate statement, the carrier said it was “troubleshooting a technology issue affecting departing flights.”

The first report identified in radio audio captured by the ATC App came at about 4:02 p.m. ET, when the crew of United flight 2787 in Denver reported trouble getting its final weights. At Chicago O’Hare, the system used to request pushbacks also went down. At Newark, a ramp controller said the outage affected how ramp crews received gate changes.

“We are having an extreme system-wide outage… which is preventing us from closing out flights, which is affecting pretty much all of our mainline departures at this point,” an O’Hare ramp controller said.

Radio reports named at least 30 United flights across 12 airports. Some crews at O’Hare and Los Angeles reported receiving final weights between 4:40 and 5:09 p.m. ET. At 5:11 p.m., an O’Hare ramp controller canceled a United flight’s pushback after it had waited about 20 minutes.

#6147. 11 Best Airbnbs in Stockholm for Historic Architecture, Saunas, and Beach Access

For a break that balances the buzz of discovering a new city with a good dose of fresh air, Stockholm’s mix of lush parks and eclectic architecture is an enduring choice. The city is formed of 14 islands, meaning you’re never too far from a waterfront to amble along. It's packed with historical charm (head to Gamla Stan to see one of Europe’s oldest medieval cobbled streets), as well as stylish boutiques and museums championing everything from Abba to the world’s best-preserved 17th-century warship. While the city is home to a slew of excellent hotels, from elegant converted townhouses to the former home of Astrid Lindgren (author of the beloved Pippi Longstocking book series), you’ll want to look to Airbnb for a real home-from-home vibe.

These 11 excellent rentals throughout the city and its outskirts balance top-notch amenities with the freedom that only comes with a private booking. True to Nordic form, there’s a clutch of homes with their own sauna and steam rooms, and all have either sea or skyline views. Below, the best Airbnbs in Stockholm to book for a weekend of weaving through medieval streets, gallery hopping, and lots of cinnamon buns.

We've vetted these listings based on Superhost status, ratings, amenities, location, previous guest reviews, and decor.

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 1.5 bathsWhy we love it: Historic architecture, prime location, dedicated workspace

Subverting traditional Scandi minimalist sensibilities, this cool retreat in the hip heart of Södermalm channels a moody, more underground kind of charm. On the top floor, light-flooded, open-plan living areas are packed with rich, creamy furnishings and crisp architectural lines—multiple previous guests say that this is one of the most stylish homes they’ve ever stayed in. Downstairs, two tranquil bedrooms are carved directly into the exposed natural rock, so you can sleep beneath historic vaulted ceilings after a long day skipping from sight to sight. On that note: Södermalm is an eclectic area of town, with plenty of vintage shops and wine bars, after which you can hole up in this cocooning, cave-like retreat, as though you’re stepping into your own secret—and very stylish—bunker.

Neighborhood: SödermalmThings to do nearby: Fotografiska, Riddarholm Church, Stockholm City Museum

Number of guests: 2Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Forest access, indoor fireplace, outdoor gas grill

Blink, and you might miss this off-grid, A-frame cabin, hidden among a thick swathe of pine trees. It’s worth searching for: Once you make your way through the foliage, you’ll find a truly wonderful Swedish escape for two. The glass-fronted structure invites in all of the elements, while inside, it’s time to switch off—there’s a crackling open hearth where you can grill all of your meals, and precious little noise other than the rustle of wind through the canopy. Fair warning: There’s a very rustic toilet and seasonal shower about a 30-second walk down the forest path, so if you’re not a DIY fan, perhaps look elsewhere. Nonetheless, for more adventurous sorts, the trade-off means absolute tranquility surrounded by happily grazing sheep and twinkly starry night skies—all within a hop and a skip of the capital.

Neighborhood: VärmdöThings to do nearby: Lillsved Beach, Buddharama Temple, Stora Sandön

Number of guests: 8Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 1.5 bathsWhy we love it: Historic warehouse, steps from the lake, wood-burning fireplace

Wood-beamed ceilings, clattering floors, a muted color scheme, and a signature bright exterior welcome you in from the cold—this former warehouse just oozes 19th-century charm the moment you round the corner. Better yet, it’s totally massive, sprawling across three roomy floors, with a prime spot perched right on the peaceful banks of Åkers canal. A snazzy and social kitchen space opens onto a central island and a fireplace, where all the family will want to gather. When it’s time to bed down, there are cozy curtained sleeping nooks and an additional attic dormitory, adding a playful, rustic vibe. You can rent canoes from host Cecile to paddle down the canal, or jump on an e-bike to explore the surrounding nature reserves. When you return, fire up the outdoor grill and gather around the dining table for a long dinner with more endless views.

Neighborhood: Norrö-StavaThings to do nearby: Prästfjärden lake, Näsudden nature reserve, Åkersbro walking trails

Number of guests: 3Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1.5 bathsWhy we love it: Sea views, sauna, hot tub

This joyfully bobbing houseboat turns the gray blue waters of the Baltic into something akin to your own front lawn—and it does so just 15 minutes from the heady sights of central Stockholm. Panoramic floor-to-ceiling glass means you feel that you’re virtually out on the water—and, of course, you can dive straight into the lake from your bedroom deck. Dry off and hop into the private wood-fired sauna to warm up. Hop off the boat, and you can sunbathe on the jetty, cook up some local catches on the barbecue, or jump into the complimentary canoe. All in all, this is an idyllic waterside playground that active types will love.

Neighborhood: BooThings to do nearby: Kringelgården bakery, Saltsjöbadens golf course, Artipelag

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 1 bathWhy we love it: Sauna, beach access, pet-friendly

Expect some truly good seascape ASMR when you stay here—you’re so close to the water you can hear the waves rolling onto the shore right from the porch. Grab the kayak from the cupboard and head down to the beach to make the most of this beautiful location. It’s a short drive from the home to Stockholm’s city center, but you’re rewarded with much serenity and glorious views instead. For those seeking a secluded family stay, this is the place.

Neighborhood: TyresöThings to do nearby: Sandholmarna nature preserve, Tyresta nature reserve, Lilla beach

Number of guests: 6Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 1.5 bathsWhy we love it: Wood stove, sauna, beach access

This spacious waterside cottage is not in Stockholm’s city center, but by compromising on a 30-minute commute into town, you gain something really special. The owners took the original 130-year-old structure down piece by piece, rebuilding it on their own property. It was worth the effort. Now, it lies surrounded by pine trees in a nature reserve beside a sparkling, clear lake, with the sea just a few steps further in the other direction. A large porch provides the spot for barbecue dinners and sunbathing sessions in the summer, and there are two spas within walking distance for those looking for their Scandi sweat fix—the sea-facing Skepparholmen Spa, and Japanese onsen-style Yasuragi. But you don't have to head that far, as the property has its own sauna. Stay in as long as you can muster, then cool off by jumping in the lake—something all the more satisfactory in the winter months.

Neighborhood: BooThings to do nearby: Boobadet Beach, Nyckelvikens wildlife refuge, Sushi Bar Namiyama

Number of guests: 2Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Rooftop views, beach access, pet-friendly

A previous guest says this flat has a New York City vibe, and we can see why—the interior space is small but stylish, with an industrial bent and views all over the coolest part of Stockholm from the balcony. It’s on the top floor of this apartment block, so the vistas can’t be beat. It’s been a winner for those on work trips, thanks to superfast WiFi and a dedicated workspace, and, unusually for Airbnb stays, you can bring your dog too.

Neighborhood: SödermalmThings to do nearby: Liljeholmsviken waterfront, Högalid Church, Skinnarviksberget

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 1 bathroomWhy we love it: Steam room, in-unit washer/dryer, fully equipped kitchen

For an Airbnb stay that’s as close to checking into a luxury hotel as possible, look to this plush apartment right in the city center. The whole place is brand new, and no expense has been spared on the fittings—there are genuine oak floorboards, Italian travertine surfaces, underfloor heating, and a slew of top-notch furniture, plus little touches such as a shower seat and a gloriously powerful rainfall shower. The best bit is the steam room; there’s no better way to decompress after a long flight or a blustery autumnal walk by the river.

Neighborhood: VasastanThings to do nearby: Vanadislunden park, Odenplan plaza, Swedish Museum of Natural History

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Proximity to metro, private patio, in-unit washer/dryer

If dopamine itself could be characterized as a building, it’d be this one. The place (all 300 square feet of it) is pure joy from top to bottom—with a pink-tiled kitchen, mint-green bathroom, and cozy bedroom nook with yellow walls and blue candy-striped bedding. Cheery artworks add a final flourish. Despite its bijou size, there’s room for two more guests on the pullout bed, and there’s a patio with twinkly fairy lights to sit out on sunny afternoons with a book, a glass of wine, or both.

Neighborhood: ÄlvsjöThings to do nearby: Älvsjö Forest Nature Preserve, Herrängens Gård, Långbro park

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Beach access, sauna, kayak

Forget your average homely fisherman’s cottage—this home here, on the cusp of the lake in the city’s swish Stocksund neighborhood, marks a newer, more modern breed of lake house. It’s chic as anything you’ll find in the city, with smooth, polished concrete floors and knotty pine walls finished with a moody, cocooning interior palette. Sweeping glass windows make the most of the beautiful views that stretch over the water and right to the city as it twinkles on the other side. Grab the kayak and spend an afternoon bobbing on the lake, then stop in for a well-deserved sweat session in the private sauna.

Neighborhood: StocksundThings to do nearby: Restaurang Hemma, Svanholmsparken park, Swedish Museum of Natural History

Number of guests: 3Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Wood-burning fireplace, Aesop toiletries, garden view

This traditional Swedish apartment has had a modern facelift recently. Now it pairs gorgeous original features, including imposing 10-foot-high ceilings and whitewashed floorboards, with a sleek new kitchen and selection of cool designer furniture pieces. There's also a truly cloudlike sofa just made for cozy nights in. The surrounding streets are just as cool as the interiors; this home is smack dab in SoFo—by far Stockholm’s trendiest district—so you're just one street over from a clutch of the best of the city’s bar, restaurant, and café scene.

Neighborhood: SödermalmThings to do nearby: Fotografiska, Stockholm City Museum, Vitabergsparken park

Alaska Airlines will add four new destinations across the U.S. to its map.

But the additions come at a cost: The carrier has discontinued four recently added routes from its hub at Portland International Airport (PDX) in Oregon.

As airline executives say, every route has to earn its place financially in a carrier’s network.

As for the four new destinations, Alaska will serve each of those with one daily flight from its Seattle-Tacoma International Airport (SEA) base. The additions are:

The carrier will also add a new nonstop from SEA to Guadalajara International Airport (GDL) in Mexico. Alaska will offer three weekly flights on Thursdays, Fridays and Saturdays with a 737-800 from March 18, 2027 through Aug. 9, 2027.

Alaska currently serves GDL from Los Angeles International Airport (LAX) and San Jose Mineta International Airport (SJC) in California's Bay Area, schedule data from aviation analytics firm Cirium shows.

The Seattle growth comes as Alaska builds its intercontinental offerings from the Pacific Northwest city. After launching its first long-haul flights in 2025 after its merger with Hawaiian Airlines, Alaska is building out a network of at least 15 intercontinental routes from SEA by 2030.

Next year, Alaska will offer nine long-haul routes from SEA with the addition of Athens International Airport (ATH), Paris-Charles de Gaulle Airport (CDG), Kansai Airport (KIX) in Osaka, Japan, and Faaʼa International Airport (PPT) in Tahiti.

Alaska plans to grow its schedule by about 4% year-over-year in 2027, with the majority in long-haul international additions.

PDX, Alaska’s wunderkind hub of recent years, is losing four recently added routes. The airline will not resume seasonal service in 2027 to:

Alaska continues to serve all four destinations from one of its other hubs.

PDX remains one of Alaska’s fastest-growing hubs as the airline shifts connections to the Oregon city. The carrier's seats at the airport are set to increase 12% in the first half of 2027 compared to this year after a 17% increase during the same period in 2026, Cirium schedules show.

"Portland is a story of focused smart growth that improves utility, strengthens the local franchise and captures the right traffic flows," Andrew Harrison, the chief commercial officer at Alaska, said in September. "[PDX] proves that Seattle and Portland are stronger together, allowing us to serve more customers, connect more traffic and improve the efficiency of our Pacific Northwest network."

As part of its PDX growth, Alaska Airlines opened a new, $18 million lounge at the airport in June.

#6144. Why Does A Plane Seem To Drop If There Are No 'Air Pockets' In The Sky?

Avgeeks are often frustrated when a layperson refers to an air pocket when they are talking about turbulence. They'll say that the airliner they were in entered a seeming vacuum in the sky, and losing lift, it dropped violently and worryingly. Enthusiasts, meteorologists, and pilots know that these air pockets don't really exist.

Air pockets are a myth, but turbulence certainly isn't. Instead of a gap in the air, we can think of turbulence as like a boat traveling through choppy seas. There are a number of factors that can cause it, such as warm air rising, wind that has been disrupted by an obstacle (like a mountain), or clean-air turbulence high in the atmosphere.

The idea that there are gaps in the air that a plane can fall through originates in the early days of flying. Airmen in early and exceedingly slow biplanes would experience a sudden downdraft, and it would feel like the plane was falling through a hole in the sky. These pilots had no instruments and a rudimentary understanding of aerodynamics.

The lack of knowledge led them to conclude that the sky has small pockets of vacuum or low-density air within it that could bring danger to an unsuspecting pilot. There would suddenly be no air to give the plane lift, meaning it could drop out of the sky or lose any semblance of control.

Despite originating over a hundred years ago, the air pocket myth is still pervasive amongst those with little interest in aviation. As part of the Ask the Expert series on its YouTube channel, Swiss International Air Lines asked various members of the public what they think an air pocket is. They seemed to parrot the myth, with statements like "an air pocket is differences in air pressure," and "it's when the plane suddenly drops."

The specific type of turbulence where an aircraft suddenly drops or rises in altitude is caused by windshear. This is a sudden change in wind speed or direction within a small amount of atmosphere. Speaking with Live Science, Guy Gratton, an aeronautical engineer, test pilot, and professor of aviation and the environment at Cranfield University, said:

"If a plane is flying along at a constant speed and height, then suddenly the headwind reduces, or it enters a descending column of air, this can cause the aircraft to suddenly descend. Conversely, if the headwind rapidly increases, or the plane enters a rising column of air, this can cause it to suddenly climb."

A common type of windshear is a microburst, which is a small column of rapidly descending air underneath a storm cloud. Airbus notes three dangerous phases that an aircraft goes through when encountering a microburst, which are particularly troublesome given that this phenomenon inherently occurs at a relatively low altitude. The table below explains these phases and how pilots respond to them.

On entering the microburst, the aircraft hits a severe headwind gust that greatly increases airspeed and lift.

The pilot reduces throttle and pushes the stick forward, forcing the aircraft's unintended ascent to stop.

Flying through the microburst, a downdraft strikes the aircraft, forcing it to descend.

The pilot adds more power and initiates a climb.

On exiting the microburst, the wind speed suddenly changes, causing a tailwind. Airspeed and lift instantly drop.

As above, the pilot must avoid the forced descent getting out of control.

There are several common locations where an airliner might encounter windshear. This includes in the vicinity of a large cumulonimbus thundercloud or at the edges of a jet stream. In both cases, an aircraft will be traveling through air that has a number of air currents going in different directions.

The air pocket myth oversimplifies turbulence, as it can actually have a range of different causes. Mechanical turbulence occurs when an obstacle disrupts the usual airflow. At high altitudes, a mountain many thousands of feet below can cause air to rise to meet the aircraft. The effect can also occur at lower altitudes because of large buildings.

Another human-made type of turbulence is wake turbulence. It happens as a result of the spiraling air currents at large planes' wingtips. As a result, turbulence occurs most often at busy airports and is most dangerous to small aircraft.

Rising air also causes a bumpy ride in the case of convective or thermal turbulence. The Earth does not heat up evenly. Hot spots on the ground cause the air directly above it to rise. This turbulence is most common on sunny afternoons, meaning fine weather does not indicate smooth flying. Cumulus clouds, which form because of ground warming, can indicate approaching turbulence.

Weather also causes frontal turbulence, happening at the boundary between a warm and a cold front. The air in the cold front can rapidly displace the warm front air, which is forced upwards. This turbulence is visible because thunderstorms often develop at these boundaries.

Air pockets may not be real, but modern aviation has seen the rise of a phenomenon that is just as terrifying. Clean air turbulence occurs without any visual warning. It can't be detected by standard weather radar systems. This means pilots often don't have the ability to warn passengers and crew members to return to their seats and put their belts on.

The table below uses Skybrary data to explain five notable incidents in the last decade that have been caused by clear-air turbulence. It shows that, while the phenomenon may not be dangerous for the entire aircraft, it can cause serious issues for those who are not expecting it.

In clean air turbulence, the first officer disengaged the autopilot without communicating with the captain. The aircraft exceeded its maximum permitted airspeed and four unsecured cabin crew were injured.

The aircraft encountered severe turbulence while crossing the Pyrenees. Two cabin crew were seriously injured, causing the aircraft to divert.

In unexpected turbulence, the senior member of the cabin crew fell and was injured. An investigation revealed the pilots had wrongfully released cabin crew from their secure positions.

During a relatively light period of clean air, a passenger was seriously injured despite wearing their seatbelt. The passenger struck their armrest, resulting in a broken rib.

During captain upgrade line training, the aircraft encountered clean air turbulence. The pilot's response was excessive, leading to a pitch change from -2.3 degrees to +6.3 degrees in one second. The unsecured cabin crew were injured.

Clear-air turbulence typically occurs at altitudes above 15,000 feet (4,570 m), often near jet streams, which cause rapid changes in wind speed. Their location is the only aspect that is predictable, so pilots can lessen the risk by changing altitude or flying around the area. They can also instruct passengers and crew members to stay seated when the aircraft is entering a high-risk area.

Data from the University of Reading's meteorology department shows that global warming has caused an increase in turbulence by 55% in some regions. Human-caused climate change intensifies jet stream currents and alters atmospheric temperatures, leading to stronger windshear. It has also increased the prevalence of clear-air turbulence. An increase in turbulence will lead to an increase in widely known turbulence-related incidents.

That could lead to a rise in wrongful assumptions that air pockets are involved, particularly with clean air turbulence being a phenomenon that can seem unexplainable. An example of one such recent notable turbulence incident happened in late October onboard a United Airlines flight from Daniel K. Inouye International Airport (HNL) to Los Angeles International Airport (LAX).

The Los Angeles Times reported that UA1157, operated by a Boeing 777-200, descended more than 3,000 feet (914 meters) in about one minute. Four flight attendants were injured, one of whom was hospitalized. All the 190 passengers escaped unscathed. However, the incident was concerning. A passenger called Marly Wadlington told ABC 7:

“I was watching a movie, and all of a sudden we just dropped. And it felt like we dropped pretty far. It started shaking, everyone was yelling. We were all super scared.”

Flights involving Hawaii have been particularly impacted by turbulence in recent years. The most worrying example was an Airbus A330-200 flight in December 2022. The turbulence incident injured 24 people, four of whom were seriously injured. SFGATE has reported a 30% increase in moderate-or-greater turbulence affecting the Hawaii and West Coast region.

#6143. Trump says no Iran deal needed after conflict drove GOP’s midterm losses

President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance salute during a Wednesday ceremony at Arlington National Cemetery in honor of Veterans Day. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)

President Donald Trump on Thursday shut down his administration’s on-again-off-again talks with Iran, saying he would not seek a deal to formally end the nine-month-old conflict with Tehran.

The possible end of the pursuit of a diplomatic solution came nine days after Trump and congressional Republicans suffered massive losses in the midterm elections. House Democrats will have more than 250 seats come January, and Senate Democrats will have at least 55 seats in the Senate — with Alaska’s competitive race still uncalled.

Polls leading up to Election Day and since have shown that a majority of voters, and a sizeable chunk of Trump’s Republican base, felt the Iran conflict was a mistake.

Vice President JD Vance penned a lengthy social media post the day after the election, blaming, in large part, the Iran war for the coast-to-coast Democratic victories. Some GOP lawmakers have also called for an end to the conflict, which drove up fuel and other commodity prices.

"The reason we lost is the war," Vance wrote the morning after the GOP wipeout. "The president himself said so last night."

Trump has said that he agrees with Vance’s assessment but that if he had to decide again whether to join Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in striking Iranian targets, he would reach the same conclusion. On Monday, he told reporters that the Iran war "militarily is effectively over."

Vance had been Trump’s designated top negotiator in the talks with Iran’s remaining leaders, but the president said Thursday on social media that he had ordered his second-in-command to instead “focus his complete and total attention on the Massive Corruption and Crime taking place in Democrat run Cities and States throughout the U.S.”

“We don’t need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed,” he added. “We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!"

The situation along the Strait of Hormuz remains contested and dangerous for commercial vessels, including ones that deliver a large amount of the world’s oil products. Iranian officials contend that they control most of the key waterway.

Trump, Vance and other administration officials have said in recent weeks that they were open to continuing talks with Iran, while criticizing Tehran's negotiating tactics. Last week, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who also is Trump’s national security adviser, told reporters that Iran's latest demands were unreasonable.

Trump’s announcement Thursday could represent his latest way to try assuaging GOP voters, including members of his “Make America Great Again” base. A Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted after the midterms and released Tuesday showed that a majority of Republicans (51 percent) want Congress to pass legislation that would end the Iran conflict. Overall, 71 percent of Americans would support such a bill, the survey found.

The conflict was front-and-center during the midterms campaign.

Republican former Rep. Mike Rogers, who lost the Senate race in Michigan to Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, called for the Iran conflict to end "quickly."

“Michigan families are struggling with the price of everyday life. Groceries cost too much. We have to bring prices down," Rogers said in one campaign ad.

On Capitol Hill, GOP lawmakers have tried giving Trump cover, while raising some concerns about high gas prices and questioning whether the president and his team have a viable exit strategy.

As the midterms campaign hit the homestretch in late September, two Iowa Republicans in tight races, Reps. Zach Nunn and Mariannette Miller-Meeks, voted with Democrats on a measure to end the conflict.

“With the negotiating window closed, sustained combat operations now require congressional authorization,” Nunn, an Air Force veteran, wrote on social media. “I will not support another open-ended war.”

Nunn and Miller-Meeks both lost their seats last week, despite breaking with the president over the war.

Trump’s declaration this week of a military end to the Iran war came more than seven years after he offered some foreshadowing during a June 25, 2019, exchange with this CQ Roll Call reporter in the Oval Office.

Asked that day what his exit strategy would be if war ever broke out with Iran, he said: “You’re not going to need an exit strategy. I don’t do exit strategies.”

#6142. Starlux Adds First Route to Australia, New Zealand

Taiwanese carrier Starlux is branching out to Australia and New Zealand with a new, one-stop connection.

Starting March 23, 2027, the airline will fly from Taipei to Sydney to Auckland. Flights will initially operate four times weekly, then switch to daily on May 1. Starlux will operate the route using Airbus A330-900 aircraft.

Taipei-Sydney-Auckland will be the airline’s first one-stop or through route; all other flights are nonstop from Taiwan. Officials said the one-stop approach will give travelers access to “two incredible destinations in one journey.”

Starlux said it is working with Qantas to arrange connecting flights to other destinations in Australia, New Zealand, and Fiji.

Starlux is headquartered in Taipei and mainly flies within East and Southeast Asia, though it also offers service to North America and Europe. In the U.S., it serves Los Angeles, San Francisco, Seattle, Phoenix, and Ontario, California.

The  is getting a significant overhaul, pairing a higher annual fee with new Atmos Rewards earning rates and a collection of perks for businesses that regularly fly on Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines.

Starting Nov. 18, new applicants can earn 10 points per dollar on qualifying flights booked through Atmos™ for Business, receive four Alaska Lounge passes annually and work toward flight discounts and bonus status points through spending.

The biggest winners may be companies with multiple employee cardholders that regularly book Alaska or Hawaiian flights. They'll pay a flat $195 annual fee regardless of how many employee cards they issue, while benefiting from new travel perks.

However, the refresh also eliminates some valuable benefits, including the annual $99 Companion Fare and the $100 discount on an Alaska Lounge+ membership. Existing cardholders won't automatically transition to the new version and can keep their current benefits.

New applicants can earn a limited-time offer of 90,000 bonus points after spending $6,000 on purchases within the first 90 days of account opening, worth about $1,440 based on TPG's November 2026 valuations. By point total, that's the largest offer in TPG's recorded history for the card, but it's not the richest because the new offer doesn't include Alaska's famous $99 Companion Fare.

Starting Nov. 18, the Atmos Rewards Business card will feature a new flat annual fee regardless of the number of cards, stronger rewards on flights booked through Atmos for Business and several new travel-day perks.

Annual fee: $195 for the company, with no additional fee for employee cards (was previously $70 + $25 per card, including for the primary cardholder)

The refresh also takes a few things away.

New cardholders will no longer earn 2 points per dollar spent on gas, electric vehicle charging, shipping and local transit/ride-hailing. New cardholders will also lose the ability to earn the annual Companion Fare through card spending and the $100 discount on an annual Alaska Lounge+ membership.

Overall, the theme is clear: The refreshed card concentrates its value around Alaska and Hawaiian travel, especially for companies willing to book through Atmos for Business and issue cards to multiple employees.

If you opened your before Nov. 18, 2026, you won't automatically receive the refreshed benefits or move to the new annual-fee structure.

Instead, Bank of America says existing cardholders will keep their current benefits, including the opportunity to earn the annual $99 Companion Fare under the previous card's terms.

If you're interested in switching to the refreshed card, you can call Bank of America at 1-800-892-3219 to explore your options.

Applications submitted before Nov. 18 will also remain under the previous card offering, even if they're still pending.

One of the biggest changes is the new annual-fee structure.

The previously charged $70 per company plus $25 per card, including the owner’s card. Now, it’s a flat $195 regardless of how many cards you have. A solo business owner will now pay more than double what they paid before, a company with five cards pays the same as before, and one with six or more pays less. This is arguably the most significant part of the refresh.

Each cardholder will continue to receive a free checked bag for themselves and up to six guests on the same reservation when the flight is paid for with the card. They also receive preferred boarding on eligible Alaska and Hawaiian flights.

That could make the card particularly appealing to small businesses with several West Coast or Hawaii-based road warriors. The more employees who consistently use the travel benefits, the easier it becomes to justify the companywide fee.

Solo owners who do not need employee cards may find one of the personal Atmos cards better suited to their needs.

In that case, you won't earn points from business spending, but you can enjoy similar perks with the Atmos™ Rewards Ascent Visa Signature® credit card for a lower annual fee or take advantage of more generous benefits (albeit with a higher fee) on the Atmos™ Rewards Summit Visa Infinite® credit card.

However, neither is a direct replacement for a business card, particularly for owners who want to separate business expenses or issue employee cards.

Related: Atmos Ascent vs. Atmos Summit: The Summit is better—but not for everyone

In addition to checked-bag and preferred-boarding perks, the refreshed card will include one Alaska Lounge pass per calendar quarter, for a total of four per account anniversary year. That cadence is best suited to a consultant or salesperson who flies throughout the year, rather than a company whose only major trip is an annual conference.

Meanwhile, the waived fee for same-day confirmed changes ($50 on most Alaska flights) could be particularly useful for employees whose meetings finish early, run late or move unexpectedly. That practical flexibility may save some employees frustration — and save the business itself money on fees.

The card also adds a $50 Instant Travel Delay Credit voucher, which can be used toward a meal or drink at the airport when an eligible flight is canceled or delayed by at least two hours on the day of travel.

Despite the new higher fee, even a solo business owner could potentially offset much of the $195 annual fee through these travel benefits. Someone who checks a bag on two round-trips would save $180; visit a lounge on each of those trips and you'll save another $130 compared to buying day passes.

Related: Alaska Airlines airport lounges: How to get access to this VIP space

Earning 10 points per dollar sounds exceptional, but it only applies to flights booked through the Atmos for Business website, the airlines’ self-managed booking platform. That means companies that don't qualify for Atmos for Business — it requires a minimum of $5,000 in annual travel spend — or businesses that book through a corporate travel agency or another platform won't earn this higher return.

Other eligible Alaska and Hawaiian purchases earn 3 points per dollar spent, dining earns 2 points per dollar spent and everything else earns 1 point per dollar. Companies with an eligible Bank of America business account also receive a 10% bonus on points earned from card purchases, effectively turning the 10-point rate into 11 points per dollar.

Lastly, travelers who select the Price Paid earning option and hold Atmos Platinum or Titanium status can earn 20 points or more per dollar on qualifying flights booked through Atmos for Business.

The card's weak general spending rate makes it better suited as a secondary card specifically for Alaska and Hawaiian spending than as a business’s only credit card.

The refreshed no longer includes its annual $99 Companion Fare (plus taxes and fees from $23), which cardholders prior to Nov. 18 earned after spending $6,000 during an account anniversary year.

That is a significant loss for owners who could redeem it for two travelers flying together. Four lounge passes and same-day change flexibility may be more useful for employees traveling alone, but they aren't an automatic replacement for a Companion Fare.

While the new discounts could be valuable for businesses with substantial spending, the $100,000 threshold is significantly higher than the previous $6,000 requirement for earning a Companion Fare.

The welcome offer drops the Companion Fare too, but it includes more points than past offers. Its 90,000 points are enough for three round-trip economy tickets between the West Coast and Hawaii on Alaska or Hawaiian, a one-way ticket on American Airlines in transatlantic business class or a round-trip premium economy ticket from Seattle to Tokyo on an Atmos partner airline.

The refreshed Atmos Rewards Business Card has a higher starting price, but it also has a clearer identity: It's built for companies with multiple cardholders and for recurring Alaska or Hawaiian travel.

Businesses that need employee cards, book substantial airfare through Atmos for Business and have employees who can use the lounge passes and same-day change waiver may come out well ahead.

However, the loss of the Companion Fare and several business spending bonus categories makes the card less appealing for some existing cardholders.

Sole proprietors or companies that don't book through Atmos for Business may still have a case for the card, but they'll need to run the numbers more carefully. And companies that rarely fly either airline or primarily need rewards on everyday operating expenses will likely find the card too specialized.

#6140. Avelo Airlines Launches 16 New Routes In 4 Weeks: See Full List Now

Newish airlines tend to grow strongly, benefiting from the revenue, unit cost, market share, and competitive advantages of doing so. For example, five-year-old Breeze Airways' passenger traffic grew by 47% in the 12 months to August. In distinct contrast, Avelo Airlines' passenger numbers fell by 15%.

Avelo has been struggling recently as it seeks to find what works. As such, it has cut many routes, including its entire international operation, and removed multiple served airports from its map. However, the airline, whose fleet consists of 17 Boeing 737-700s and 737-800s, will launch 16 new routes in November and December. Still, compared to the same two months in 2025, 30+ routes have been removed.

Analysis of the airline's schedule submission to Cirium Diio has been explored. This compared the budget operator's network between January 2025 and October 2026 with what is set to operate in November 2026. The process found that the following ten routes will launch. This includes a return to the Caribbean. However, as the two routes will be to Aguadilla, Puerto Rico, they'll be domestic. Aguadilla is a brand-new destination for Avelo.

Half of the entries will be from McKinney (DTX), where Avelo's latest base just opened. Located around 34 miles (54 km) north of downtown Dallas, McKinney's passenger terminal opened on November 11. Not surprisingly, that was exactly when the ultra-low-cost carrier Avelo began flying from the airport. In doing so, the carrier now serves three airports in the Lone Star State: Dallas/Fort Worth, McKinney, and Houston Intercontinental.

McKinney is near Dallas, Concord is near Charlotte, and Lakeland is between Orlando and Tampa

Initially, Avelo had one aircraft based at McKinney. However, that'll jump to two this month and, eventually, three. When a trio of aircraft are stationed there, nearly a third of the budget carrier's fleet will be there, which perhaps illustrates the challenges that it has faced.

Simple Flying's Live Flight Tracker shows that the N801XT and N803XT, both of which are 737-800s, will be there this week, although the specific airframes may change in the future. Generally, each aircraft has four legs per day. For example, on November 19, the 20.8-year-old N803XT, which is ex-Turkish Airlines, will fly McKinney-Orlando-McKinney-Las Vegas-McKinney.

As part of the announcement, Allegiant will pull out of Chicago Midway. Find out more now!

They will all be from McKinney and, like the five mentioned earlier, will be brand-new markets. Significantly, it'll be the first time that Avelo has flown to Denver, albeit only with one route and four weekly departures. It'll mark Avelo's return to Colorado after last flying there in September 2024 from Burbank to Colorado Springs.

Previously, the airline also flew from Burbank to Grand Junction and from Burbank and Las Vegas to Fort Collins. The new route contributes to Avelo having a record number of flights to Atlanta, the world's busiest airport for passengers but not for flights

However, context is needed. Only three markets will exist: Lakeland, McKinney, and Tweed New Haven. Previously, Avelo flew there from Wilmington, Delaware. Things are not this simple, as it appears that Lakeland-Atlanta service will end in early January 2027. No flights are scheduled beyond there, but that might change.

US Department of Transportation (DOT) information currently extends to August 2026. In the 12 months to that summer month, Avelo transported nearly 2.3 million round-trip passengers. Compared to the prior 12 months, traffic fell by 15%. While not a like-for-like comparison, Breeze grew by 47%.

Avelo's average load factor is 77.7%. While that is low compared to many budget operators around the world, it is relatively normal for US airlines. As the number of seats for sale fell by 16%, the smaller reduction in traffic (-15%) means that the load factor improved to the highest level since the 12 months to August 2023. What is not known is how fares changed.

#6138. Transfer Amex Points To Avianca Lifemiles With 10% Bonus: Worth It?

The Amex Membership Rewards program has just introduced a new bonus for points transfers to Avianca Lifemiles. While this is hardly the biggest bonus, something is better than nothing, and the program is useful for Star Alliance redemptions.

Between November 16 and December 16, 2026, it’s possible to receive a 10% bonus when moving points from Amex Membership Rewards to Avianca Lifemiles. This is being offered on Amex’s end, so when you go the points transfer page, make sure that you see this offer available.

Ordinarily points transfer between programs at a 1:1 ratio (in increments of 1,000 points), while through this promotion you’d get 1,100 Lifemiles for every 1,000 Amex Membership Rewards points transferred. Points transfers from Amex to Avianca are typically instant, and the bonus miles will post the same time as the standard miles.

We see transferable points currencies frequently offer bonuses on transfers to Lifemiles, and we’ve seen such promotions from most major transferable points currencies in the past year.

Avianca is in the Star Alliance, which means you can redeem Lifemiles on all Star Alliance airlines without any fuel surcharges. Really this is the core value proposition of the program, since this is a great way to book Star Alliance premium cabin seats at a huge discount. Check out my guide on how to redeem Lifemiles for ideas on how to use these miles.

With a specific use in mind, this could represent a great value, whether you’re looking at traveling first class on All Nippon Airways, or are looking at traveling in business class on a countless number of airlines. Everyone has to crunch the numbers for themselves and decide whether this makes sense or not.

Let me emphasize that in some cases, Lifemiles doesn’t have access to the same award availability as Star Alliance partners, for better or worse. Sometimes Lifemiles doesn’t have access to partner awards that other programs do have access to, and other times the inverse is true.

That’s why I always recommend doing some “dummy” award searches before buying miles, so you can get a sense of how award availability lines up with your needs.

Through December 16, 2026, the Amex Membership Rewards program is offering a 10% bonus on points transfers to Avianca Lifemiles. If you’re looking to redeem on Star Alliance partners, there’s definitely some value to be had here.

With the 10% bonus, you can potentially get a very reasonably priced award on Avianca or one of its Star Alliance partners. As always, the challenge is actually finding award availability. Admittedly I wouldn’t make a speculative points transfer, though, as we have seen some bigger transfer bonuses in the past.

Do you plan on taking advantage of this Amex transfer bonus to Avianca Lifemiles?

#6137. Former Maine Gov. Paul LePage declared winner of open House seat

Former Maine Gov. Paul LePage, fifth from right, joins incoming members Thursday for their freshman class photo on the House steps outside the Capitol. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

Paul LePage, the former Maine governor who once said he was “Donald Trump before Donald Trump,” is heading to Congress.

The Associated Press called the race for the open 2nd District on Thursday after the Maine Secretary of State’s office tabulated the votes under the state’s ranked choice voting system. LePage ended up ahead of Democratic state Auditor Matt Dunlap 50.8 percent to 49.2 percent.

Dunlap had already conceded the race to LePage, who will succeed retiring Democratic Rep. Jared Golden in the sprawling district, which includes much of Maine outside the Portland and Augusta areas.

“Paul LePage is already hard at work for the people of Maine attending Congressional orientation, meeting with national leaders, and making it clear the political parties need to work together for the American people,” Brent Littlefield, a senior adviser to LePage, said in a statement Thursday. “As Paul said, he will work with anyone, regardless of Party, to put Maine first.”

LePage’s win is a glimmer of good news for Republicans, who saw massive losses across the country in last week’s midterm elections. He is one of three Republicans, along with Texas’ Jace Yarbrough and Tennessee’s Brent Taylor, to have flipped a House seat, although Maine’s 2nd District is the only one of the three that wasn’t redrawn to favor the GOP.

LePage’s win also means that at least one Republican will continue to represent New England in Congress, taking up the mantle from Maine Sen. Susan Collins, who lost her own reelection bid last week.

Golden, who was first elected in 2018, had been a top Republican target throughout his time in Congress. But the lawmaker, known for bucking his party, proved difficult to unseat in the past two election cycles.

“I also know a thing or two about winning in tough circumstances. So, I know you have to tip your hat to Paul LePage for winning in the midst of this Blue Tsunami,” Golden said in a social media post last week.

Dunlap initially launched his campaign as a primary challenge to Golden in the fall of 2025, only for the congressman to announce his retirement a month later. Dunlap went on to win a four-way contest for the Democratic nomination.

#6136. Transfer Capital One Miles To Qatar Airways Privilege Club With 15% Bonus: Worth It?

The Capital One mileage program has just introduced a new bonus for points transfers to Qatar Airways Privilege Club. While the percentage bonus amount isn’t huge, there’s potentially value to be had, especially given the flexibility these rewards offer.

Between November 15 and December 14, 2026, it’s possible to receive a 15% bonus when moving points from Capital One to Qatar Airways Privilege Club. This is being offered on Capital One’s end, so when you go the mileage transfer page, make sure that you see this offer available.

Ordinarily rewards transfer between programs at a 1:1 ratio (in increments of 1,000 miles), while through this promotion you’d get 1,150 Qatar Airways Privilege Club Avios for every 1,000 Capital One miles transferred. Points transfers from Capital One to Qatar Airways are typically instant, and the bonus rewards will post the same time as the standard rewards.

We see transferable points currencies frequently offer bonuses on transfers to a variety of Avios currencies, and you can of course move rewards between those various currencies. We’ve definitely seen bigger than 15% bonuses in the past, but there’s no guarantee we’ll see a higher offer return anytime soon.

I’d argue that the Qatar Airways Privilege Club program is pretty lucrative nowadays. For one, keep in mind that Qatar Airways uses Avios as its rewards currency, so it’s possible to transfer Avios at a 1:1 ratio between the various programs that earn Avios. That includes Aer Lingus AerClub, British Airways Club, Finnair Plus, and Iberia Plus.

This means that you could use this offer to indirectly convert Citi ThankYou points into British Airways Avios with a 15% bonus as well. That’s something that will no doubt interest some.

However, there’s also huge value directly with the Qatar Airways Privilege Club program. Privilege Club has decent award pricing on Qatar Airways flights, and also has access to more business class award availability than partner programs (though availability still isn’t great). Privilege Club also has several unique airline partners, ranging from JetBlue, to RwandAir, to Virgin Australia, opening up valuable redemption opportunities.

Through December 14, 2026, the Capital One program is offering a 15% bonus on points transfers to Qatar Airways Privilege Club. If you’re looking to acquire any “flavor” of Avios, this could be a great value, as this is also a way to get rewards with British Airways, Iberia, etc.

However, if you’re thinking of making a speculative transfer to earn Avios, I might wait for a bigger offer, as we do sometimes see 30%+ bonuses on transfers to some Avios currencies.

Do you plan on taking advantage of this Privilege Club transfer bonus?

#6135. Hello, OMAAT Readers! How I Got Here And What’s Next

Isn’t this a little surreal? After years of reading OMAAT, here I am writing my very first post.

First of all, a huge thank you to Ben for such a lovely introduction, and for everyone who gave me such a warm welcome in the comments already. I’m really looking forward to getting to know the OMAAT community Ben has built over the years.

In the first of what will undoubtedly be a lot of posts for One Mile at a Time, I thought I’d share a bit about who I am and what you can expect from me going forward.

I’m literally asking myself that as I write this.

Funnily enough, it was never my dream to be a writer, journalist, blogger, or anything similar. The only thing I can ever remember wanting to be “when I grew up” was a pilot. Despite several applications and reaching the final stage of cadet schemes with Aer Lingus and British Airways, it didn’t work out for me.

Determined to work in the industry, I quit my soul-destroying city job in London to do a Master’s in Air Transport Management at the University of Loughborough in the U.K. I was then offered 2 very different jobs: a junior marketing role with Air Transat, or to be part of a small team starting up TPG’s U.K. office. As a natural risk-taker, I took the latter. After almost 8 years of writing for various publications and dabbling in some video content, I’ve realized that this is what I was meant to be doing all along — the job just didn’t exist when I wanted to be a pilot as a kid.

So why OMAAT? Why now? I spent the last 2 years traveling the world, working remotely, in search of somewhere I felt connected enough to call home. In my heart of hearts, I always knew that was going to be Rio, so I moved here in September this year. I’ve also been considering a more permanent home for my writing and my online presence, so when happenstance did its thing and Ben offered me a full-time online home at OMAAT, it was the perfect opportunity.

I’m honored to have been entrusted to write alongside Ben, whose expertise I’ve learned from over the years. While I don’t promise to be an expert on everything, my almost 8 years of experience in this industry should hopefully mean my expertise meets the standard expected here.

What started out as a passion for planes and aviation has turned into a love of all things travel, loyalty, and the miles and points that help make it happen. I’m really looking forward to sharing some of my learnings, experiences, and tips and tricks from the past couple of years that should complement Ben’s breadth of knowledge.

To start with, much of what you’ll see from me will be written. But as Ben said, the plan is to gradually bring in more video and social content, which I’m really looking forward to helping OMAAT with.

I’m also a self-proclaimed expert on Rio and Brazil (I’ve been coming here since 2009), so if there’s any specific Rio, Brazil, or wider South American travel advice, reviews, or insights you’d like, I’d be more than happy to help, even if it means I have to hop a plane for the research. 😝

I’ll leave it at that for now, as I need to get packing to fly across the Pond for an exciting aviation event this week. All will be revealed soon. 🤓✈️

I’m very excited and honored to be Ben’s first full-time writer in a very long time. Today is the first day of a new adventure for myself, Ben, and the OMAAT behind-the-scenes team, and I can’t wait to bring you, the readers, along for the ride.

#6134. Alaska Airlines Eyes New Long-Haul Boeing 787 Route: But There's A Major Twist

Alaska Airlines is keen to fly to Lisbon, which is the capital of Portugal and an important destination for tourism. The oneworld member has previously expressed interest in flying there. A major ongoing stumbling block is the lack of slots, at least until, and if, Lisbon's new airport opens in many years.

As Ishrion Aviation has pointed out, Alaska Airlines applied for slots for a daily service to Lisbon. Unsurprisingly, it was not granted any of them. Slots do exist, but only in limited numbers and at particular times. It is likely that the growing US operator would either have to reduce its request substantially (say, to a logical three weekly flights) or accept inferior times, as WestJet did. Given Alaska Airlines' hub structure, a poor schedule would not be sensible.

The carrier has big plans for its long-haul network, although it is finding the going tough for now. Recently, it called its long-haul routes 'a drag', but they'd always take time to develop, even before the rise in the price of fuel. Against this backdrop, it'd be reasonable to question the appeal of potential future flights between Seattle, obviously Alaska Airlines' primary hub, and the Portuguese capital.

In the 12 months to September 2026, booking data via OAG shows that 22,700 round-trip passengers flew indirectly between the two cities. Obviously, that volume is small, although nonstop flights, along with hopefully strong promotions, would easily grow that by 40% to 50% in the first season.

Nonetheless, the supposed daily frequency would be highly excessive (three weekly flights would make much more sense). As such, it would therefore rely even more than usual on lower-yielding transfer traffic via Seattle.

Despite the low existing traffic, Lisbon is Seattle's third-largest unserved European market, excluding places like Athens, which Alaska Airlines has already announced. Zurich was the top unserved market (36,100 passengers), which stopped having nonstop flights with the Swiss leisure operator Edelweiss in 2025, followed by the oneworld hub of Madrid (25,500).

Of course, traffic (both existing and likely stimulated) is just one part of it. Across all airlines, cabins, and passengers, the average fare to Lisbon was $641 one-way (excluding a fuel surcharge, taxes, and add-ons). That was similar to Barcelona, to which Delta Air Lines began flying this year, almost certainly to get in before Alaska Airlines announced the route. However, Lisbon flights would cover less distance and be less expensive to serve.

The airline's international expansion continues.

More notably, and perhaps worryingly, Seattle-Athens had an average one-way fare of $646, which was less than 1% higher than Lisbon's. However, flights to the capital of Greece, which Alaska Airlines will begin on May 12, 2027, will cover 19% more distance and be much more expensive to operate. Of course, in these instances, and elsewhere where it is the only operator, it should get a reasonable price premium for the convenience of flying nonstop.

The carrier's debut to Europe took place in April 2026, when the first flight from Seattle to Rome took off. The launch came after Alaska Airlines began its first-ever long-haul service, which was to Asia. The first route was from Washington State to Tokyo Narita in May 2025, followed by Seoul Incheon four months later.

Alaska Airlines' Planned Operations To Europe: July 2027

Faces British Airways, Delta, and Virgin Atlantic

After Rome came London Heathrow (May 2026), followed by Reykjavík (May 2026). Next year, Alaska Airlines will begin flying to Athens (May 2027) and Paris CDG (May 2027). When writing, the carrier currently plans five transatlantic routes, with a big emphasis on leisure markets, just like WestJet from Canada to Europe. This is perhaps why Alaska Airlines has not announced flights to Madrid, in what would be a logical tie-up with fellow oneworld member Iberia.

Let's narrow the focus to mid-July 2027. In that week, Alaska Airlines will be one of 12 airlines flying from Seattle to Europe, which will collectively have 147 weekly departures (21 daily). Discover Airlines will be there, as the Lufthansa Group's leisure unit is replacing Lufthansa itself. Alaska Airlines will have 28 weekly departures (four daily) and rank second behind Delta (35 weekly; five daily).
