#6121. Delta Air Lines' Basic Business Fare Keeps The Lie-Flat Seat, But Lounge Access Ends In 2027

Delta Air Lines has introduced a cheaper way for passengers to experience its Delta One business class cabin, but the lower price comes with some significant compromises. Its new Basic Business fare retains the features that matter most to many premium travelers, such as the lie-flat seat, alongside premium dining and priority boarding. However, passengers choosing this entry-level ticket will receive fewer benefits before and after their flight, with restrictions covering seat selection, flight changes, frequent flyer earnings, and eventually lounge access.

The most important change is scheduled for January 19, 2027, when Basic Business passengers will lose access to Delta One Lounges and dedicated Delta One check-in facilities. Until then, travelers can still enjoy these ground services, creating a temporary period in which the product offers more than its long-term structure promises. The development highlights how airlines are increasingly dividing business class into different price levels without necessarily changing the onboard experience.

Delta Air Lines introduced Basic Business in July 2026, with the fare becoming available for flights from September. The new option is designed to attract passengers who want a premium long-haul experience but are unwilling to pay the higher prices associated with traditional business class tickets. Rather than removing the lie-flat seat, Delta Air Lines has chosen to unbundle several benefits traditionally associated with its Delta One cabin.

This means passengers still receive the central feature of business class, allowing them to recline into a fully flat sleeping position on applicable aircraft. Premium dining also remains included, meaning travelers do not have to sacrifice the main onboard comforts that distinguish Delta One from economy and premium economy. Zone 1 boarding is another benefit that remains available, giving Basic Business passengers priority when boarding begins. However, the lower fare is not simply a discounted version of the existing Delta One ticket. It introduces restrictions that affect the journey at several stages, particularly when passengers want greater control over their seats or need to change their travel arrangements. These differences matter because business class travelers often value flexibility just as much as comfort, especially when flying internationally for work.

The distinction also gives Delta Air Lines another way to manage demand across its premium cabins. Some passengers may accept fewer benefits in exchange for a lower ticket price, while others will prefer paying extra for a more comprehensive experience. By introducing multiple fare levels within the same cabin, the SkyTeam carrier can appeal to both groups without redesigning its existing business class product.

The decision to retain the lie-flat seat is arguably the most important part of the Basic Business offering. For passengers traveling overnight or on long international routes, the ability to sleep horizontally can make a considerable difference to the journey. Removing this feature would have made the cheaper fare considerably less attractive, particularly when competing airlines continue to promote their premium cabins as places where passengers can rest comfortably.

Basic Business travelers also retain access to Delta One's premium dining experience. This means the cheaper ticket does not automatically translate into a reduced meal service, with passengers continuing to receive the elevated onboard food and beverage experience associated with the cabin. For travelers who primarily judge business class by the quality of the seat, food, and sleeping arrangements, this could make the entry-level fare appealing.

Zone 1 boarding is another important inclusion because it allows passengers to board ahead of most other travelers. This can be particularly useful on busy international departures, when finding overhead storage space and settling into a seat without unnecessary delays can improve the experience. Retaining this priority also means Basic Business passengers will not feel entirely separated from other Delta One travelers when entering the aircraft.

The latest data from ch-aviation shows that Delta Air Lines currently operates a fleet of 1,005 aircraft, with a further 319 on order, including 20 Airbus A350-1000 and 30 Boeing 787-10 aircraft, as shown in the table below:

*Not all aircraft of this type feature Delta One

Nevertheless, the similarities largely end with the onboard experience. Passengers choosing Classic or Extra fares retain additional benefits that are no longer included with Basic Business, making the differences between ticket categories more noticeable outside the aircraft. The product is therefore designed for travelers who prioritize the physical business class experience but are comfortable giving up some traditional premium conveniences.

The US legacy carrier is slashing business class prices.

One of the clearest restrictions concerns seat assignments, which are only provided after check-in for Basic Business passengers. This is a meaningful difference from more expensive Delta One fares, where travelers generally have greater control over selecting their preferred seats before departure. Passengers who want a particular position in the cabin may find the arrangement inconvenient.

Some markets may offer the opportunity to purchase advance seat selection separately, but this does not change the underlying structure of the fare. Travelers will need to consider whether paying extra for a specific seat makes the cheaper ticket worthwhile, particularly when comparing the final cost against the Classic option. For couples and colleagues, the uncertainty could be an important disadvantage.

Basic Business also excludes same-day confirmed flight changes and standby options. These benefits can be valuable when business meetings finish earlier than expected, connecting arrangements change, or passengers want to take an earlier departure. Without these options, travelers have less flexibility to adjust their plans on the day of travel, even when alternative flights have available seats.

Importantly, Delta Air Lines has confirmed that Medallion status does not restore these excluded same-day benefits. This is a significant departure from the expectations of frequent flyers accustomed to receiving additional flexibility through their loyalty status. Even passengers with an established relationship with the airline must accept the Basic Business restrictions, making the choice of fare particularly important for those whose schedules frequently change.

The most significant upcoming change involves access to Delta One Lounges and dedicated Delta One check-in facilities. Basic Business passengers currently retain these privileges, meaning travelers purchasing the entry-level fare can still enjoy the premium airport experience during the initial introduction period. However, this benefit will not continue indefinitely, with January 19, 2027, established as the cutoff date. From that date, passengers traveling on Basic Business tickets will no longer qualify for Delta One Lounge access through their fare. The dedicated Delta One check-in experience will also disappear from the package, creating a more noticeable difference between the entry-level ticket and higher-priced alternatives. The change effectively moves Basic Business further away from the traditional all-inclusive business class experience. The importance of this restriction becomes clearer when considering the role airport facilities play in premium travel. Delta One Lounges provide an environment where eligible passengers can relax, eat, and prepare for long-haul journeys away from busier public terminal areas. Dedicated check-in facilities also make the airport experience more convenient, particularly during busy departure periods.

For passengers booking flights before the deadline, the timing of travel will matter considerably. A ticket purchased months in advance will not necessarily guarantee lounge access if the journey takes place after January 19, 2027. Travelers comparing Basic Business with Classic should pay particular attention to the departure date rather than assuming that the benefits currently available will remain attached to the fare.

Delta Main Basic is one of the most restrictive fares in the US.

The financial differences between Delta Air Lines' business class fare categories extend to its SkyMiles loyalty program. Basic Business passengers earn just two SkyMiles per dollar spent, compared with five miles per dollar for Classic and seven miles per dollar for Extra. This creates a substantial difference in the rewards accumulated from otherwise similar journeys in the same premium cabin.

For occasional travelers, the reduced earning rate may not be especially important, particularly if Basic Business delivers meaningful savings. However, frequent international travelers who regularly purchase business class tickets could accumulate considerably fewer miles over time. Those miles contribute toward future flights and other redemption opportunities, making the difference relevant to passengers who actively participate in the loyalty program.

The reduced earning rate reinforces the idea that Basic Business is aimed at customers who primarily want the seat rather than the broader collection of premium benefits. Delta Air Lines is effectively placing a lower value on the loyalty contribution of passengers purchasing its cheapest business class product. This reflects the wider industry trend toward offering different rewards depending on how much customers spend.

Passengers will therefore need to compare immediate ticket savings against the longer-term value of the miles they would otherwise earn. Someone booking an occasional holiday might find the difference relatively insignificant, while a regular corporate traveler could lose a meaningful amount of potential rewards. The more expensive fare categories may consequently offer better overall value for passengers who prioritize loyalty benefits.

Delta Air Lines is not alone in experimenting with cheaper, unbundled business class products. United Airlines has introduced Polaris Base, while JetBlue has launched Mint Base, both offering lower-priced entry points into their respective premium cabins. These products reflect a broader industry shift toward separating the physical comfort of business class from additional services traditionally included in one comprehensive fare.

However, the different airlines do not necessarily apply identical restrictions. United Airlines' Polaris Base, for example, continues to permit access to standard United Clubs, demonstrating that lounge eligibility can vary depending on the product and the airline's wider premium travel strategy. Passengers should therefore examine the precise conditions rather than assuming every basic business class ticket follows the same rules.

For Delta Air Lines, the January 2027 lounge cutoff is particularly significant because lounge access remains available during the initial introduction period. This temporary arrangement could make Basic Business more attractive to travelers booking journeys before the deadline, although passengers should avoid treating the current benefits as permanent features of the fare. The eventual restrictions are an important part of understanding what the product actually offers.

Found an error? Send it info@simpleflying.com so it can be corrected.

Ultimately, Basic Business gives Delta Air Lines another way to compete for customers who want a lie-flat seat without paying for every traditional business class benefit. Premium dining and Zone 1 boarding help preserve the appeal of the onboard experience, but reduced mileage earnings, restricted flexibility, and the removal of lounge access create clear differences. From January 19, 2027, the fare will become a considerably more stripped-back proposition, leaving passengers to decide whether the seat alone justifies the price.

#6120. Van Hollen announces bid for majority leader, but Schumer says he has the votes

Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., left, has announced a challenge to current Senate Minority Leader Charles Schumer, D-N.Y. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call file photo)

Sen. Chris Van Hollen announced Thursday night that he would run for Senate majority leader, launching a challenge to Sen. Charles E. Schumer of New York, the current Democratic leader.

Van Hollen, a Maryland Democrat first elected to the Senate in 2016, served in leadership in the House and has been chairman of both the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee. He has said since the midterm elections he was listening to fellow Senate Democrats about the possibility of a run for the top job.

“In this election, the American people called for change. They called for a change from Donald Trump’s disastrous policies but even bigger than that, a change from the status quo that isn’t working for working people,” Van Hollen said in a statement. “It’s now on us to meet this moment, and to do that we need new leadership. This is not about any one person – it’s about answering the call of the American people. That is why I’m running for Senate Majority Leader.”

Schumer has already said he has the votes needed to continue serving as the leader.

“I welcome any discussion about the future of our caucus and the important work ahead. I’m proud of what we’ve accomplished together — 55 seats and counting is an amazing result — and I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic Leader. I look forward to leading our new Democratic majority and delivering for the American people,” Schumer said in a statement.

Schumer's supporters were quick to highlight the success at the ballot box in 2026, with the Democratic caucus potentially growing to 56 seats if former Rep. Mary Peltola prevails in Alaska.

“Chuck has outlined an aggressive plan for the new Democratic majority which is directly responsive to the message we heard from the voters, and he has the experience and unique mastery of the Senate process to make it happen,” Sen. Angus King, a Maine independent who caucuses with the Democrats, said in a statement. “Why would you fire the manager when you just won the World Series?”

In keeping with the World Series theme, Sen. Tammy Baldwin, D-Wis., echoed King with her own statement of support for Schumer.

“The Brewers just had a record season, and next year is not the time to change our management," Baldwin said. "The same is true in the Senate.”

In an interview with MS NOW about his run, Van Hollen conceded that Schumer would be the favorite in the secret-ballot contest, which will take place in December.

“Am I the underdog? Yes,” Van Hollen said. “You’re talking about an incumbent who uses the power of incumbency to, you know, provide deals to people.”

Van Hollen outlined legislative priorities including restoring Medicaid funding that Republicans cut in last year's budget reconciliation law and extending Affordable Care Act tax credits. But he suggested Democrats need to go further.

"We need to extend tax credits for the Affordable Care Act, but we can’t stop there, right? We have a completely broken health care system. It’s become profits, not people. And so my view is, we also need in the first 100 days to make health care more affordable for tens of millions of people," Van Hollen said. "We need to immediately make it clear that nobody’s going to pay one penny to subsidize data centers. ... We need to make sure that we have a livable minimum wage."

He also said he would not take sides in contested Democratic primaries, and he would make sure the DSCC did not take money from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, or AIPAC.

Van Hollen's early backers include progressive Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed, who emerged from a hotly contested Democratic primary in Michigan while the Senate Democratic political apparatus was backing Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich.

“In April, I was the first candidate in the country to call on Senator Chris Van Hollen to lead Senate Democrats, and I am proud to stand with him in his bid to become Senate Majority Leader,” El-Sayed said in a statement. “Michiganders demand money out of politics, money in pockets, and Medicare for All. Sen. Chris Van Hollen offers both the courage to go toe-to-toe with the Trump administration to deliver for working people and the experience to maneuver the Senate caucus. It’s why he has my full support to lead our caucus.”

#6119. Wow: Lufthansa Adds Premium Business Seats On Some Short Haul A320 Flights!

Lufthansa has just announced plans to introduce “real” business class seats on some of its narrow body planes, and that’s a really exciting development, given the typical business class standard on narrow body aircraft in Europe!

Interestingly, this is a concept that was initially trialed on Lufthansa Group low cost subsidiary Eurowings, and we knew at the time it was being used as a test for a more widespread implementation across the airline group. I’m delighted to see this become more widespread, and I hope this is just the start of a bigger trend.

Lufthansa has revealed that it will expand its premium offering on short and medium haul routes. With the introduction of the new Premium Business Seat, passengers will get more personal space than they’re used to on short haul aircraft.

Historically, business class on Airbus A320-family aircraft has consisted of standard economy seats with a blocked middle. So that means with the 3-3 layout, four seats were only sold per row. What’s happening is that the first three rows on some aircraft are being replaced with two rows of recliner seats, meaning the per-seat footprint is around 50% bigger than in standard business class.

At launch, the new Lufthansa Premium Business Seat will be available on six Airbus A320 aircraft (and these planes will also be equipped with Starlink). The seat will feature significantly more space, with nearly one meter of legroom, plus extra recline. This doesn’t replace the standard business class product, but instead, is an upsell option.

This new product is now available for sale for flights as of March 1, 2027, on routes between Frankfurt (FRA) and Athens (ATH), Cairo (CAI), and Nice (NCE). However, the first plane with the seats will already be in service as of December 16, 2026, and as of February 2027, it’ll be deployed on the above routes (but tickets are only on sale as of March as of now).

If a flight has this product available, you’ll see the “Premium Business Seat” designator during the booking process.

The process of actually booking a Premium Business Seat is essentially an upgrade cost on top of the standard business class fare. For example, looking at a Frankfurt to Athens route, I see an upgrade cost of €139, which frankly seems quite reasonable for a flight of this length.

Lufthansa is for the time being describing this as a commercial test, with the aim of examining demand for additional comfort on these routes, and the results will form the basis for deciding whether to expand the offering.

You’ll see many people refer to short haul business class in Europe as a “scam” (I don’t agree, but people say that), and they’re shocked to find economy seats with blocked middles. Admittedly product standards differ vastly around the globe.

The reason that airlines in Europe can get away with this product is threefold:

Keep in mind that most of the network carriers in Europe don’t make much money on short haul flights (or even lose a lot of money), given high costs and fierce competition from ultra low cost carriers.

With that in mind, I think Lufthansa is going about this exactly right:

I’d love to see more airlines introduce something similar. In particular, Air France, as Europe’s most premium airline, seems best positioned to do this, and could do it with very little opportunity cost. Why?

Honestly, if I were Air France, I’d just introduce this throughout the A220 fleet, and it would be a major point of differentiation, competitively. No airline could do it as efficiently as Air France, and every A220 flight has at least two rows of business class, so the opportunity cost is minimal.

Lufthansa will be introducing “real” business class seats on a subfleet of its Airbus A320s. As of the spring of 2027, expect these planes to be flying from Frankfurt to Athens, Cairo, and Nice. This Premium Business Seat concept will complement the existing business class, and will be available as a buy-up for business class passengers.

I’m very happy to finally see some more comfort on flights within Europe, and I imagine this will prove successful. If it doesn’t, I suspect it would be due to a lack of people knowing about this, rather than there not actually being demand.

What do you make of the Lufthansa Premium Business Seat concept?

#6118. New Resy Rewards Program Offers 4x Bonus Amex Points For Dining Out

Resy has just launched the Resy Rewards program, which lets American Express card members in the United States earn an extra 4x points per dollar spent at participating Resy restaurants, on top of their credit card rewards. As you’d expect, it’s not quite that straightforward, but I’d still consider this to be pretty exciting!

American Express owns both Resy and Tock (which is now being integrated into Resy), as part of its larger “lifestyle” play for attracting card members. So along with that, Resy is leaning more into the rewards program side of things, with the new Resy Rewards program offering an extra 4x Amex points per dollar spent at eligible Resy restaurants.

Resy Rewards is first launching in New York City, where users will see a new “Rewards” tab within the Resy iOS app, where they can browse and book eligible restaurants. Restaurants participating in the Resy Rewards launch include Carne Mare, Le Crocodile, Hearth, Kiko, OPTO, Le Pavillon, and more. In 2027, Resy Rewards plans to expand to additional U.S. cities, and select Tock venues will become eligible to participate in the program.

So, how exactly does Resy Rewards work? Card members need to enroll a US-based Membership Rewards program eligible card in Resy Rewards, then book a Resy Rewards reservation through the “Rewards” tab in the Resy iOS app, and then pay the bill for the dining experience with the enrolled card. So this requires a little more jumping through hoops than just using an Amex card Resy credit, for example.

These rewards are in addition to whatever the standard rewards are on an Amex card. For example, the American Express® Gold Card (learn more) ordinarily earns 4x points at restaurants globally, so if you dined at a restaurant eligible for Resy Rewards, you could be earning 8x points per dollar spent, which is pretty awesome.

Here’s how Pablo Rivero, CEO of Resy and SVP of American Express Global Dining, describes this:

“For the first time, we’re bringing American Express’s industry-leading Rewards program into the Resy iOS app and connecting two things our Card Members value deeply: great dining experiences and meaningful rewards. As we’ve seen with the success of the Resy Credit, rewarding diners while driving demand and revenue to Resy restaurants is a win on both sides of the table.”

I’m delighted to see Amex introduce an opportunity to earn points for dining out, beyond the bonus categories already offered on some of the issuer’s most popular cards. For the time being, this is rather niche, given that it’s limited to select restaurants in New York City, but the expectation is that it will expand more broadly in 2027 (though it remains to be seen how broadly).

Essentially think of this as being similar to a dining rewards program, as the idea is that restaurants have to opt-in to participate in this, with the hope being that this drums up business for them (and presumably they pay Amex and Resy something extra in exchange for that).

Furthermore, you do have to specifically reserve your reservation through Resy to qualify for this, so if you don’t have a reservation made through the “Rewards” tab on Resy, then you won’t earn bonus points.

I’m happy to see this, as earning 8x points on dining when paying with the Amex Gold Card is quite a great deal. Then again, so much of my dining out is through InKind, which is my favorite dining rewards program, given the excellent selection of restaurants the program has in Miami, and it’s tough to compete with the rewards offered by the program.

The new Resy Rewards program offers bonus Amex points when you make a reservation at an eligible restaurant and then pay with your eligible Amex card. The idea is that you can earn an extra 4x points per dollar spent on purchases at eligible restaurants, which is pretty awesome.

The catch is that this is initially launching in New York City, only “eligible” restaurants qualify, and you need to reserve through Resy and then pay with the same linked card in order to earn the bonus points. It’s nice to see this launch, and I look forward to it expanding to more markets.

An airport lounge membership, hotel perks and a handful of statement credits used to be enough to set a premium travel rewards card apart. These days, that sounds like the starting point.

The faces competition from the (see rates and fees), Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card and (see rates and fees). All four offer transferable rewards and airport lounge access, along with benefits designed to offset their high annual fees.

Still, the Platinum makes a compelling case for a place in a frequent traveler's wallet. Its strengths include extensive lounge access, generous earnings on flights booked directly with airlines and hotel benefits that can make a stay considerably more comfortable.

At $895 a year (see rates and fees), it's also the most expensive of these four cards.

Here's where the Platinum stands out — and where another premium card might be a better fit.

Complimentary Priority Pass lounge access is a shared benefit across these cards (enrollment required). What makes the stand out is the additional lounges available through the American Express Global Lounge Collection.

The American Express Global Lounge Collection includes Centurion Lounges, eligible Delta Sky Clubs and other participating partner lounge networks.

The Centurion network has a larger footprint than either Capital One’s or Chase’s own branded lounge network. Citi doesn't operate its own network, although cardholders receive four Admirals Club passes per calendar year.

For me, the Centurion Lounges at Dallas-Fort Worth International Airport (DFW) and George Bush Intercontinental Airport (IAH) in Houston are particularly useful when connecting to and from Austin. I enjoy the food at the lounges, but after an international flight, the opportunity to shower before my final flight of the day is what I appreciate most.

Delta Sky Club access is another reason to consider the Platinum. Cardmembers receive 10 visits per benefit year when flying on eligible itineraries. (Basic economy tickets don't qualify, and unlimited visits require $75,000 in eligible annual spending.)

There are other limits to consider. Centurion guest access costs extra unless you meet a spending requirement, and the biggest network won't necessarily be the most useful at your home airport.

Check the lounges along your regular routes before choosing a card based on access alone.

The offers up to $600 in annual lodging statement credits, split into two allowances of up to $300: one from January through June and another from July through December.

Eligible purchases include prepaid Fine Hotels + Resorts and The Hotel Collection bookings through American Express Travel®, plus qualifying prepaid Airbnb Luxe stays booked through AmexTravel.com or the Amex Travel App™.

THC and eligible Airbnb Luxe bookings require stays of at least two nights. Starting Jan. 1, 2027, FHR bookings will also require a two-night stay to qualify for the lodging credit.

I tend to use my credit for THC stays because I often find lower prices than at FHR properties. For January, I've booked two nights at The Standard, Bangkok Mahanakhon for $362. After applying the $300 credit, the stay will cost me $62 out of pocket.

My stay includes daily breakfast for two and a $100 credit toward eligible on-property charges, which I plan to use at an on-site restaurant or for room service. I'll also be eligible for early check-in, late checkout and a room upgrade (subject to availability). Breakfast is an additional benefit at this particular property; it isn't standard across THC.

FHR offers a more consistent package, including daily breakfast for two and guaranteed 4 p.m. checkout. That last benefit can be especially useful before an evening flight.

Competing premium cards have their own hotel programs. The Platinum's appeal is the combination of its credit and booking benefits. Just make sure to compare the total price with other available rates before deciding how much you're saving.

The earns 5 Membership Rewards points per dollar spent on flights booked directly with airlines or through Amex Travel (on up to $500,000 of airfare purchases per calendar year, then 1 point per dollar spent).

The ability to book directly is a meaningful advantage. You can earn generously while dealing with the airline directly if you need to change your reservation or something goes wrong.

The earns 4 points per dollar spent on flights booked directly. It earns a higher 8 points per dollar through Chase Travel℠, while the earns 6 points per dollar spent on flights through Citi Travel.

Those points offer plenty of redemption options.

Membership Rewards airline partners provide access to Oneworld, SkyTeam and Star Alliance flights through programs such as British Airways Club, Air France-KLM Flying Blue and Air Canada Aeroplan. Hotel partners include Hilton Honors and Marriott Bonvoy.

All four cards have useful transfer partners, so consider which programs you actually use. A strong earning rate matters more when it earns points you know how to redeem.

The high spending requirement deserves attention. Make sure you can meet it through purchases you already planned to make, and assess the card's ongoing value separately from its first-year bonus.

The 's long list of credits makes more sense when you focus on the ones that fit your existing spending.

Its up to $300 annual digital entertainment credit is one I particularly like. It provides up to $25 monthly toward eligible purchases with participating providers.† I use it for YouTube Premium and Disney+/Hulu; the monthly allowance is shared across eligible subscriptions.

#6116. Calls for Nvidia probes, new chip export limits intensify

“The bottom line is we need to understand the magnitude of this with respect to Chinese intelligence, possible chip diversion,” said Rep. John Moolenaar, R-Mich., seen above. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call file photo)

The resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang on Thursday did little to quell bipartisan demands from Congress for an accounting of potential national security fallout from his affair with an alleged Chinese spy and talk of adding tougher chip export controls to the annual defense authorization bill.

Huang admitted on Sunday to having an affair, and reports say that it was with Alice Huang, an executive at Singaporean tech company and Nvidia customer Megaspeed, whom the U.S. government believes spied for China, according to recent reports. The New York Times and Reuters reported he also had affairs with two Nvidia employees.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., told reporters Thursday that he supports the Senate investigating Huang’s potential influence on U.S. artificial intelligence and chip policy.

“I think that it would make sense because of the… nature of the association… and the governments and the national security interests we were talking about here,” Thune said, though he said he thought it would be “wrong” to make assumptions about how close Huang’s relationship with President Donald Trump has been.

Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., echoed the need for lawmakers to delve into the scandal, saying in a post on X that “Congress must demand answers.”

“The Trump administration must also answer for what it did once it learned about Mr. Huang’s relationship with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset. Were government officials told not to investigate because of Trump’s relationship with Mr. Huang? What did Trump know when he personally invited Mr. Huang aboard Air Force One?” Schumer wrote, referring to the president having invited Huang to accompany him to China in May.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., said at a press conference that Reps. Gregory W. Meeks, D-N.Y., and Jim Himes, D-Conn., the ranking members of the Foreign Affairs and Intelligence committees, respectively, are leading Democrats’ efforts to “get to the bottom of what has happened.”

“We need a classified briefing made available to members of Congress as it relates to the Nvidia situation,” Jeffries said. “And to the extent that our national security has been compromised, the American people deserve answers, and we're going to work to make sure that happens.”

The investigations look likely to begin before control of Congress changes hands in January.

Rep. John Moolenaar, R-Mich., who chairs the House select China committee, told reporters that his panel, along with House Foreign Affairs and Intelligence, are in negotiations with Huang to find a date for his testimony before Congress.

“The bottom line is we need to understand the magnitude of this with respect to Chinese intelligence, possible chip diversion,” Moolenaar said. “What ways is Chinese intelligence influencing his perspective, his perspective influencing national security policy?”

Last week, the chairs of the three committees sent a letter to Huang requesting that he appear at a joint closed-door briefing. Moolenaar said that if Huang does not agree to a date, the committees will subpoena him.

Late Thursday, he joined with House Foreign Affairs Chairman Brian Mast, R-Fla., and House Intelligence Chairman Rick Crawford, R-Ark., in sending a new letter to Huang seeking a closed-door transcribed interview on Dec. 1. They also wrote to Nvidia General Counsel Tim Teter seeking a similar interview on Dec. 2. Separately, Mast wrote to Jeffrey Kessler, the Commerce Department undersecretary for industry and security, seeking his appearance at a committee hearing on Dec. 3.

Moolenaar also said that Congress needs to understand what privileged information Chinese intelligence may have gained access to through Huang and how they may have tried to influence U.S. policy.

“We need to have strong safeguards when it comes to our technology and export controls,” Moolenaar said. “And [Huang has] been one of the strongest proponents for not having export controls. This shines a whole new light on that discussion.”

Also late Thursday, Senate Banking Chairman Tim Scott, R-S.C.,  sent a letter to Huang calling on him to appear at a Dec. 3 committee hearing and another letter to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to testify at a Dec. 10 hearing "regarding recent public reports about NVIDIA and the Department of Commerce's role that raises national security concerns."

A proposed manager’s amendment to the Senate's fiscal 2027 National Defense Authorization Act bill (S 4784) contains several possibilities for those safeguards, including requirements for chip security mechanisms that would allow for verification if semiconductors are diverted to countries of concern and a ban on exporting certain very powerful chips to those countries. The House NDAA does not contain similar language.

However, House Armed Services Chair Mike D. Rogers, D-Ala., is open to the restrictions. He told reporters Wednesday that he “would like to see” semiconductor export controls in the NDAA, but that the Huang scandal had not changed his position.

Democratic Caucus Vice Chair Ted Lieu, D-Calif., told reporters on Thursday that after reports that the federal government had been aware of Huang’s affair with the alleged spy, the administration should have shared the information with Congress.

“The administration needs to be investigated for hiding this information from Congress and the American people,” he said.

Lieu also suggested that Nvidia’s reported donation to the White House ballroom project influenced the Trump administration’s decision to allow the export of some powerful Nvidia chips to China.

“There is no reason to do that. That hurts our national security, and we have an opportunity right now to fix that in the upcoming National Defense Authorization,” Lieu said.

Mast said the Huang revelations could give new momentum to including chip export rules in the NDAA. He also said that his “directive” on the issue came “straight from the admin” and informed his objectives on the committee.

“Don't let chips be smuggled to China. Make sure that American companies get to buy them first,” Mast said. “Make sure that the machines that make them don't get sold to them, even though it's the Dutch that make the machines. Make sure that they can't access it remotely.”

Mast’s committee has advanced many of those priorities, including some of the language included in the NDAA.

In March, the committee on a unanimous vote advanced legislation known as the Chip Security Act, which would require chip security mechanisms to verify that certain semiconductors subject to export controls aren’t diverted to countries of concern, including China and Iran.

The committee also advanced bills to require the Bureau of Industry and Security and the State Department to work with allied suppliers of semiconductor manufacturing equipment to implement export controls to prevent the equipment from going to countries of concern, and to require licenses for the export of certain powerful chips, including banning exporting certain chips to countries of concern.

Versions of all three bills are included in the Senate manager’s amendment to the NDAA.

The scandal has also led to calls for oversight of the Commerce Department, including Secretary Howard Lutnick, for its handling of export policy and actions around Huang.

Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., told reporters Thursday that Lutnick and Nvidia should testify “before Democrats can set the narrative.”

“If there is some reasonable basis or some way to discount some of the reporting, the best way to do it is request a meeting with us and give us a briefing,” Tillis said. “Because otherwise, you're going to get what you get in an oversight hearing in about six weeks.”

Asked about oversight of the Commerce Department’s role in the Huang scandal, Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, who chairs the Commerce Committee, said his panel “has engaged in vigorous oversight under Republican presidents and Democrat presidents and will continue to be [engaged in it].”

On Wednesday, prior to Huang’s resignation, Senate Banking ranking member Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., and Sen. Chris Coons, D-Del., sent a letter to Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller requesting that they “preserve all documents, communications, records, and other materials regarding the export of NVIDIA’s advanced AI chips to China or to entities that may divert such chips to China.”

“This incident raises significant concerns about the federal government’s ability to effectively enforce our export controls and protect our national security,” the senators wrote.

In a statement Thursday, Warren said that Huang’s resignation did not “absolve” him of the need to answer questions. She also called for the passage of stricter export controls, including the bill to ban the export of certain chips to China.

Sen. Michael Bennet, D-Colo., sent his own letter on Wednesday to Lutnick, Rubio, Attorney General Todd Blanche and Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, requesting an update on the Justice Department’s investigation into Megaspeed for possibly diverting U.S. chips to China.

Savannah Behrmann, John M. Donnelly, Jacob Fulton and David Jordan contributed to this report.

#6115. Delta SkyMiles & World Of Hyatt Partnership Live: Dual Earning, Milestone Rewards, & Linking Accounts

In September 2026, Delta SkyMiles and World of Hyatt unveiled plans to launch a new, long term strategic partnership. This announcement came just shortly after American AAdvantage and World of Hyatt announced that they will be ending their partnership.

At the time, we didn’t actually have any details as to what the partnership would entail, but that has now changed, as additional information has been revealed. Parts of the partnership are even now live, and members can already link their accounts.

Delta and Hyatt are launching a new loyalty program collaboration, which comes with a “shared ambition to create additional value, recognition and engagement opportunities across more of the travel journey.” This includes reciprocal opportunities to earn rewards, and also reciprocal opportunities to select perks with the partner brand.

Here’s how Laurie Blair, Hyatt’s SVP of Global Marketing and Loyalty, describes this:

“World of Hyatt and Delta SkyMiles were each built to make travel more meaningful and rewarding, which makes this collaboration feel meant to be. By connecting the Delta flight and Hyatt stay, we are helping members get more from the journeys they are already taking while opening the door to new experiences, destinations and memories. It is an exciting next step in our commitment to caring for members throughout the full travel journey, from takeoff to check out.”

Here’s how Dwight James, Delta’s SVP of Customer Engagement & Loyalty, describes this:

“At Delta, we know loyalty is something we earn by delivering meaningful value and experiences that make our Members want to keep choosing us. Our relationship with World of Hyatt gives us another way to do that by recognizing and rewarding Members across more of their travel, while creating new ways to earn, engage and experience both brands.”

Effective immediately (as of November 17, 2026), elite members of both loyalty programs can earn simultaneously with the new “Dual Earn” benefit. Members must link their accounts, and can then earn additional rewards.

World of Hyatt members can earn bonus points on eligible Delta flights (which includes Delta Comfort, Delta Premium Select, Delta First Class, and Delta One), as follows:

Delta SkyMiles members can earn bonus miles on eligible Hyatt stays (which includes qualifying room rates, qualifying incidental spend, and qualifying non-stay charges at participating Hyatt properties, eligible Mr & Mrs Smith spend booked through Hyatt, and eligible spend at The Venetian booked through Hyatt):

As of 2027, eligible elite members of both World of Hyatt and Delta SkyMiles will gain access to new milestone reward choices, giving people more ways to earn, and more flexibility in how they use their loyalty benefits. This would apply to World of Hyatt Milestone Rewards, and Delta SkyMiles Choice Benefits.

As of January 1, 2027, World of Hyatt members will be able to choose Delta awards as they reach qualifying Milestone Rewards thresholds. The first Delta award choice will become available at 20 qualifying nights or 35,000 base points, with additional choices as members progress through the program, including:

As of February 1, 2027, Delta SkyMiles members will be able to choose Hyatt awards as they reach qualifying Choice Benefits thresholds. Members will be able to select free night awards, as follows:

To celebrate the start of this partnership, Hyatt and Delta are offering limited time offers for members who link their accounts.

First, from November 17 through December 31, 2026, linked members can register to earn one additional World of Hyatt elite night after completing their first qualifying Hyatt stay during the offer period. Taking advantage of this should be a no-brainer.

Next, from January 4 through February 15, 2027, linked members can:

Basically, Hyatt has dumped American in favor of Delta. Admittedly the partnership between American and Hyatt had already been scaled back over time. The two programs used to offer a dual accrual opportunity as well, but that was eventually cut.

After all, companies only want to offer perks like that if they’re driving incremental business, and I imagine at some point it’s hard to justify that expense, when you feel like there’s not much upside left:

Now the Delta and Hyatt partnership is starting out in a similar way to how the American one did, with one major exception. On the dual accrual front, SkyMiles elite members are lucky, as they earn rewards on all qualifying Hyatt spending. Meanwhile World of Hyatt members only earn rewards when booking premium tickets, which is a bit disappointing. And here I was thinking that all seats on Delta aircraft are premium!!

I do have to say, as much as I’m a World of Hyatt loyalist, the program has certainly become less differentiated over time. While Delta can argue all it wants about how premium it is, SkyMiles simply isn’t as good of a loyalty program as AAdvantage. So perhaps this swap reflects the direction Hyatt is trying to head on loyalty… I dunno.

Delta and Hyatt have launched an exclusive new partnership, which explains why American and Hyatt cut ties. The partnership is now live, and it includes dual points accrual opportunities, reciprocal milestone perks, and some limited time opportunities.

At a minimum, it’s definitely worth linking accounts. And if you’re a World of Hyatt member with a stay planned before the end of the year, be sure to register for an extra elite night, as there’s no reason not to take advantage of that.

What do you make of this new Delta and Hyatt partnership, and American being dumped?

#6114. The New Changes That Could Make The US Air Force's C-17 Globemasters Become Fighters Instead Of Transport Aircraft

Bluebearwing | Shutterstock, Simple Flying

Chris earned a Master’s degree in Defense and Strategic Studies (Highest Honors) from the University of Texas at El Paso.

His graduate work concentrated on Global and National Security, Low-Intensity Conflict, Modern Warfare, and US grand strategy. He also undertook extensive regional studies, analyzing how key regions integrate into the broader US security architecture.

This rigorous program provided him with a comprehensive understanding of U.S. military operations, global strategy, and weapons systems. Additionally, he gained a strong appreciation for great power competition.—an increasingly central force shaping international relations and conflict for the foreseeable future.

The United States Air Force is exploring a concept that could fundamentally change how it generates long-range strike capabilities by turning conventional cargo aircraft into formidable missile-launching platforms. Known initially as Rapid Dragon and now progressing under the Dragon Cart initiative, the program uses specially configured pallets to deploy multiple air-launched cruise missiles from aircraft such as the Lockheed Martin C-130J Super Hercules and Boeing C-17 Globemaster III.

Rather than developing entirely new combat aircraft, the concept leverages the existing air mobility fleet to provide commanders with additional precision-strike capacity. With growing demand for affordable, mass-produced munitions and the need to expand the US military's weapons stockpile, this approach could give the Air Force a significant advantage in future high-intensity conflicts.

In 2019, the Air Force Research Laboratory (AFRL) initiated experiments that could, if successful, transform conventional transport aircraft such as the C-17 and C-130 into dual-use aircraft with immense firepower. Once deployed, these cargo haulers will be able to carry significant numbers of rapidly producible cruise missiles and saturate a battlespace, augmenting strike aircraft and heavy bombers.

The AFRL noted that the program has brought together more than "30 stakeholders, including Air Force Major Commands, the Test and Evaluation Enterprise, Program Offices, Mission Planners, other Services, Foreign Partners & Allies, and Industry to develop and demonstrate the capability through modeling, simulation, analysis, demonstration, and flight tests."

The project began as Rapid Dragon and is now known as Dragon Cart. The project tested the possibility of loading palletized munitions, such as JASSM-ER cruise missiles, into C-130s and C-17s. Air & Space Forces Magazine states that the "Rapid Dragon program performed several tests on the C-130 and C-17, including a live-fire test at Eglin Air Force Base, Florida, in December 2021." AFRL has also stated that Rapid Dragon has employed the palletized munitions concept on three separate continents, including the EUCOM and INDOPACOM theaters.

According to CENTCOM Citadel, a C-130J Super Hercules can carry two pallets, each containing six missile tubes, enabling the aircraft to deploy up to 12 air-launched cruise missiles. Meanwhile, the C-17 Globemaster III, with a maximum payload capacity of 170,900 lb (77,519 kg), could theoretically accommodate five nine-missile pallets carrying up to 45 JASSMs. This substantial weapons payload could temporarily transform the cargo aircraft into a formidable standoff strike platform.

The US Air Force Research Laboratory is at the cutting edge of weapons and general technology development for the US military and partner states.

As demonstrated by Operation Epic Fury, during which US strike aircraft deployed approximately 1,100 JASSMs, from an estimated inventory of 4,400, the need for affordable mass in this category of munitions has become increasingly apparent. Further, the ability to deploy these weapons flexibly would allow US commanders to strike targets without placing additional demands on bomber, fighter, and strike aircraft crews.

Due to the need for an expanded stockpile of missiles, particularly more affordable varieties, Dragon Cart dovetails with the Air Force's investment in its Family of Affordable Mass Missiles (FAMM) program. This initiative is designed to expand the service's munitions stockpile with comparatively inexpensive, less exquisite air-to-ground missiles. To this point, Air&Space Forces Magazine reports that just last July, the "Pentagon announced framework agreements for multiyear deals with three companies to produce and develop two versions of FAMM weapons—FAMM-Lugged, for fighter aircraft, and FAMM-Palletized, for airlifters."

As part of this plan, the Air Force has requested $355 million in its FY2027 budget to procure 1,000 weapons under the broader FAMM program. Its five-year budget projections call for the purchase of 28,000 missiles for $12.6 billion, as detailed by Defence Industry Europe.

The massive buildup of precision missiles will be supported by companies such as Anduril, whose Barracuda cruise missile recently received certification as the Air Force's first large-scale production munition compliant with open systems architecture. This certification provides a clear path forward for the new weapon, which offers commanders greater flexibility, as technicians can swap out payloads and reconfigure other features depending on mission requirements.

Under the FAMM program, Air&Space Forces Magazine states that "Anduril, CoAspire, and Zone 5 Technologies were selected. The agreements call for the three companies to produce 8,000 missiles annually once production ramps up. That timeline targets 5,300 missiles in 2028, rising to 8,000 by 2031." Anduril is slated to deliver its first Barracuda missiles to the Pentagon in early 2027.

Comparing France's exquisite omnirole jet to the leading fighters.

With the missiles getting ever closer to delivery and the capability already within the Air Force's grasp, the service is planning to field this new weapon system in 2027, according to Defence Blog. Regarding the impending deployment of the missile delivery system, General Kenneth S. Wilsbach, US Air Force Chief of Staff, stated: “As you might gather, capabilities like FAMM-P blur the distinction between our combat air forces and mobility air force mission sets. That’s a cultural shift we need to be prepared for, and I need every mobility Airman in the room to embrace that change.”

Regarding this blurring of the line between combat and air mobility, this new weapons capability could potentially turn suitably equipped C-130s and C-17s into platforms capable of striking targets across a given theater. Between its active-duty, Air National Guard, and Reserve units, the Air Force operates 428 C-130s and 222 C-17s. That's a substantial number of potential missile-launching platforms. Another consideration is that any adversary will now have to devote resources and plan for the possibility that cargo aircraft operating in the area could be carrying a devastating payload of cruise missiles, placing high-value targets under potential threat.

Manufactured with a longer fuselage, C-130J-30 for combat delivery

Special Operations; aerial and ground refueling (US Air Force-only variant)

Search and rescue support missions; aerial and ground refueling (US Air Force-only variant)

Search and rescue/maritime support missions (US Coast Guard–only variant)

Civil-certified multipurpose air freighter

If the aircraft are called upon to strike hostile military sites, the missile pallets are loaded like standard cargo through the aircraft's Cargo Handling System and secured in place using pallet locks and a restraint system. Once over the designated launch area, the crew pushes the pallet or pallets out through the rear cargo door, much like any other airdropped load. Once clear of the aircraft, the pallet deploys a parachute, allowing the missiles to be released into the air. Their engines then activate, and the missiles maneuver toward their designated targets.

One of the program's greatest advantages is that, during contingency operations or high-intensity conflicts, the Air Force could support ground operations and provide substantial follow-on strikes without placing additional demands on its dedicated strike aircraft and heavy bomber crews. Further, using cargo aircraft as precision-strike platforms could provide commanders with highly accurate firepower against multiple targets, offering considerable value in support of ground operations.

Over 2,700 C-130-family aircraft have been produced so far, with production expected to run into the 2030s.

Despite the advantages of converting transport aircraft into missile-launching platforms, the concept is not without operational challenges. The C-130J Super Hercules and C-17 Globemaster III were designed primarily for air mobility, not penetrating heavily defended airspace. Consequently, these aircraft would need to operate at considerable standoff distances from hostile air defense systems, relying on the extended range of their cruise missiles to engage targets without entering contested airspace. This places greater importance on missile range, accuracy, and mission planning.

Further, deploying palletized munitions requires coordination between aircraft crews, mission planners, intelligence personnel, and weapons operators. Although the Cargo Handling System allows missile pallets to be loaded using conventional cargo procedures, aircraft must accommodate specialized release equipment, parachute deployment, and systems to coordinate missile launches. Additionally, cargo aircraft assigned to strike missions would temporarily be unavailable for traditional responsibilities, potentially placing additional demands on an already heavily tasked air mobility fleet.

Another consideration is the availability of suitable weapons and the ability to integrate different missile systems across multiple aircraft platforms. Rapid Dragon and the broader Dragon Cart initiative aim to make this process more flexible through palletized configurations and modular weapons architectures. However, individual aircraft and missile combinations still require testing, integration, and operational certification. The Air Force also has to ensure sufficient missile inventories are available to support conventional strike operations and expanded palletized weapons deployment. These considerations will determine how effectively the concept transitions from experimental demonstrations into a dependable component of US long-range strike capabilities.

The Rapid Dragon concept represents a significant shift in how the US Air Force could generate and deploy long-range strike capabilities. By adapting existing cargo aircraft to launch palletized cruise missiles, the service could substantially expand its available weapons-delivery platforms without relying exclusively on traditional bombers and fighter aircraft. The transition toward Dragon Cart, alongside the development of affordable, mass-produced munitions such as Anduril's Barracuda, further demonstrates the growing importance of flexible weapons deployment.

Although operational challenges involving aircraft availability, weapons integration, and survivability remain, the potential benefits are considerable. With hundreds of C-130s and C-17s across its active-duty, Air National Guard, and Reserve fleets, the Air Force has a substantial transportation infrastructure that could serve an additional combat role. Ultimately, Dragon Cart could reshape how the US generates strike capacity in future conflicts.

#6113. Aer Lingus to Introduce First Premium Economy Cabin

Aer Lingus is moving to upgrade the widebody aircraft operating its transatlantic network.

The carrier said Wednesday that it will introduce its first-ever Premium Economy cabin on 10 refurbished Airbus A330s. The aircraft will also get upgraded Business Class seats – now enclosed as suites – and an improved Economy section.

“[This] is a transformation of the entire experience across our A330 fleet, elevating Business Class, Economy, and, for the first time in Aer Lingus history, introducing Premium Economy,” CEO Lynne Embleton said in a news release. “We want to give our customers greater choice, comfort, and connectivity while creating an experience that feels unmistakably Aer Lingus.”

The upgraded Business Class will have 28 Collins Elevation suites in a 1-2-1 configuration, giving each passenger direct aisle access. Each seat will have a fully flat bed, a closing door, enhanced bedding, and “well-being amenities.” A self-service snack and refreshment bar will also be available.

The carrier will also roll out new Economy seats with more personal space and six-way adjustable leather headrests.

New interior elements will tie the three cabins together, officials said. Plans call for mood lighting, artwork reflecting Irish landscapes, and custom fabrics in colors inspired by the sea.

All seats will have larger 4K high-definition entertainment screens, Bluetooth headphone connectivity, USB-C charging ports, and access to Starlink wireless internet. Starlink is already available across all of Aer Lingus’ transatlantic routes.

The first of the overhauled A330s will reenter service in October 2027, flying between Dublin and New York-JFK. The new cabin experience will become available on additional North American routes as work on the remaining A330s is completed.

Aer Lingus serves a total of 20 destinations across the U.S., Canada, and Mexico, including Boston, Newark, New Jersey, Miami, Los Angeles, Toronto, and Cancún.

#6112. Earning World Of Hyatt Elite Nights & Status With Credit Cards: Worth It?

Chase and Hyatt have two co-branded credit cards — the World of Hyatt Credit Card (learn more) and World of Hyatt Business Card (learn more). I’d consider these to be among the more lucrative hotel credit cards out there, particularly the personal version of the card.

One of the awesome things about Hyatt’s two credit cards is that they can earn you elite nights, making it easier to qualify for status in the World of Hyatt program. In this post, I’d like to get into the nitty-gritty of how earning Hyatt elite status with credit cards works, and discuss whether it’s worth it.

Chase and Hyatt have both the World of Hyatt Credit Card (a personal card) and the World of Hyatt Business Credit Card (a business card). Both cards have valuable benefits, though I think the personal card is considerably more compelling than the business card. Let me start by just briefly recapping the perks of the two cards.

The World of Hyatt Credit Card has a $95 annual fee and offers:

This means that you’re getting five elite nights toward status and a Category 1-4 free night award every year just for having the card. To me that more than justifies the annual fee, by a long shot (I consistently get $250+ of value out of the free night certificate alone). That doesn’t even factor in the incremental perks you can get for spending on the card.

The World of Hyatt Business Credit Card has a $199 annual fee and offers:

The business version of the card isn’t quite as rewarding as the personal version of the card, especially if you’re not a big spender. However, for businesses that spend quite a bit on credit cards, this can be the best card for earning elite status.

Both the World of Hyatt Credit Card and World of Hyatt Business Credit Card offer the ability to earn elite nights. However, the ways in which you earn elite nights differ between the two cards, so let’s go over those details.

The World of Hyatt Credit Card offers qualifying nights toward Hyatt status in two ways. First of all, the World of Hyatt Card offers five elite nights annually just for having the card. There’s no spending required to earn these five elite nights, and you receive them for each calendar year in which you have the card, including the year in which you open the card.

Beyond that, the World of Hyatt Card offers two elite nights for every $5,000 spent on the card (in other words, that’s up to one elite night per $2,500 of spending). There’s no limit to how many elite nights you can earn this way, and the elite nights earned through spending on this card aren’t in any way tied to the calendar year. In other words, if you spent $2,500 on the card in 2026 and then spend $2,500 on the card in 2027, you’d earn two elite nights at that point.

The World of Hyatt Business Credit Card offers five elite nights for every $10,000 spent on the card in a calendar year (in other words, that’s up to one elite night per $2,000 of spending). On this card, the spending counter resets at the beginning of the calendar year. In other words, if you spent $8,000 on the card in 2026, you’d still have to spend a full $10,000 in 2027 to earn five elite nights.

As you can see, this card offers elite nights for spending at an accelerated rate, though unlike the personal card, it doesn’t offer the five elite nights annually just for having the card.

How soon do elite nights post from the World of Hyatt Credit Card and the World of Hyatt Business Credit Card?

While the above covers the basics, I’d like to now analyze the overall value proposition of earning World of Hyatt elite status by spending on the World of Hyatt Credit Card or World of Hyatt Business Card, including addressing some of the most common questions and scenarios that come up.

With Hyatt, not all elite perks are tied directly to having status, but rather some require earning a certain number of elite nights in a year, known as the Milestone Rewards program. The Milestone Rewards program is how you earn perks like suite upgrade awards, club access awards, Guest of Honor awards, and more.

Hyatt elite nights earned through Hyatt credit cards would count toward Milestone Rewards the same as any hotel stays would, which adds further value to credit card spending.

One of the perks of both Hyatt credit cards is that you receive Discoverist status for as long as you have the card. Discoverist status ordinarily requires 10 elite qualifying nights or 25,000 base points per year. As a reminder, here are World of Hyatt’s elite thresholds:

One common point of confusion is that people assume these cards really come with up to 15 elite nights per year. They assume you already get Discoverist status, and that any elite nights are on top of that. Note that while these cards offer Discoverist status, you don’t get the elite nights that correspond to that.

This means that if you have a Hyatt credit card, you’ll receive Discoverist status on an ongoing basis (and five elite nights every year if you have the personal card), but you’ll still need to qualify for Explorist or Globalist status based on the full criteria.

Hyatt’s lifetime Globalist status is based on earning one million base points in the program. World of Hyatt members earn five base points per dollar spent on Hyatt stays, meaning you essentially have to spend $200,000 at Hyatts to earn lifetime Globalist status.

Credit card spending, and any elite nights earned through Hyatt credit cards, won’t count toward lifetime Globalist status. That’s because the qualification criteria is based solely on base points, and not based on elite qualifying nights (in which case it would count).

World of Hyatt Globalist is my favorite top tier hotel status, and what I love is that Hyatt’s co-branded credit cards make it easier to earn that. Let’s look at the best strategy for earning Globalist status with the card. Hyatt Globalist status ordinarily requires earning 60 qualifying nights in a year. So how much would you have to spend on a Hyatt credit card to earn that status?

On the World of Hyatt Credit Card, you’d need to spend $140,000 to earn Globalist status:

Meanwhile on the World of Hyatt Business Credit Card, you’d need to spend $120,000 to earn Globalist status:

As you can see, the personal credit card offers more elite nights upfront, while the business credit card offers elite nights at a faster pace for spending (assuming you can reach the thresholds).

When you’re analyzing the value of spending your way toward status, don’t forget that even beyond the general status perks, the Milestone Rewards perks could really add up. For example, if you make it to 60 elite nights, you could select five suite upgrade awards and four club access awards, and would also receive a Category 1-7 free night award, a Category 1-4 free night award, and three Guest of Honor awards.

Then on the personal version of the card, you also receive an additional Category 1-4 free night award when you spend $15,000 on the card in a year. The value of all of those perks really adds up.

Hyatt counts award nights toward status, and just for having the World of Hyatt Credit Card, you get a free night every year, plus the opportunity to earn a further three free nights for spending $15,000, earning Explorist status, and earning Globalist status.

On top of that, presumably you want to earn Globalist status because you actually intend to stay at Hyatts with some frequency. Hotel status is worthless if you don’t actually stay at that brand.

To be realistic, let’s assume that long term you’re earning 30 elite nights per year through actual stays. There are so many great Globalist benefits to use (like suite upgrade awards and free night awards), so if you’re staying at Hyatts less than that I question whether Globalist is worth it for you.

If you earned 30 of the required 60 elite nights through credit card spending, you’d need to spend the following:

Given all the incremental perks you’re picking up with Milestone Rewards, I’d say the math could really check out.

When deciding if it makes sense to spend money on the World of Hyatt Credit Card or World of Hyatt Business Credit Card, consider the opportunity cost of the spending. For easy math purposes, I tend to consider the opportunity cost of credit card spending to be around 3.4%.

That’s because based on my valuation of miles & points, most transferable points currencies are worth 1.7 cents each, and you have some cards offering 2x points per dollar spent. Meanwhile I value World of Hyatt points at 1.4 cents each.

If we were to theoretically assume you’re spending $60,000 on a Hyatt credit card per year (give or take) in order to earn Globalist status, what’s the opportunity cost of that spending? By my math, you’re looking at an opportunity cost of up to 2% (the spread between a 3.4% return and 1.4% return). That’s around $1,200, if you value things the way that I do. But that’s not factoring in the value of all the other perks mentioned above:

For many, I think the above perks could more than justify the difference in return on spending otherwise.

There are many things to love about the World of Hyatt Credit Card or World of Hyatt Business Card, though the ability to get a fast track toward status is probably my favorite perk. I absolutely love Hyatt Globalist status, and credit cards have historically helped me requalify for status. If you’re a Hyatt loyalist and don’t yet have the hotel group’s co-branded credit cards, they’re seriously worth considering.

What has your experience been using World of Hyatt Credit Cards to earn elite status?

#6111. American to Renovate, Expand Phoenix Lounges

American Airlines plans to refresh and expand its three Admirals Club lounges at Phoenix Sky Harbor International Airport.

The carrier said Tuesday that it will add seating, upgrade amenities, and improve food and beverage service across all three spaces in Terminal 4.

In the near term, the Admirals Club lounge in Concourse A between gates A19 and A21 will get a new servery area, infrastructure enhancements to support expanded food and beverage offerings, and facility updates to improve the overall customer experience.

Longer-term plans call for nearly tripling the combined footprint of the Concourse A lounges, the other being above gates A7-A9. New furniture and finishings will be brought in, and seating capacity will expand by 150%.

The lounge in Concourse B, between gates B5 and B7, will get a new self-service food and beverage area and have its seating capacity increased by 20%.

“Phoenix continues to be an important hub in our network, and these investments reflect our commitment to giving customers more space, comfort, and convenience when they travel through PHX,” American Chief Customer Officer Heather Garboden said in a news release. “While we look forward to the development of the new West Terminal, these enhancements will help create an even more seamless travel experience for the millions of customers who pass through Phoenix each year.”

The planned West Terminal will be built on the west side of the airport between Terminal 3 and Taxiway U. American is expected to serve as the terminal’s primary carrier.

According to the airport’s timeline, the project should be finished by 2033.

#6110. Legislative Branch bill would hold off on GAO cuts

A group of visitors walks past the Capitol on Sept. 22. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call file photo)

With stopgap funding set to expire in less than a month, Senate Republican appropriators Thursday unveiled a roughly $5.3 billion draft fiscal 2027 Legislative Branch spending bill that would boost security funding and sidestep contentious debates over a key watchdog.

The proposal would provide $965 million for Capitol Police, a nearly $83 million hike from fiscal 2026, but still short of the more than $1 billion the department requested as threats against lawmakers rise.

And it would bump funding for the Government Accountability Office up to $860 million, an increase of nearly 6 percent from fiscal 2026. That stands in contrast to the version of the bill advanced by the House Appropriations Committee in May, which floated slashing the GAO by 25 percent.

It joins several other draft spending bills released this week by Senate Appropriations Chair Susan Collins, R-Maine, who is trying to kickstart bicameral negotiations as lawmakers stare down a Dec. 11 deadline to fund the government.

Her committee ran into a stalemate on topline numbers earlier this year that stopped it from marking up any of the 12 annual bills, but lawmakers nipped the threat of a government shutdown in the bud ahead of the midterm elections by pushing through a continuing resolution. With that funding now set to expire next month, appropriators are hoping they can wrap up at least some of the bills while punting the rest into the next Congress with another stopgap.

The Legislative Branch bill is the smallest of the 12 appropriations bills and typically among the least controversial. But debates over the GAO have become a sticking point during the Trump administration as the agency accuses the White House of violating budget laws — a move the Office of Management and Budget has pushed back on, arguing the GAO has no authority over the administration since it is part of the legislative branch.

The GAO has been without a permanent head after its longtime leader Gene L. Dodaro retired last year, although Republicans are now making a last-ditch effort to get one confirmed during the lame-duck session before Democrats take power.

The House version of the spending bill sought to bar the comptroller general from suing under the 1974 budget law restricting presidential impoundments, unless specifically authorized by Congress. But the Senate proposal includes no such language, and overall, it appears designed to avoid drastic or contentious moves.

It would also leave in place a provision that would block cost-of-living adjustments for members of Congress, whose pay has been frozen since 2009.

Senate Democrats, however, criticized the bill text after its release, saying it wouldn’t invest enough in the legislative branch.

“The Legislative Branch bill underfunds key work to support oversight of the Executive Branch, and it underfunds important efforts to keep the Capitol complex safe,” Senate Appropriations ranking member Patty Murray, D-Wash., said in a statement.

The Architect of the Capitol would get $762.5 million, though funding for House office buildings is not included in that total. The agency is requesting $1.6 billion as it seeks to begin large-scale renovations of the Rayburn House Office Building. The architect has repeatedly warned lawmakers that parts of the Capitol complex are in need of critical infrastructure upgrades, arguing that delaying renovations will only make them more expensive as things continue to deteriorate.

The bill’s $5.3 billion proposal represents funding for the Senate and legislative branch agencies, while excluding House-only funds, which are typically added later.

#6109. Tulum Is Losing Airlines Fast: Why The Hyped New Airport Is Failing

In late 2023, we saw the opening of the Felipe Carrillo Puerto International Airport (TQO), in Tulum, Mexico. For those not familiar, Tulum is located on the eastern coast of the Yucatan Peninsula, and for years, it was a growing tourist destination.

While it could previously be accessed via Cancun International Airport (CUN), the hope was that by opening a new international airport, visitor numbers would expand massively. Unfortunately what has actually happened is exactly the opposite, as airline after airline has pulled out. What exactly is going on here? I think it makes for an interesting story, and thanks to TravelinWilly for flagging this.

In 2023, we saw airline after airline announce flights to Tulum. Among US carriers, we saw American, Delta, JetBlue, and United, all launch flights to Tulum, while Spirit announced flights, but never launched them.

That was only a small part of the overall international service to the airport, as we also saw flights to Tulum on Air Canada, Air Transat, Avianca, Copa, Discover, and WestJet, along with flights on domestic carriers like Aeromexico, Mexicana de Aviacion, Viva, and Volaris.

Less than three years after the airport opened, where do things stand? When it comes to international year-round service, we’ve now gone from service to 12 airports, to service to four airports, which is an absolutely massive reduction:

Just to put this into numbers, in the first half of 2026, the airport saw a 33.2% reduction in passengers. June 2026 was the worst month to date, with a 44.8% drop, as there were just 47,600 passengers, compared to 86,200 passengers the year prior.

It goes without saying that for a newly built airport, this is rather catastrophic, and not what you hope to see.

In some ways, it feels like the whole concept behind Tulum Airport was sort of unnecessary. That’s also easily explained by the fact that the airport was well over a decade in the making, so while I can see how it might’ve seemed like a good idea at some point, tourism trends do evolve over time.

The reality is that there was a point where Tulum was cool, edgy, and a bit off the beaten path, compared to… whatever it is now. But when it comes to the struggles that airlines have had with flying to Tulum, it seems like the problems have been endless:

It’ll be interesting to see if Tulum can reverse any of these trends, and regain visitors…

A few years ago Tulum Airport opened to some fanfare, as a good number of airlines rushed to add service there. Unfortunately the excitement didn’t last long, as the airport has gone from a dozen year-round international routes, to just four.

This reduction in demand particularly evident from the United States, as soon there will just be nonstop service on American and Delta, and even that will be with reduced frequencies and routes.

Tulum Airport is facing endless challenges, not the least of which is a decline in visitors to Mexico from the United States, combined with increasing competition for those fewer visitors. Mexico just isn’t a value destination in the way that it used to be in places like Cancun, Tulum, Los Cabos, etc., and that’s understandably impacting demand.

I’m curious if Tulum can find a way to turn things around, but it’s not a good situation.

What do you make of the Tulum Airport demand problem?
